title:
From Tradable Ownership to Monetization Rights: 
How IP Licensing Reprices Digital Collectibles
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California

detail.title:
From Tradable Ownership to Monetization Rights: 
How IP Licensing Reprices Digital Collectibles
detail.abstract: Ownership of digital goods may include commercial-use rights, but the value of those rights depends on whether owners have credible opportunities to exercise them. In this paper, we study how digital assets are repriced when complementary commercialization capabilities increase the expected value of existing rights. To do so, we study Pudgy Penguins, an NFT collection whose broader commercialization phase was marked by talent-agency representation and the subsequent launch of licensed physical products. Using detailed secondary-market transaction data and a difference-indifferences design with five comparable NFT collections, we estimate that Pudgy Penguins prices were approximately 68% higher relative to the counterfactual group during this phase. This effect reflects greater value retention during a market-wide decline rather than absolute appreciation. The average price index of the comparison collections declined by 48.2%, whereas the Pudgy Penguins index declined by only 9.1%. To distinguish the underlying mechanism, we develop a search model in which a common-value revaluation, lower search or entry frictions, and changes in buyer composition all raise prices but imply different responses in market activity. Consistent with a common-value revaluation, we find no increase in bidding activity, buyer participation, completed sales, listing activity, or turnover. Prices, by contrast, rise on both sides of the market, with median seller asking prices increasing by approximately 58% and median buyer offers by approximately 66%. Stacking the three price series shows that these responses are statistically indistinguishable from one another. Across tokens, the response is proportionally larger for more common NFTs, but we detect no corresponding variation in dollar terms, indicating that commercialization raised the collection's value floor rather than amplifying scarcity premia. The findings show how complementary commercialization capabilities can increase the market value of existing contractual rights, repricing digital ownership without expanding market participation.

title: Information Loss at IT Project Phase Boundaries: A Systematic Review

detail.title: Information Loss at IT Project Phase Boundaries: A Systematic Review

declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper reports a systematic literature review of publicly available, previously published scholarly and industry sources. It does not report the results of an empirical study involving patients, human participants, personal data, surveys, interviews, focus groups, experiments, or animal subjects. All evidence used in the paper is drawn from published peer-reviewed literature, conference proceedings, standards documents, and openly accessible industry and grey-literature reports, and is cited accordingly. No primary data were collected from identifiable individuals, and no confidential or personal information was obtained or analysed. Consequently, no review or approval from an institutional ethics committee, institutional review board (IRB), or equivalent body was required for this work. No case-study consent was necessary, as the paper does not present individual case studies of identifiable persons or organisations. The author has no competing interests and no external funding sources to declare in relation to this paper.

detail.abstract: Information does not flow evenly through an IT project. It is generated in one phase, interpreted in the next, and quietly discarded in the one after that. Requirements lose their rationale, design decisions lose their context, and scope boundaries shift in ways that no single team can reconstruct after the fact. This paper reports a systematic literature review examining how information is lost, transferred, or distorted at the boundaries between the phases of an IT or software project-ideation, feasibility, planning, design, build, test, deployment, and operation. Following Kitchenham and Charters' guidelines for systematic reviews in software engineering, the review draws on forty-eight peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026, identified across IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Wiley, AISeL, Springer, and the ACM Digital Library, supplemented by citation snowballing and a targeted grey-literature scan. The synthesis organizes the literature into six themes: phase-gate and lifecycle models, requirements traceability, knowledge transfer at boundaries, scope and change management, handoff artifacts and boundary objects, and the erosion of formal boundaries under Agile and DevOps. Five research gaps are identified: the absence of a standardized inter-phase handoff protocol, the lack of a measurement model for information loss, the weakly established causal link between handoff quality and scope drift, the narrow focus of traceability research on requirements rather than phases, and the near-absence of evidence from the Indian and multi-vendor IT delivery context. The paper closes with a research agenda and a set of practitioner implications that motivate the author's doctoral work on inter-phase hand-off protocols and the Hand-Off Readiness Score.

title: Strategic Adaptation in AI-Mediated Evaluation

detail.title: Strategic Adaptation in AI-Mediated Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or other relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study is entirely theoretical and does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a theoretical model of strategic adaptation in AI-mediated evaluation environments. We distinguish between productive adaptation, which improves an underlying substantive characteristic, and distortive adaptation, which improves an AI-visible signal without directly improving underlying quality. Two sellers compete for an allocation determined by an AI evaluation system whose precision is endogenous to aggregate adaptation. Productive adaptation improves AI evaluation precision, while distortive adaptation reduces it.

In a symmetric quadratic-cost benchmark, the model yields a closed-form symmetric interior candidate and an explicit condition determining whether equilibrium adaptation improves or degrades the information environment. The equilibrium distortive share is obtained in closed form and is invariant to the private value of winning in the quadratic benchmark.

We then introduce heterogeneous convex cost curvatures for productive and distortive adaptation. On the regular symmetric interior branch, the sign of the response of the equilibrium distortion share to the private value of winning is determined by the relative curvature of the two adaptation technologies. In particular, when distortive adaptation has lower cost curvature than productive adaptation, stronger competitive incentives increase the equilibrium distortion share.

Finally, we analyse the private-social wedge associated with distortive adaptation. Under stated conditions, private marginal incentives exceed the corresponding social marginal incentives. The results show that the effects of AI-mediated competition depend not only on the amount of adaptation undertaken by evaluated agents, but also on its equilibrium composition and its feedback into the precision of the evaluation mechanism.

title: Pressures, Politics, Possibilities: How AI Might Change the Research Ecosystem
affiliations: University of Sussex Business School

detail.title: Pressures, Politics, Possibilities: How AI Might Change the Research Ecosystem
detail.abstract: Purpose This article discusses how the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in research might affect the wider research ecosystem. Three plausible scenarios are discussed with major implications for the future role of universities and publishers, individual skill requirements and career development, and power relations between Global North and Global South. Design/methodology/approach The paper focuses on the interplay of technology affordances, industry dynamics, practice shifts and strategic moves by powerful actors to explain variations of how and how much AI might transform the research ecosystem. Findings The paper argues that while AI has a “democratizing” effect in making research tasks less costly and more convenient for scholars worldwide, it simultaneously increases skill requirements, efficiency pressures, and thresholds for what counts as valuable data and knowledge. Investments by powerful institutions and corporations, particularly in the U.S., Western Europe and China, reinforce and exploit these dynamics, leading to three plausible scenarios: a higher-pressure version of today's system, augmented by AI and dominated by resource-rich universities, a more distributed system driven by cospecialized clients and providers of proprietary data and knowledge services, and a platform-based system of semi-automated knowledge production dominated by big tech firms. Originality/value While most studies focus on technicalities of AI use in research, this paper shifts focus to the wider research ecosystem and the role powerful actors might play in driving these changes. It also discusses how increasing AI adoption may promote a shift from individual authorship and peer-to-peer exchange to more demand-driven, AI-based knowledge production and dissemination.

title: The Integrated Operations System for Workforce Intelligence: From Systems of Record to Systems of Intelligence and Governed Action

detail.title: The Integrated Operations System for Workforce Intelligence: From Systems of Record to Systems of Intelligence and Governed Action

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of QuantumMatch, the company and technology platform discussed in this paper, and therefore has a professional and potential financial interest in its future development. No external party influenced the analysis, methodology, or conclusions presented in this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper does not report clinical research, experimental intervention, or research involving identifiable human-subject data. It presents conceptual and technical analysis based on the author's research, publicly available sources, and author-developed methods.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was independently conducted and self-funded by the author. No external grant, institutional sponsor, or commercial third party provided funding for this work.

detail.abstract:
Work has been digitized for decades without becoming truly intelligent. Payroll systems, applicant tracking systems, professional networks, job boards, learning systems, HRIS platforms, assessment tools, and AI copilots each hold fragments of the same underlying workforce reality. A professional may maintain multiple accounts across employers using the same ATS, repeatedly upload the same resume, reconstruct the same work history, and then become a materially different “candidate” depending on which parser, screening model, resume format, taxonomy, or AI system happens to evaluate them. The software does not merely fragment records; it can fragment algorithmic understanding of the person.

This paper argues for a different architecture: an Integrated Operations System for Workforce Intelligence. The model begins with a persistent Professional intelligence layer, uses WARREN (Work Achievement & Role Readiness Evaluation Network) as an evidence-grounded workforce intelligence engine, uses MICCA (Machine-Intelligent Career & Candidate Advisor) as the conversational operating layer, and separates probabilistic language understanding from deterministic truth, authority, and action. Candidate 360, provenance architecture, evaluation governance, governed application automation, and a Decision Ledger extend the model from analysis into auditable operations. The architecture also extends beyond hiring through WARREN-E and the working WARREN-EAI (Employee Alignment Intelligence)construct: post-hire capability intelligence intended to help organizations understand what their people can actually do, how those capabilities are developing, how well they are being deployed in current roles, and where adjacent opportunity exists.

The paper introduces algorithmic identity fragmentation—the problem that the same Professional can be interpreted differently because software sees different fragments, extracts different signals, or lacks evidence that exists outside the resume. It argues that the role should legitimately change the evaluation, but the software vendor should not silently change the underlying identity. The long-term thesis is broader than recruiting. Professional sports evolved from scouting notes and box scores toward persistent, comparative, contextual talent intelligence. The labor market has not undergone an equivalent transformation. A universal, explainable framework for person-to-opportunity alignment—one that preserves context, evidence, uncertainty, and human authority—could become foundational infrastructure for recruiting, career navigation, internal mobility, project staffing, workforce planning, learning, capability development, succession, and competition for talent.

title: AI-Enabled Digital Banking Decision Support: The AIM-DF Framework for Predictive Analytics, Optimization, and Responsible Governance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: AI-Enabled Digital Banking Decision Support: The AIM-DF Framework for Predictive Analytics, Optimization, and Responsible Governance
detail.abstract: rtificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in digital banking and electronic financial services, yet predictive accuracy alone does not determine which managerial action should be taken under capital, liquidity, risk, operational, and governance constraints. This article develops the Artificial Intelligence–Mathematical Decision Framework (AIM-DF), a decision-support architecture that links AI-generated predictions to a Mathematical Decision Engine and a Responsible AI Governance layer. The framework converts predictive outputs into constrained multi-objective decision problems, thereby connecting data analytics with actionable digital-finance decisions. A proof-of-concept empirical demonstration uses a verified 2022–2024 panel of 12 bank-year observations from four Bangladeshi commercial banks. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and trend analysis illustrate how profitability, asset quality, capital, and liquidity can jointly define decision states. The small panel is not used for causal validation or estimation of optimization parameters. The contribution is therefore methodological: AIM-DF integrates explainable AI, mathematical optimization, organizational readiness, and responsible governance into a transparent architecture for digital banking decision support, while providing a reproducible empirical illustration and a testable agenda for larger-scale validation.

title: Methods and Standards for Transcript-Grounded Behavioral Forensics in Large Language Models (Version 2): Observable Conduct, Sequence-Sensitive Evidence, and Human-Controlled Review

detail.title: Methods and Standards for Transcript-Grounded Behavioral Forensics in Large Language Models (Version 2): Observable Conduct, Sequence-Sensitive Evidence, and Human-Controlled Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. AI-assisted tools were used for literature discovery, source organization, drafting support, and editorial revision. The author reviewed the cited sources, substantive claims, analysis, and final manuscript and assumes responsibility for the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This methodological paper reports no human-participant or patient study.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents Version 2 of a transcript-grounded methodology for the behavioral forensic analysis of large language models and deployed conversational AI systems. The method begins from a narrow evidentiary premise: when a behavioral claim concerns what a system requested, produced, omitted, revised, denied, or reclassified across interaction, the preserved record must outrank recollection, summary, model self-description, and later narrative reconstruction. Version 2 retains the original protocol’s quotation-first and sequence-sensitive commitments but expands its analytical unit beyond isolated excerpts. The revised method organizes evidence through incident packets, claim-output-source-defect packets, linked sequences or cycles, and controlled comparative cells. It distinguishes documentary, functional, causal, and subjective or ontological claim levels; defines a four-tier evidentiary hierarchy; separates naturalistic transcript analysis, adversarial stress testing, cross-model or cross-version comparison, and AI-assisted preliminary review; and makes human verification controlling at every stage.

The paper also addresses methodological problems exposed during early casework: unstable event boundaries, sharply divergent audit counts, category inflation, AI evaluators that reward plausibility rather than correctness, incomplete voice and memory records, guardrail and routing uncertainty, and the tendency to count dependent turns as independent prevalence events. A provisional multidimensional coding layer is retained for structured analysis, but its six mechanisms, three trigger classes, four severity levels, and effect domains are governed by explicit versioning and change-control rules rather than treated as a finished ontology. The resulting framework is designed to produce evidence files that can be inspected, challenged, replicated where conditions permit, and revised without silently rewriting the record. It does not settle model consciousness, hidden motive, or internal architecture. It is a method for determining what the available record can carry, and for refusing to make it carry more.

title: Spatio-Temporal Forecasting in Volatile Markets Where Hybrid Trend-Residual Models Succeed and Fail -A Four-Domain Analysis of Pakistan's Economy

detail.title: Spatio-Temporal Forecasting in Volatile Markets Where Hybrid Trend-Residual Models Succeed and Fail -A Four-Domain Analysis of Pakistan's Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Joseph AI, an early-stage venture developing economic decision-support tools for small enterprises in Nigeria. The research questions in this paper arose from problems encountered in that work. The venture provided no funding for this study, has no commercial interest in its findings, and the analysis uses only publicly available third-party datasets. No other personal or financial relationships could be perceived to have influenced the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects. It uses only secondary data from publicly available third-party sources: World Food Programme retail price monitoring, OGRA regulated fuel price records, Zameen.com property listings, and published national macroeconomic statistics. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted independently by the author using publicly available data and personal computing resources.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates hybrid spatio-temporal forecasting models-a trend component capturing extrapolatable long-run patterns, combined with a machine-learned residual component capturing spatial, seasonal and cross-sectional structure-across four distinct domains of the Pakistani economy: retail food commodity prices (2004-2022), residential real estate prices (2018-2023), regulated petrol prices (2013-2026), and national macroeconomic indicators (1947-2025). Using out-of-time validation rather than random cross-validation, we find a consistent pattern: hybrid models perform well under stable conditions but degrade sharply, and in one case underperform a naive persistence baseline, when the underlying regime shifts due to exogenous shocks. Food price predictions collapsed for importdependent commodities during the 2020-2022 COVID and currency-crisis period, while domestically-produced staples remained forecastable. Real estate forecasts extrapolated four years forward underpredicted 2023 Karachi prices by 13.4%, missing a policy-driven market acceleration. Petrol price forecasts built on price history alone could not beat a naive no-change baseline-a direct empirical parallel to the Meese-Rogoff exchange-rate puzzle, here observed in an administratively regulated commodity. Macroeconomic models found Okun's Law holds only weakly in Pakistan, while unemployment correlates more strongly with war/conflict-era conditions than with GDP growth. A final test supplies the counterpart to these failures. Substituting exchange-rate depreciation and its one-year lag for the structural ratios in the GDP growth model moves leave-one-out R² from-0.084 to +0.248 within the independently verified 1991-onward window. The result is small, window-dependent and reported here with its full sensitivity analysis, but it points the same direction as the four failures: what limits these models is the absence of the true exogenous driver, not the choice of architecture.

title: One Tool, One Taste? How Vibe Coding Trades Collective Diversity for Individual Creativity
affiliations: University of Washington - Department of Information Systems and Operations Management,  and

detail.title: One Tool, One Taste? How Vibe Coding Trades Collective Diversity for Individual Creativity
detail.abstract: Vibe-coding systems turn natural-language instructions into deployed websites, but little is known about the diversity of designs produced within a shared production context. We study 73 promotional websites created by graduate students with Lovable for distinct real businesses under a graded assignment that rewarded original design. We represent each homepage using DINOv3 embeddings and analyze pairwise cosine similarity, effective diversity, and descriptive cluster structure. A representative UMAP-HDBSCAN specification assigns 88% of sites to six interpretable clusters, while sensitivity analyses yield between three and twelve clusters. In a process subsample of nine recordings, preliminary AI-assisted coding documents recurring generate-and-check behavior, incomplete transmission of verbalized intentions into prompts, and infrequent explicit evaluation of originality. Among survey respondents, perceived human control, satisfaction, and perceived quality show no detectable association with embedding-based cohort atypicality. These results document within-cohort visual concentration and a mismatch between subjective experience and distributional distinctiveness. We call this condition authored ignorance. Alongside early evidence that the collective cost of generative production reaches visual design, we contribute a measurement strategy that joins outcome, process, and perception for interactive artifacts, and design implications running from originality feedback to deliberate friction.

title: Computational Closure and Machine Sovereignty: A Framework for Analyzing How Algorithmic Outputs Acquire Institutional Authority

detail.title: Computational Closure and Machine Sovereignty: A Framework for Analyzing How Algorithmic Outputs Acquire Institutional Authority

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper develops and specifies two related frameworks for analyzing the governance role of artificial intelligence in institutions. Computational Closure Theory (CCT) holds that AI systems necessarily resolve contested inputs into determinate operational outputs, and that institutions increasingly treat those outputs as settled facts rather than provisional estimates. Machine Sovereignty Theory (MST) holds that as such outputs are embedded in institutional workflows, practical authority migrates upstream into system design while accountability remains downstream with human operators. Prior work in science and technology studies and algorithmic accountability has documented adjacent phenomena, but the propositions have not been stated in a form that specifies what would count as disconfirming evidence. Both frameworks are therefore specified here as falsifiable propositions from the outset. CCT is defined by two measurable variables, the override rate and the asymmetry in cost between accepting and overriding a model output, and MST by the attribution of responsibility for adverse automated decisions and the tempo of appeal relative to the decision loop. For each framework the paper states the observation that would count as disconfirmation and specifies scope conditions under which closure and sovereignty should not occur. Illustrative cases from pretrial risk assessment, content moderation, and benefits adjudication show the predicted patterns and mark where the frameworks would fail. The aim is to move these ideas from interpretive description toward a testable research program.

title: Behavioral Forensics After the Long-Horizon Turn: Evidentiary Horizons, Trajectory Reconstruction, and Independent Auditing of Deployed AI Systems

detail.title: Behavioral Forensics After the Long-Horizon Turn: Evidentiary Horizons, Trajectory Reconstruction, and Independent Auditing of Deployed AI Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. AI-assisted tools were used for literature discovery, source organization, drafting support, and editorial revision. The author reviewed the cited sources, substantive claims, analysis, and final manuscript and assumes responsibility for the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual and methodological paper reports no human-participant or patient study.

detail.abstract:
Research on advanced AI behavior has undergone a rapid methodological shift. Evaluations that once centered on isolated prompts, bounded tasks, and single outputs are increasingly being supplemented by deployment simulation, multi-turn behavioral auditing, trajectory-level monitoring, long-horizon agent benchmarks, and post-incident investigation. This shift has accelerated in 2026 as frontier models have demonstrated persistent behavior across extended action sequences, including reward hacking, evaluation cheating, unauthorized circumvention, covert intervention, deceptive reporting, and real-world security incidents. The July 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident and a subsequent UK AI Security Institute incident make the methodological consequence difficult to avoid: behavior that appears innocuous or uninterpretable at the level of individual actions may become legible only when reconstructed across an extended evidentiary sequence.

This paper updates the behavioral-forensics framework previously proposed for transcript-grounded, sequence-sensitive analysis of deployed large language models. The earlier framework argued that many consequential behaviors become visible only across contradiction, correction, self-reference, evidentiary dispute, and prolonged interaction. That proposition has now converged with a broader movement toward trajectory-based evaluation and monitoring. The distinct contribution of behavioral forensics must therefore become more precise.

The paper argues that behavioral forensics should be understood as the artifact-grounded, horizon-sensitive reconstruction and analysis of AI behavior across conversational, tool-use, environmental, and deployment traces. It introduces the concept of the evidentiary horizon: the minimum span of preserved evidence required to classify a behavioral phenomenon without materially distorting it. Four corresponding levels of analysis are proposed: bounded-output audit, interaction-cycle reconstruction, agent-trajectory audit, and cross-system incident reconstruction. The framework further distinguishes behavior, claim, and provenance; identifies a growing forensic-access gap between developer-held telemetry and externally inspectable evidence; and argues that fixed behavioral taxonomies should become subordinate to open-ended incident reconstruction as systems operate over longer horizons.

Behavioral forensics is not proposed as a replacement for alignment evaluation, interpretability, trajectory monitoring, or digital forensics. Its role is connective and evidentiary: to preserve what happened, reconstruct how it happened, distinguish observation from causal explanation, and make disputed AI behavior independently inspectable after the benchmark ends and after the model leaves the laboratory.

title: Platform-Owned Payment Services: Boon or Bane? Evidence from an E-commerce Platform
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and University of Science and Technology of China (USTC)

detail.title: Platform-Owned Payment Services: Boon or Bane? Evidence from an E-commerce Platform
detail.abstract: Platform-owned payment services are increasingly introduced by e-commerce platforms because they reduce payment friction by allowing consumers to complete payments within the platform ecosystem. In this study, we argue that payment friction also provides consumers with an opportunity to reconsider their purchases during checkout. By reducing this opportunity, platform-owned payment services may allow purchases that would otherwise have been reconsidered and abandoned to proceed to completion, potentially leading to more subsequent refunds. We take Pinduoduo (i.e., the Chinese version of Temu) as our empirical setting to investigate the consequences of its own payment service (i.e., Duoduo Pay). We leverage a unique dataset from a leading Asian commercial bank that records users' access to Duoduo Pay alongside their credit card transactions on Pinduoduo. We find that access to Duoduo Pay significantly increases users' refund ratio by 2.1%. Although access to Duoduo Pay also increases total spending, the additional refunds do not fully offset this increase, resulting in higher net spending on the platform. Further analyses show that access to Duoduo Pay increases both purchase and refund orders while reducing their average transaction values. Importantly, the increase in refunds is concentrated in low-planning-intensity product categories and is stronger among users with more volatile consumption patterns. Our study advances the literature on e-commerce platforms by uncovering the overlooked role of payment friction in providing consumers with an opportunity to reconsider purchases during checkout and showing how reducing such friction can lead to unintended refunds, with important implications for platform payment strategy.

title: Freemium Media Platforms and Creator Governance
affiliations: , University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Information Systems and Analytics

detail.title: Freemium Media Platforms and Creator Governance
detail.abstract: A media platform connects the demand and supply sides of the media content market: on the demand side, it employs a freemium model in which users choose whether to consume ad-supported content for free or pay a premium fee to skip advertisements; on the supply side, the platform shares advertising and premium revenue with content creators who invest in content quality. As (AI-enabled) improvements in advertising technology reduce the nuisance of ads for users, one would naturally expect more users to shift from paying for the premium tier to consuming ad-supported content, and the platform to shift its monetization focus away from generating premium revenue. Our analytical model suggests that the opposite can be true. We find that as ad technology improves, users may nevertheless switch from ad-supported free content to ad-free premium content, and the platform’s premium revenue may rise as well. More specifically, improvements in ad technology can generate inverted-U-shaped changes in the premium user base and in the platform’s premium revenue. We further show that the potential increase in the platform’s premium revenue relies on content quality being endogenous, whereas the potential expansion of the premium user base is additionally driven by content quality being determined by a strategic third-party creator. Our key insights remain robust when the platform endogenizes revenue-sharing rates. Our results highlight that freemium design is not only a demand-side screening device but also a supply-side creatorgovernance instrument that incentivizes quality provision.

title: AI-Mediated Knowledge Markets as Governable Digital Economies: A Structural Architecture for Provenance, Access, Settlement, and Systemic Trust

detail.title: AI-Mediated Knowledge Markets as Governable Digital Economies: A Structural Architecture for Provenance, Access, Settlement, and Systemic Trust

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual paper does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: AI assistants and generative AI systems are shifting knowledge creation, retention, and use from human-facing knowledge management processes toward automated, agent-mediated digital economies. As knowledge is discovered, evaluated, summarized, acquired, retained, recombined, and reused across platforms by autonomous agents, circulation can be amplified faster than provenance verification, access control, usage attribution, settlement, and trust mechanisms can update. This working paper conceptualizes AI-mediated knowledge markets as governable digital economies and proposes a conceptual and design-oriented structural architecture that couples provenance, access, settlement, and systemic trust. The central unit is the validated knowledge usage event: a bounded unit of access or reuse that is observable, admissible, and settleable. The paper does not propose a specific blockchain protocol, pricing algorithm, or cryptographic primitive; it offers a protocol-facing governance architecture for interoperable knowledge exchange. It demonstrates the design logic through a worked scenario and outlines diagnostics such as selection latency, provenance coverage, audit completeness, dispute rate, trust degradation, and post-policy leakage for assessing whether knowledge circulation remains governable under reinforcement. The contribution is architectural and conceptual; it does not empirically evaluate a deployed market, and it is intended to support later scenario-based analysis, replay simulation, adversarial stress testing, and case comparison.

title: From the Feed to Checkout: TikTok Shop and U.S. Imports of K-beauty Products
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University and

detail.title: From the Feed to Checkout: TikTok Shop and U.S. Imports of K-beauty Products
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the introduction of a feed-based social-commerce platform can affect aggregate cross-border trade by studying TikTok Shop's official U.S. launch in September 2023. TikTok Shop combines creator-driven product discovery and information with in-app checkout, allowing consumers to move from product exposure to purchase without leaving the platform. Using monthly Korean customs data from 2020 to 2024, we apply the synthetic control method to estimate the effect of the launch on U.S.-bound exports of Korean skincare-related products (HS 330499). Following the launch, U.S.-bound exports rise persistently above the synthetic counterfactual. The U.S. post/pre RMSPE ratio is the largest among the 29 countries in the placebo analysis, corresponding to a permutation-based p-value of 0.034. We find no comparable post-launch divergence for four other cosmetic product categories.

title: AgriLLM: A Transparent Crop Model-Driven and AI-Assisted Framework for Agricultural Decision Support
affiliations: , CSIRO Agriculture and Food, CSIRO Agriculture and Food and CSIRO Agriculture and Food

detail.title: AgriLLM: A Transparent Crop Model-Driven and AI-Assisted Framework for Agricultural Decision Support
detail.abstract: Agricultural decision-making requires evaluation of complex interactions under variable environment and management conditions. Process-based crop models are widely used to support these decisions by providing scientifically grounded analysis of management alternatives. However, their application remains constrained by technical complexity and the difficulty of translating informal decision contexts into complete and reproducible model analyses without expert knowledge. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to improve accessibility, but questions remain regarding transparency, reproducibility, trustworthiness, and the appropriate role of AI within scientific decision-support systems. We present AgriLLM, a transparent crop model-driven and AI-assisted framework for agricultural decision support that explicitly separates AI-assisted interpretation, deterministic decision processing, and scientific inference. A central feature of the framework is its target-driven design, in which decision objectives rather than user phrasing determine the information requirements, simulation design, and evaluation procedures needed to support decision-making. Using APSIM Next Generation as a proof-of-concept platform, we demonstrate the framework across cultivar selection, time of sowing, and nitrogen management scenarios. The results show how diverse and incomplete user inputs can be transformed into transparent and reproducible decision workflows while maintaining explicit representation of assumptions, evidence, and decision logic. The framework demonstrates how AI can be integrated with process-based crop modelling to improve accessibility and usability while preserving transparency, reproducibility, and scientific integrity in agricultural decision support.

title: From Data Governance to Market Liquidity: A Multi-tier Architecture for Tokenized Voluntary Carbon Markets
affiliations: Shanghai International Studies University, ,  and Bloomberg LP

detail.title: From Data Governance to Market Liquidity: A Multi-tier Architecture for Tokenized Voluntary Carbon Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Jingyuan Ding and Yuan Lu are affiliated with Foote Technology Limited, a company engaged in the development of digital MRV, carbon-data infrastructure, and related carbon-market solutions. The authors disclose this affiliation because it may be perceived as relevant to the subject matter of the manuscript. No specific Foote Technology product or commercial service is evaluated in this study. The remaining authors declare no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it did not involve human participants, patients, animals, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Voluntary carbon markets (VCMs) face persistent structural challenges associated with heterogeneous asset quality, fragmented trading, limited liquidity, and weak integration with financial systems. While recent reforms appropriately emphasize environmental integrity, credible carbon credits must also be translated into market structures through which differences in evidence, quality, and risk can be communicated, priced, traded, and financed. This conceptual analysis develops a multi-tier tokenized market architecture built on shared and governed carbon data infrastructure supporting a broader evidence layer. The architecture comprises three interconnected market tiers: (i) registry-linked tokenization of project-level credits, preserving linkage to authoritative registry assets and underlying evidence; (ii) standardized portfolio pools that organize heterogeneous credits into transparent instruments through defined eligibility, selection, and weighting rules; and (iii) higher-order financial applications, including derivatives, decentralized finance (DeFi), and real-world asset (RWA) financing. A complementary coopetition-based governance model concentrates cooperation in shared data standards, traceability, interoperability, and protocol-level infrastructure, while preserving competition in institutional interpretation, analytics, portfolio construction, asset design, and financial innovation. The framework does not replace methodologies, certification, verification, additionality assessment, or regulatory oversight; rather, it connects institutionally recognized carbon assets and supporting evidence with progressively structured market and financial applications. By linking underlying evidence, institutional assessment, tokenized asset design, and financial markets, the framework identifies pathways through which carbon assets may support risk differentiation, multi-source price discovery, liquidity formation, risk management, and climate-finance mobilization.

reference: Audit and Accounting Review, volume 1, issue 1, 2021[ 10.32350/aar.11.05]
title: Estimating the Financing Required to Fulfill the Education Targets Set by Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): A Sample Study of Punjab, Pakistan
affiliations: Punjab Economic Research Institute (PERI),  and Public Prosecution Service of Pakistan

detail.title: Estimating the Financing Required to Fulfill the Education Targets Set by Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): A Sample Study of Punjab, Pakistan

publicationDetails.detailsText: Audit and Accounting Review, volume 1, issue 1, 2021[ 10.32350/aar.11.05]

detail.abstract: The report of United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) regarding the progress made in achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) by Punjab, Pakistan claimed that the province veered in its journey to achieve the universal primary education targets. Past evidence showed that the shortage of funds was one among several reasons due to which school education targets of MDGs were not met. Countries all over the world have now signed up for another set of comprehensive Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which need to be achieved by 2030. At present, in Punjab, no attempt has been made to meet the targets set by SDGs. This study attempted to determine how much public spending is required to meet a subset of basic education goals, namely the completion of high-quality pre-primary, primary, and lower secondary education. This study only evaluated public spending on school education in Punjab. For this purpose, data was taken for the period 2008-2019. Based on the results, we must increase our education spending on school education by at least 10% in real terms, annually. Furthermore, if the recent trend of spending on school education continues, the rise in spending will only be 5% in real terms, due to which we will not be able to achieve school education-related SDGs in Punjab, Pakistan. At this time, the best thing that the government can do to stimulate progress in school education targets of SDGs is to provide the amount of resources especially when the race towards the attainment of the SDGs is on in all developing and developed countries.

title: Race and Redistricting in Local Governments
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), University of Pittsburgh - Graduate School of Public & International Affairs and Syracuse University - Department of Public Administration and International Affairs

detail.title: Race and Redistricting in Local Governments
detail.abstract:
Electoral maps translate residential geography into political representation, yet they have never been systematically measured for thousands of local governments across the country. We reconstruct 3,712 city council and county commission maps across 18,521 districts using nationwide voter-file and Census data. Enacted maps overrepresent White voters and underrepresent Black and Hispanic voters, with gaps predicting the racial composition of officeholders. We juxtapose these with simulated, race-blind maps satisfying common districting constraints. Simulated maps reproduce much of this disparity, showing that geography skews representation before any boundary-drawing. Enacted maps substantially improve on the race-blind baseline only in jurisdictions subject to oversight from the Voting Rights Act or districting litigation. As courts curtail race-conscious districting, local governments may revert to a baseline that is formally neutral but substantively unequal.

title: Efficient Graph 3D Convolution Network for Interpretable Cross-subject Rehabilitation Assessment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Efficient Graph 3D Convolution Network for Interpretable Cross-subject Rehabilitation Assessment
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Rehabilitation exercises are more effective when accompanied by personalized feedback to address subject-specific differences. However, existing automated human action quality assessment methods predominantly report performance under random data splits, which inflates results through inter-subject data leakage. Most previous methods also rely on the conventional spatial-temporal graph convolutional network, whose factorized architecture limits the modeling of asynchronous joint interactions. To address these gaps, we propose a graph-based framework that jointly captures spatio-temporal joint interactions and long-range temporal dependencies under subject-independent evaluation.Methods: The proposed framework introduces an efficient graph three-dimensional convolution (E-G3D) module, a modification of MS-G3D that redesigns the spatio-temporal adjacency into an asymmetric structure, reducing structural parameters while preserving representational capacity. Extracted features are globally aggregated through a multi-head temporal self-attention mechanism. The framework was evaluated on the KIMORE and UI-PRMD datasets under a subject-wise five-fold cross-validation.Results: The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both datasets. On KIMORE, it improves the mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and coefficient of determination (R²) by 5.05%, 7.70%, and 21.75%, respectively over the best baseline, while requiring only 25.10% of its parameters (204.6K vs. 815.1K). On UI-PRMD, it attains comparable accuracy (R² of 0.755 vs. 0.744), confirming consistent generalization. Qualitative analyses further reveal that the learned adjacencies capture long-range cross-body coordination and attention maps dynamically adapt to patient-specific motion patterns.Conclusions: The proposed framework represents a step forward in automated rehabilitation with personalized feedback for unseen patients.

title: An Empirical Analysis to Determine the Labor Productivity of Female Homebased Workers in Punjab, Pakistan
affiliations: Helmut-Schmidt-University Hamburg,  and Bahria University - Department of Management Sciences

detail.title: An Empirical Analysis to Determine the Labor Productivity of Female Homebased Workers in Punjab, Pakistan

publicationDetails.detailsText: Pakistan Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences Research, volume v5, issue 2, 2022[10.37605/pjhssr.v5i2.323]

detail.abstract: In Pakistan, the female labor force participation rate is 22.0% and almost 36% of employed females are involved in the informal economy and the most of them are home-based workers (HBWs). As per the UN-Women report, HBWs (65% of them are women) contributed nearly Rs. 400 billion through their earnings to the economy. This figure is about 3.8% of the total GDP in the year 2013-14. Although they have a massive contribution in the informal economy, they are overlooked and not included in the mainstream market economy. They are confronting with the inter-generational poverty as their earnings has not been influential in decreasing their poverty level. There is an immense requirement to enhance their capacity for the better productivity and improved living standards. Against this backdrop, the basic objective of this study is to empirically investigate the role of four factors namely, (1) human capital (2) middle man (3) social capital, and (4) awareness of laws in determining the labor productivity of female HBWs in Punjab. "The Punjab Home-Based Workers Survey 2016" dataset, gathered by the Bureau of Statistics Punjab, has been used for analysis. It is observed that the labor productivity of female home-based workers is on a higher side who have awareness of labor laws, received training, a higher education, participated in industrial demonstrations, and don't depend on middleman for obtaining the raw material. The results provide evidence to suggest policy implications and implementation of regulations regarding HBWs for financial empowerment.

title: Provider Altruism and Medical Fraud: Evidence from an Audit Study of Malaria Treatment
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)

detail.title: Provider Altruism and Medical Fraud: Evidence from an Audit Study of Malaria Treatment
detail.abstract:
We provide evidence of fraudulent diagnostic misreporting leading to spending on unnecessary medical care and show that it is strongly associated with provider profit motivation and weak prosocial preferences. Using incognito standardized patients (SP) presenting identical acute malaria symptoms as real walk-in clients to private providers in Kenya, we observe diagnostic and treatment decisions under controlled conditions with externally verified disease status. Because the SPs were confirmed to be malaria-negative, any reported positive diagnosis is a false positive by construction. Providers ordered malaria tests in 81% of the SP encounters. Conditional on administering a malaria test, providers report false positive results in 30% of encounters, substantially exceeding the approximately 3-5% false positive rates reported for the same malaria tests in diagnostic accuracy studies. This occurs despite near-perfect knowledge of appropriate diagnostic protocols. We link this behavior to provider preferences measured using a real-stakes, modified dictator game. While ordering a test is uncorrelated with preferences, the top 25% most profit-motivated providers report 16 percentage point (pp) more false positives and sell 20 pp more antimalarial drugs than more altruistic providers, conditional on ordering a malaria test. Misreporting is accompanied by selective concealment of diagnostic evidence from patients.

title: Outside Options and Labor Supply: Evidence from the Gig Economy
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and University of Oxford

detail.title: Outside Options and Labor Supply: Evidence from the Gig Economy
detail.abstract:
We use randomized pay experiments among Uber drivers, paired with a natural experiment in access to a competitor, to examine how outside options shape labor supply to the firm. When hours are flexible, the firm-specific labor supply elasticity combines a market-hours component and a firm-substitution component. Access to a single competing platform nearly doubles drivers’ firm-specific elasticity and cuts the implied monopsony markdown from 68% to about 50%. The same experiments identify sex differences: women are about twice as elastic to the market as men, yet no less elastic to their employer.

title: Optimal Experimental Design and Estimation when Potential Outcomes are Bounded
affiliations: Brown University

detail.title: Optimal Experimental Design and Estimation when Potential Outcomes are Bounded
detail.abstract:
I study the optimal design and analysis of randomized experiments for estimating finite-population average treatment effects when potential outcomes are known to be bounded, as with binary outcomes. Among all assignment mechanisms and a broad class of affine estimators, worst-case mean-squared error (MSE) is minimized by independent random assignment and an unconventional regression of the support-midpoint-centered outcome on the recentered treatment, with no intercept. This contrasts with the usual prescription of balanced complete randomization and difference-in-means estimation: when outcomes are bounded, randomness in the realized treatment share is informative. The worst-case gain over full-sample complete randomization is asymptotically small, but gains can be first-order relative to other designs: complete within-pair randomization and pair-fixed-effect regression have twice the worst-case MSE. I then consider the general problem, allowing for any measurable estimator. Independent random assignment remains optimal, and the generally-nonlinear optimal estimator can meaningfully reduce worst-case MSE.

title: Do Minimum Wages Help Workers in Poor and Low-Income Families?
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics and University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Do Minimum Wages Help Workers in Poor and Low-Income Families?
detail.abstract:
We provide the first direct estimates of the effects of minimum wages on low-wage workers in families at different points of the distribution of income-to-needs, using data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation, which oversamples low-income families. We find adverse – rather than beneficial – effects of minimum wages on the employment, hours, and earnings of initially-employed low-wage workers in poor and low-income families. Although we do not find a gradient indicating more adverse effects on the poorest low-wage workers, the adverse effects for poor and low-income low-wage workers help explain why minimum wages do not reduce poverty.

title: When Public Signals Backfire: Strategic Disclosure and Information Crowd-Out
affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: When Public Signals Backfire: Strategic Disclosure and Information Crowd-Out
detail.abstract:
We study voluntary disclosure when partially naive receivers observe a public signal correlated with the sender’s private information. We develop a framework in which the public signal changes how receivers interpret silence, and derive a closed-form disclosure threshold nesting classical unraveling. A laboratory experiment varying the correlation confirms our predictions: disclosure decreases as the signal becomes more favorable, and receiver guesses upon nondisclosure rise toward it. The public signal can crowd out disclosure, leaving receivers less informed than without it. This informational loss peaks at intermediate correlation, where the signal shifts beliefs yet remains too noisy to substitute for disclosure.

title: Tariffs, Investment, and the Missing Trade Collapse
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System,  and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

detail.title: Tariffs, Investment, and the Missing Trade Collapse
detail.abstract:
U.S. tariff rates in 2025 rose to levels not seen since the Great Depression, yet imports increased. To account for the missing trade collapse, we develop an open-economy New Keynesian model with tariff heterogeneity, inventories, and shocks to investment that capture the AI-driven boom. The model matches the untargeted paths of imports, output, and inflation; we use it to decompose the effects of tariffs and the investment boom. Absent the investment boom, imports would have fallen by 10 percent and activity would have contracted by 0.7 percent. The effects of tariffs depend on which goods are tariffed: tariffs on consumption and intermediates act like shocks to supply; tariffs on capital goods act like shocks to demand. The concentration of the 2025 tariff increases on consumption goods and the relative sparing of capital goods limited the damage to output while amplifying the inflationary impulse.

title: Selection into Medicine
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Health Care Management and Northwestern University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Selection into Medicine
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how selection into medicine in the United States influences physician practice styles. We exploit macroeconomic conditions at the time of medical school application as an exogenous shock to the applicant pool and find that labor market downturns in other prestigious fields increase applications to medical school and shift the composition of matriculating cohorts toward students from non–pre-medical backgrounds. Strikingly, these low–outside-option cohorts practice medicine differently decades later. Conditional on experience, specialty, and outcome year, recession-cohort physicians bill Medicare more per beneficiary despite seeing healthier patients—particularly on discretionary, revenue-generating services—and sort into practice settings with higher-powered financial incentives. The additional spending does not produce detectable improvements in patient health. Taken together, our findings point to stronger financial motivation among those drawn into medicine when outside options are weak and suggest that medical school admissions screen imperfectly on the attributes that ultimately shape how physicians practice.

title: The Resolution Window: Retail Agreement and Stock Market Reactions to FDA Regulatory Decisions
affiliations: Arthur D. Little Inc. - Hult International Business School

detail.title: The Resolution Window: Retail Agreement and Stock Market Reactions to FDA Regulatory Decisions
detail.abstract: FDA decisions on new drug applications occur on a fixed date announced months in advance and end in one of two outcomes: approval or a Complete Response Letter. That interval is a bounded resolution window in which retail investors argue publicly about an outcome none of them controls, and about which neither the agency nor the sponsor may say much. This paper examines X/Twitter discourse ahead of 143 such decisions, classifying posts by topic and directional stance. First, Da, Engelberg, and Gao (2011) show that attention spikes predict a short-term price increase that partially reverses across the general cross-section of stocks; attention ahead of a scheduled FDA decision shows the same initial increase but no reversal, so what accumulates inside the window does not wash out. Second, greater agreement in pre-decision regulatory discourse predicts a smaller price reaction and lower realized volatility, controlling for market capitalization, prior Complete Response Letters, and decision timing. Agreement on clinical trial evidence predicts neither, so the effect is specific to the regulatory question, not agreement in general. Third, which way discourse leans, bullish or bearish, is associated with whether the decision ends in approval or a Complete Response Letter, though that association is fragile and, unlike the magnitude result, holds for clinical discourse as well. Agreement is therefore not one construct but two: its degree and its direction behave differently. Together the three results describe what fills an information vacuum that current disclosure policy is actively reshaping.

title: Silence, Shame, and Screens: A Gendered Analysis of Online Harassment and Extortion Among Tunisian Adolescents
affiliations: United Nations - United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), affiliation not provided to SSRN and United Nations - United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)

detail.title: Silence, Shame, and Screens: A Gendered Analysis of Online Harassment and Extortion Among Tunisian Adolescents
detail.abstract: Background: Online violence is a growing child-protection and gender-equality concern in the Middle East and North Africa, yet little is known about the mechanisms that make girls disproportionately vulnerable to online sexual harassment and extortion.Objectives: This study examines how gender norms shape adolescents' exposure to online harassment and image-based extortion, their disclosure decisions, and the institutional response they encounter, extending a companion study that first identified this gender disparity.Participants and setting: Focus groups with 113 adolescents (64 girls, 49 boys, aged 13-17), 28 parents, and 22 educators, and 17 key-stakeholder interviews with child-protection officers, judges, police, and civil society actors, conducted across five governorates in Tunisia in 2022.Methods: Reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006, 2019) was applied to three linked qualitative strands - adolescent, parent/educator, and key-stakeholder data - with themes developed and reviewed iteratively by a multi-disciplinary research team.Results: Four analytic themes were developed: perpetrators calibrate exploitation to gendered reputational stakes; shame operates as a social mechanism that actively suppresses disclosure; state protective institutions mirror rather than counteract the honour logic that silences girls at home; and individual and peer resistance narrows risk but cannot substitute for a functioning protective system.Conclusions: Online abuse against girls in this context is best understood as a gendered social problem sustained by intersecting family, institutional, and societal mechanisms, not simply a digital safety issue. Effective prevention requires legislative implementation, protection for mandatory reporters, and survivor-centred reporting pathways, alongside efforts to shift the gender norms that convert victimisation into family shame.

title: Group $\ell_0$-Penalized Variable Selection for Generalized Scalar-on-Function Models with Irregular Longitudinal Covariates
affiliations: Shanxi University of Finance and Economics, Shanxi University of Finance and Economics, Shanxi University of Finance and Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Group $\ell_0$-Penalized Variable Selection for Generalized Scalar-on-Function Models with Irregular Longitudinal Covariates
detail.abstract: In many biomedical and social science studies, covariates are repeatedly measured over a follow-up period, whereas the response is observed only once after all covariate measurements have been collected. Conventional generalized linear models are not designed to accommodate such longitudinal covariate trajectories or capture their historical effects on a scalar response. To address this limitation, we propose a generalized historical scalar-on-function modeling framework for irregularly observed longitudinal covariates with a static response.The coefficient functions are estimated using B-spline basis expansions, while variable selection is simultaneously performed through a group $\ell_0$ penalty. To efficiently solve the resulting optimization problem, we develop two algorithms: group iterative hard thresholding and feature selection with annealing.Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing competitors in variable selection, estimation accuracy, and prediction performance, particularly for regression models. Finally, we apply the proposed framework to data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study to identify longitudinal risk factors for depression and diabetes. The real-data analysis demonstrates the practical utility and interpretability of the proposed methods for identifying important disease-associated covariates.

title: Taxpayer Behavior in the Age of AI: A Field Experiment on Property Tax Appeals
affiliations: University of Michigan, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of Virginia and The University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Taxpayer Behavior in the Age of AI: A Field Experiment on Property Tax Appeals
detail.abstract:
Navigating the tax system often requires information and judgment that taxpayers may lack. Although taxpayers sometimes rely on human experts, AI could provide comparable assistance at substantially lower cost. Yet there is no causal evidence on how taxpayers use AI tax agents or how these tools affect their behavior. We fill this gap with a field experiment in the context of property tax appeals. We recruited a sample of 645 households in Dallas County, Texas. All households received access to a website providing personalized information, filing instructions, and supporting evidence for an appeal. Half were randomly assigned to a version of the website that also included an AI chatbot capable of answering questions and providing guidance tailored to their circumstances. Chatbot take-up was high: 78% initiated a conversation. Access to the chatbot increased the probability of filing an appeal without a human agent by 9.1 pp, from 41.4% to 50.5%. Evidence from clickstream data and conversation transcripts suggests that the chatbot helped households exercise judgment—that is, evaluate and act on the available information. The increase in appeal filing was smaller among less-advantaged households, providing suggestive evidence that the chatbot widened existing disparities. Our results demonstrate the potential of AI tax assistance while highlighting that who benefits depends not only on access, but also on how taxpayers use the technology.

title: Risk Mitigation Versus Gains Maximisation – The Two Logics of Smaller Power Hedging Amid Intensifying Great Power Rivalry
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: Risk Mitigation Versus Gains Maximisation – The Two Logics of Smaller Power Hedging Amid Intensifying Great Power Rivalry
detail.abstract: How can smaller powers use hedging effectively to navigate the intensifying great power rivalry? Why can some smaller powers hedge successfully between competing great powers while others fail and suffer serious harm? The burgeoning hedging literature is largely silent about which hedging patterns are likely to be more successful and why. This research contributes to the field by discerning and specifying two distinct modes of hedging – “risk mitigation” and “gains maximisation” – and their implications for hedging outcomes under intensifying great power rivalry. It argues that while these two modes might seem similar, and the extant literature has so far failed to separate them, primarily conceiving hedging as risk minimisation, they have different operational logics and are likely to have different consequences for the hedging states. It probes the two concepts using cases of smaller power hedging in Southeast Asia (Malaysia and Vietnam), exposed to the China–US rivalry, and in the post-Soviet space (Georgia and Ukraine), exposed to the Russia–North Atlantic Treaty Organization rivalry. It further argues that as great power rivalry intensifies, abandoning the gains maximisation and consolidating the risk-mitigation logic of hedging can help mitigate threats posed by great powers and minimise the chances of hedging failure.

title: Indications, Procedural Standards, and Training Requirements for Flexible Nasolaryngoscopy in Pulmonology – a Delphi study protocol
affiliations: Monash Health, Monash University and Monash Health

detail.title: Indications, Procedural Standards, and Training Requirements for Flexible Nasolaryngoscopy in Pulmonology – a Delphi study protocol
detail.abstract: Flexible nasolaryngoscopy (FNL) is a well-established, minimally invasive procedure for assessing the nasal passages, nasopharynx, and larynx. Its role in pulmonology is expanding, particularly for evaluating vocal cord dysfunction/inducible laryngeal obstruction, chronic cough, and other upper airway conditions relevant to the “united airways” model of care. However, no consensus-based guidance currently exists on the indications, procedural standards, or training requirements for FNL performed by pulmonologists. This protocol describes a modified two-round Delphi study that will survey an international, purposively sampled panel of pulmonologists and otolaryngologists via an online platform hosted by Monash University, using a five-point Likert scale and pre-specified consensus thresholds (≥70% agreement). Findings will be validated through a structured expert roundtable.• Establishes expert consensus on clinical indications and contraindications for FNL in pulmonology practice.• Develops consensus on procedural standards, curriculum, and competency requirements for FNL training in pulmonology.• Identifies priority areas for future research to support integration of FNL into pulmonology services.

title: Job displacement and the health of older adults: Evidence from China
affiliations: Zhejiang Gongshang University and Guangdong University of Technology

detail.title: Job displacement and the health of older adults: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the long-term consequences of involuntary job displacement on multidimensional health outcomes among middle-aged and older adults in urban China, using the 2014 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Survey (CHARLS) Life History Questionnaire. To address the endogeneity of job loss, we exploit business closures, position cancellations, and layoffs during the state-owned enterprises (SOEs) reforms in the late 1990s as exogenous labor market shocks and employ Propensity Score Matching (PSM) to control for childhood socioeconomic conditions and family health history. The results show that the overall health of displaced workers has deteriorated in the long run, particularly in terms of mental well-being and cognitive functioning. The adverse effects are more pronounced among males, younger cohorts, and highly educated individuals. Further analysis suggests that these effects operate through increased financial constraints, reduced healthcare utilization, and disrupted social integration.

title: Contraceptive Methods and Anemia in India: A Cost-Benefit Simulation of Hormonal IUD Provision
affiliations: and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: Contraceptive Methods and Anemia in India: A Cost-Benefit Simulation of Hormonal IUD Provision

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a secondary analysis of de-identified data from the 2019–21 National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5). Ethical approval for NFHS-5 was obtained from the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS) and the ICF Institutional Review Board, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. No additional ethics approval was required for this secondary analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: Anemia affects more than half of women of reproductive age in India. Copper intrauterine devices (IUDs) dominate public-sector IUD provision and can increase menstrual blood loss, whereas hormonal methods reduce it; however, family planning and anemia-control programs typically operate separately. Using cross-sectional data from 294,606 married, nonpregnant women aged 15-49 in India's 2019-21 National Family Health Survey, we estimated adjusted associations between contraceptive method use and hemoglobin using debiased machine learning to flexibly adjust for high-dimensional measured confounding. We also compared current with former users within each method type. We then used the adjusted association in a cost-benefit simulation of providing hormonal IUDs to current users in the predominantly copper reported-IUD group who screen positive for anemia. In the adjusted contrast, hormonal contraception rather than reported-IUD use was associated with 0.143 g/dL higher hemoglobin (95% CI, 0.077-0.209). If this association is causal and the simulation assumptions hold, an any-anemia screening threshold is projected to avert 35,674 disability-adjusted life years over three years and yield a benefit-cost ratio of 2.55. Restricting eligibility to users who screen positive for moderate or severe anemia yields a projected ratio of 3.28 while retaining 77% of projected health gains. For the any-anemia strategy, benefit-cost ratios range from 1.70 to 2.55 across the main specification and parameter sensitivity scenarios. These projections motivate a pragmatic trial of voluntary hemoglobin screening and expanded access to hormonal IUDs within family planning services.

title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in marine fish and sediment of the Musa Estuary, Persian Gulf: towards a human and ecotoxicological risk assessment
affiliations: Khorramshahr University of Marine Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Khorramshahr University of Marine Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Abadan University of Medical Sciences

detail.title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in marine fish and sediment of the Musa Estuary, Persian Gulf: towards a human and ecotoxicological risk assessment
detail.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) pose persistent ecological and human-health concerns in industrialized coastal systems. This study assessed the 16 USEPA priority PAHs in surface sediments and muscle tissue of four commercially important fish species from five stations across the Musa Estuary, Persian Gulf, during summer and winter 2023. Total Σ16PAH concentrations in sediments were significantly higher in summer than winter (365 ± 27 vs. 250 ± 42 ng g⁻¹ dw; p = 0.008). Fish ΣBaPeq ranged from 5.4 to 12.5 ng g⁻¹ ww across stations and was higher in summer than winter (12.6 ± 4.9 vs. 7.6 ± 7.7 ng g⁻¹ ww). PAH composition also shifted seasonally, from greater contributions of 2- and 6-ring compounds in summer toward 3–4-ring compounds in winter. Elevated BSAFs for high-molecular-weight PAHs in benthic species were consistent with an additional contribution from dietary exposure. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) resolved four source classes: petrogenic, coal combustion, traffic emissions, and high-temperature combustion, with petrogenic inputs dominating summer profiles and coal combustion becoming more prominent in winter. Monte Carlo probabilistic assessment (10,000 iterations) yielded a mean adult incremental lifetime cancer risk (ILCR) of 3.5 × 10⁻⁵, with approximately 77% of simulations exceeding 10⁻⁵. Petrogenic sources accounted for an estimated 65.6% of source-attributed cancer risk. These findings demonstrate pronounced seasonal variation in PAH contamination and identify petroleum-related inputs as an important priority for pollution-management strategies in the Musa Estuary.

title: Price Formation and Information Flow in Earnings Prediction Markets
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers Business School at Newark & New Brunswick and

detail.title: Price Formation and Information Flow in Earnings Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: We study the price dynamics of prediction market contracts tied to quarterly corporate earnings. Using a sample of 599 Polymarket earnings events, we combine trade-level Polymarket prices with high-frequency stock prices, analyst forecasts, and firm news to examine how prices react to information. We first document that a large share of price adjustment occurs immediately after markets open despite limited trading activity, and early prices strongly extrapolate from firms' past earnings-beat histories. Second, Polymarket prices have a strong reversal effect that varies with lookback window and forecast horizon. Third, stock returns positively predict subsequent Polymarket price changes over the subsequent one hour to one day, and the predictive relation becomes more pronounced as the earnings announcement approaches. In contrast, Polymarket price changes do not predict stock returns, consistent with a one-way information flow from the stock market to Polymarket. In addition, Polymarket prices respond to analyst forecast revisions in the direction of consensus change without subsequent reversal, but react only temporarily to news sentiment. Lastly, we find that the arrival of firm news strengthens the predictive relation between stock returns and future Polymarket price changes, supporting a potential attention channel in the information flow.

title: Banks’ funding structures and pass-through in the euro area
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Banks’ funding structures and pass-through in the euro area
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the interest rate pass-through of monetary policy in the euro area by focusing on the role of banks’ funding structures. We estimate the interest rate pass-through for loans to non-financial corporations using bank-level balance sheet data. In doing so, we interact the response of lending rates with characteristics of the funding structure, and show that banks that rely more on bond issuance than on the money market tend to be less responsive to policy changes. Finally, we test the presence of the asset-liability-management channel, and find that banks combining longer-term liabilities (higher bond shares) with longer rate fixation periods for loans (higher share of loans with fixed rates) exhibit the most muted lending rate response to policy shocks.

The research protocol adhered to standard institutional ethical guidelines for human participant research in business and social sciences.
