detail.abstract: Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) are critical catalysts for capital mobilization and structural equity growth in emerging markets, yet retail investor engagement remains highly stratified. This study investigates the behavioral, cognitive, and demographic micro-determinants of IPO participation among retail investors in the South Gujarat region-a primary industrial and commercial hub in India. Utilizing a primary dataset of 485 retail investors collected via a stratified random sampling design across urban and suburban agglomerations (2024-2025), we deploy structural equation modeling (SEM) and multivariate logistic regression to isolate participation dynamics. The empirical results demonstrate that risk perception operates as the primary inhibitor of market entry (𝛽 =-0.412, 𝑝 < .001), decreasing the likelihood of participation by 33.7% for each unit increase on the psychometric risk scale. Conversely, financial literacy exerts a major positive influence (𝛽 = +0.487, 𝑝 < .001), rendering highly literate individuals 1.63 times more likely to execute IPO investments. Information source credibility and behavioral path-dependency (prior experience) further amplify participation probabilities. The integrated behavioral framework accounts for 61.4% of the variance in participation (𝑅 2 = 0.614), offering significant improvements over traditional single-theory cross-sectional frameworks. These insights provide stock exchanges, financial technology platforms, and regulatory authorities with a clear empirical framework for designing riskmitigating disclosure systems and targeted investor education programs.

title: The TANKFULL Model: Distributionally Weighted Investment and the Limits of Two-Type Aggregation

detail.title: The TANKFULL Model: Distributionally Weighted Investment and the Limits of Two-Type Aggregation
detail.abstract: Two-Agent New Keynesian (TANK) models provide a tractable middle ground between representative-agent New Keynesian models, which suppress household heterogeneity, and heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) models, which retain rich household distributions at substantially greater analytical and computational cost. TANK models preserve economically important differences between two household types and can reproduce important aggregate implications of richer heterogeneous-household economies. Their very tractability, however, creates a potential limitation: compressing household heterogeneity to two types may discard distributional information that matters for productive investment. I develop the TANKFULL model to determine exactly how much investment-relevant distributional information a two-type New Keynesian model can preserve. I incorporate distributionally weighted investment, under which equal units of income received by different household groups can generate different marginal effects on productive investment because the groups differ in expenditure responses, expenditure incidence, and exposure to firms with different investment responsiveness. I establish both a positive result and a sharp dimensional limit. Two household types are sufficient for distribution to affect investment: an income-preserving reallocation changes investment whenever the types have different residual investment weights. But when their conventional marginal propensities to consume differ, aggregate disposable income and aggregate consumption jointly span the two-dimensional household-income space, leaving no independent residual income-distribution direction. I show that at least three independent household-income dimensions are generically required for a redistribution to leave both aggregate disposable income and aggregate consumption unchanged while still altering investment. More generally, when K locally independent aggregate statistics summarize an N-dimensional heterogeneous state, the residual state space has dimension N-K. TANKFULL therefore identifies both the additional distributional content available within the tractable TANK model and the precise dimensional boundary beyond which richer household heterogeneity becomes necessary.

title: Hidden in the aggregate: the cyclicality of EU labour force participation
affiliations: and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Hidden in the aggregate: the cyclicality of EU labour force participation
detail.abstract: We estimate the cyclical response of labour force participation to growth shocks across EU regions. We use a shift-share instrumental variable approach and local projections on EU Labour Force Survey microdata covering 15 countries and 114 regions over 2000–2020. The aggregate labour force participation rate is remarkably resilient, a clear contrast to the highly cyclical participation rate documented for the U.S. However, this resilience masks pronounced demographic heterogeneity. Men’s participation declines significantly while women’s remains stable, reflecting sectoral segregation and the added worker effect. Young workers exhibit the most persistent responses, with effects lasting up to eight years, consistent with hysteresis through human capital erosion. Less-educated and non-native workers bear disproportionate employment costs. The findings imply that aggregate slack measures may miss important distributional dimensions relevant for monetary, fiscal, and structural policy.

title: Lagged and Non-Linear Climatic and Environmental Determinants of Malaria Incidence in Sindh, Pakistan: A Distributed Lag Nonlinear Modelling Study
affiliations: University of Karachi, People’s Primary Healthcare Initiative, Aga Khan University, PATH, University of Karachi, People’s Primary Healthcare Initiative, People’s Primary Healthcare Initiative, Aga Khan University - Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Northumbria University, PATH, Fudan University - Key Laboratory of Public Health Safety and Aga Khan University

detail.title: Lagged and Non-Linear Climatic and Environmental Determinants of Malaria Incidence in Sindh, Pakistan: A Distributed Lag Nonlinear Modelling Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: Research reported in this study was supported by the Fogarty International Center of the National Institutes of Health under Award Number D43TW012733.

detail.abstract:
Background: Malaria is a major public health problem in Sindh, Pakistan, where seasonal, climatic variability and ecological heterogeneity sustain transmission. Environmental effects are often delayed and non-linear, limiting the value of simple linear models for early warning.

Material and methods: We analysed monthly malaria case counts from 17 high-burden districts of Sindh from 2013 to 2024, linked with satellite/reanalysis-derived temperature, rainfall, relative humidity and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI). Cross-correlation and Granger causality analyses explored lagged predictive relationships. Distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) estimated exposure-lag-response associations over lags of up to four months, adjusting for seasonality, long-term trends and district-level heterogeneity.

Results: Malaria burden varied substantially across districts, with median monthly cases ranging from 329 in Hyderabad to 5,472 in Sanghar; the all-district median was 1,904 cases. Relative humidity and NDVI showed the most consistent temporal predictive associations. Relative humidity showed significant Granger associations in 15/17 districts and the strongest spatial consistency, while NDVI was significant in 13/17 districts and showed the strongest province-level predictive signal (F=62.44, p<0.001). Rainfall peaked at a two-month lag in the combined analysis (r=0.371, p<0.001), while temperature showed weaker and more heterogeneous associations. DLNM results showed increased malaria risk under humid conditions, with high relative humidity associated with incidence rate ratios of 1.75-1.78 at one- to two-month cumulative lags. High rainfall showed elevated risk at one- to two-month lags (IRR 1.80 and 1.72), while very high temperature was largely suppressive.

Conclusion: Malaria risk in Sindh is shaped by delayed and ecologically mediated environmental processes. Relative humidity and NDVI appear particularly useful for climate-informed early warning, offering an operational lead time of approximately four to eight weeks.

title: Integrating spatial histological feature-associated modules with habitat radiomics for subtyping thymic epithelial tumors: a retrospective cohort study
affiliations: Jiangxi Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Jiangxi Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, Jiangxi Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital and Zhejiang Cancer Hospital

detail.title: Integrating spatial histological feature-associated modules with habitat radiomics for subtyping thymic epithelial tumors: a retrospective cohort study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All other authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
Background: Thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) comprise heterogeneous World Health Organization (WHO) histological subtypes with overlapping epithelial cell subtypes and lymphocytic features, making reliable subtype classification challenging. Herein, we integrated spatial organization pathology feature modules with CT habitat radiomics (HR) and knowledge distillation to develop a novel, non-invasive, and repeatable diagnostic model for subtyping TETs.

Methods: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) and paired preoperative non-contrast-enhanced CT images from multi-center were enrolled in this retrospective study. CONCH-based visual features, four diagnostic semantic prompts, and cellular pathomic features were integrated to derive eight interpretable spatial histopathological feature (SPF) modules and develop the pathology model. CT-based HRs were subsequently trained using deep learning with or without SPF module knowledge to develop models for evaluating prediction performance across multiple datasets.

Findings: Eight SPF modules based on TET pathological diagnostic elements were defined and quantified in each WSI. SPF module-based model achieved subtype-specific areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.703–1.000 in the internal JX test cohort, 0.880–0.978 in the external ZJ cohort, and 0.843–0.939 in the TCGA-THYM cohort. Profiling of the paired CT-based HRs and SPF modules showed differences in correlation between histological subtypes. Sankey diagram and correlation matrix revealed potential digital information across the two modalities. Moreover, the SPF-guided distillation model performed better than the SPF-unguided distillation model in both the JX cohort (0.911 vs 0.832) and ZJ cohort (0.929 vs 0.702), and also outperformed the predictive value of Transfer learning and Multi-task learning.

Interpretation: The modules of spatial-organizational pathological features are a novel digital label that can be used to develop pathological subtype prediction models. The SPF modules may also serve as a bridge to optimize knowledge training for the CT branch, thereby enhancing the specificity and sensitivity of CT-based non-invasive prediction of TET pathological subtypes.

title: Corporate Tax Cuts, Firm Growth, and Workers' Earnings
affiliations: , Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Government of the United States of America - Joint Committee on Taxation and Joint Committee on Taxation, US Congress

detail.title: Corporate Tax Cuts, Firm Growth, and Workers' Earnings
detail.abstract: We study the effects of the largest corporate income tax cut in U.S. history on firms and workers. To identify causal effects, we use employer-employee matched tax records and event studies comparing similarly sized firms in the same industry that faced divergent tax changes due to their pre-existing legal status. Tax cuts cause increases in firms' investment, sales, profits, employment, and payrolls, with earnings gains concentrated among highly paid workers. In the short-run, 87% of private income gains flow to the top 10% of the income distribution.

title:
From European Social Housing Models to Societal Impact in Greece: 
A Policy Pathway for Social Economy-Led Housing
affiliations: University of West Attica (UNIWA) - Department of Business Administration

detail.title:
From European Social Housing Models to Societal Impact in Greece: 
A Policy Pathway for Social Economy-Led Housing

declarations.ethicsApproval: NO ETHICAL ISSUES
declarations.funderStatement: NO

detail.abstract: Europe's housing crisis is placing growing pressure on welfare systems, urban cohesion, and the capacity of low-and middle-income households to secure stable and affordable homes. This paper translates comparative evidence from Vienna, Brussels, Barcelona, and Zurich into a societal-impact pathway for Greece. It asks how social economy organisations, municipalities, and central government could jointly develop housing arrangements that protect long-term affordability while strengthening participation, community stability, and institutional capacity. The analysis draws on comparative public-policy and institutional evidence concerning municipal and limited-profit housing, Community Land Trusts, collaborative housing, and cooperative housing ecosystems. The paper identifies four transferable mechanisms: long-term stewardship of land and housing, limits on speculative gains, participatory governance, and durable public-community partnerships. On this basis, it proposes a phased Greek policy pathway built around pilot sites, access to public and municipal property, transparent beneficiary criteria, technical support, and measurable social outcomes. The anticipated impacts include reduced housing-cost pressure, greater residential stability, stronger community participation, and improved capacity to deliver socially oriented housing. The paper does not present the social economy as a substitute for public responsibility. It positions it as an institutional partner that can help convert public assets and policy commitments into locally governed, socially sustainable housing solutions.

title: The Behavioural Economics of Decision-Making in a Crisis:,Lessons from the Covid Era
affiliations: UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics and University of Nevada, Reno - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Behavioural Economics of Decision-Making in a Crisis:,Lessons from the Covid Era
detail.abstract: The Covid era provided an exceptional opportunity to record and examine decision-making in a crisis. We analyse the features of decision-making during the Covid era through the lens of behavioural economics. Covid-era decision-making processes and outcomes deviated acutely from what was recommended by Western public health authorities prior to mid-March 2020. We find that several behavioural economics concepts – including several concepts that we each individually identified as important early in the Covid era (e.g., in Foster 2020 and Pingle 2022) – explain why decision-making processes and the decisions made deviated from what had been considered best practice, often producing results that increased harm rather than ameliorating it. We reflect on how we might reduce the chance of repeating the types of mistakes made during the Covid era when a future similar crisis arises. Because human social planners are not immune to behavioural tendencies as economic analysis traditionally assumes, we find that we must plan to address our human frailties if we are to plan and act effectively the next time a crisis looms.

title: Development and Validation of a Questionnaire for Community-based Screening of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome in Women Aged 18-45 Years in Odisha, India: A Validation Study

detail.title: Development and Validation of a Questionnaire for Community-based Screening of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome in Women Aged 18-45 Years in Odisha, India: A Validation Study

detail.abstract:
Background: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age. Early identification remains challenging, particularly in resource-limited settings with limited access to diagnostic services. This study aimed to develop and validate a simple, symptom-based community screening questionnaire for identifying women at increased risk of PCOS.

Methods: A four-phase development and validation study was conducted. Candidate items were generated through literature review and qualitative interviews with women diagnosed with PCOS. Following content validation by a nine-member expert panel, face validation, and cognitive debriefing, the final questionnaire was administered to 160 women aged 18-45 years in Odisha, India. The 2018 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS served as the reference standard. Predictors were selected using bivariate, LASSO, and multivariable logistic regression. Separate universal and married-women prediction models were developed, each with unweighted and integer-weighted risk scores. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, diagnostic accuracy measures, calibration assessment, 2000-bootstrap internal validation, and test-retest reliability.

Findings: The initial pool of 124 items across 13 domains was refined to a 16-item questionnaire covering five domains. Two scoring approaches were developed for universal and married-women models. In the universal model, unweighted and weighted scores achieved AUCs of 0.950 and 0.964, respectively, while the married-women model achieved AUCs of 0.949 and 0.957. At optimal cut-offs, the universal unweighted score showed 96.2% sensitivity and 75.9% specificity, whereas the weighted score achieved 90.4% sensitivity and 87.0% specificity. Calibration assessment demonstrated good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities across both models. Bootstrap validation showed minimal optimism, and both models demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.963 and 0.968).

Interpretations: The validated questionnaire demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance, reliability, and feasibility for community-based PCOS screening. This simple, low-cost, non-invasive tool may facilitate early identification and referral, particularly in resource-limited settings. Further external validation is warranted.

title: Technology and Jobs: Is Automation Increasing Inequality in India? A Panel Data Analysis of Automation, Job Polarization and Income Inequality (2007–2024)
affiliations: Mahatma Gandhi University

detail.title: Technology and Jobs: Is Automation Increasing Inequality in India? A Panel Data Analysis of Automation, Job Polarization and Income Inequality (2007–2024)
detail.abstract: Automation is increasingly transforming the structure of employment, altering the demand for different types of labour and raising concerns about inequality in developing economies. While the literature on technological change and employment is extensive for advanced economies, empirical evidence on the long-run sectoral effects of automation in India remains comparatively limited, particularly with respect to low-skill employment, income inequality, financial conditions, and inter-sectoral spillovers. This study examines whether automation contributes to job displacement and widening income inequality across major sectors of the Indian economy. The analysis covers six sectors—agriculture, manufacturing, construction, retail, IT/BPO, and healthcare—over the period 2007–2024, producing a balanced sector-year panel of 108 observations. A composite sectoral automation index is constructed using sector-specific indicators of technological adoption, with principal component analysis employed to combine standardised components and reduce arbitrary weighting. The empirical framework employs two-way fixed-effects models with sector and year effects, complemented by an instrumental-variable strategy to address potential reverse causality and omitted-variable bias. A Bartik-style shift-share instrument is constructed using sectoral exposure to automatable tasks and foreign robot installation growth. Additional analyses employ method-of-moments quantile regression to examine heterogeneity across the distribution of low-skill employment, while interaction models investigate the roles of sectoral credit access and social protection expenditure. Input-output linkages are further incorporated to identify automation spillovers across sectors.The findings indicate a substantial negative relationship between automation and low-skill employment. The baseline fixed-effects estimates suggest that a one-unit increase in the automation index is associated with a 16.9 percentage-point reduction in the low-skill employment share, while automation increases the high-skill employment share by approximately 4.3 percentage points. The instrumental-variable estimates remain statistically significant, although smaller in magnitude, indicating that the relationship is not driven solely by broader modernisation trends. Automation is also associated with higher income inequality, with the baseline Gini coefficient estimate indicating a statistically significant positive effect. Quantile estimates reveal considerable heterogeneity: the negative effect on low-skill employment becomes stronger at higher quantiles, suggesting that sectors with greater concentrations of low-skill workers are particularly vulnerable to technological displacement. The interaction between automation and the COVID-19 period further indicates that the pandemic intensified automation-related reductions in low-skill employment. Financial conditions also matter: greater sectoral credit availability amplifies the inequality effect of automation, whereas higher social protection expenditure significantly mitigates it. The spillover analysis demonstrates that automation in one sector can reduce low-skill employment in connected downstream sectors, indicating that the effects of technological adoption extend beyond the sectors in which automation occurs directly.The study concludes that automation in India is associated not merely with technological upgrading but with a significant restructuring of empl

title: The social cost of plastic waste
affiliations: University of Strasbourg

detail.title: The social cost of plastic waste
detail.abstract: We integrate material flows into a growth model and derive a formula for the social cost of waste. We calibrate the model on historical plastic use data, which show sharply increasing plastic dependency and substantial future income losses due to plastic waste if not addressed. The social cost of plastic waste is in the range of plastic market prices and rises sharply. Our results indicate a need for urgent policy intervention.

publicationDetails.journalName: Wharton Pension Research Council / Boettner Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The pension sector is an important investor group in global financial markets and a key holder of government and corporate debt. This article examines the evolution of pension fund asset allocations around the globe and documents two important structural changes. First, pension investors have shifted portfolio share allocations away from fixed income securities. This trend is robust across Defined Contribution (DC) and Defined Benefit (DB) programs as well as country groups. Second, pensions have instead shifted allocations into riskier investments within mutual funds as well as alternative investments. We hypothesize that a global decline in interest rates is one potential driver of this change. Using a global sample, we show that declining local currency government bond yields are associated with lower bond pension portfolio shares and higher holdings shares of mutual funds and foreign assets. We discuss the potential implications of these trends for borrowing costs. The declining holding share of pension as a long-term investor group implies a lower cost increase in response to new debt issuance, but it may come at a cost of higher yield sensitivity to global uncertainty.

title: Socioeconomic Inequality in Anemia Severity among Women in the Terai Region  A Concentration Index Approach
affiliations: Patna University and Deen Dayal Upadhyay Gorakhpur University

detail.title: Socioeconomic Inequality in Anemia Severity among Women in the Terai Region  A Concentration Index Approach
detail.abstract: ​Background:   Anemia remains an important public health concern among women, with the burden often greater among socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Examining the socioeconomic distribution of anemia severity can provide information beyond overall prevalence and help identify groups that bear a disproportionate burden.Objective:       This study assessed wealth-related socioeconomic inequality in anemia severity among women in the Terai region and examined whether the observed pattern was consistent with socioeconomic differences in severe anemia.Methods:         The study used secondary data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21), restricted to women aged 15–49 years residing in the Terai region. Anemia was classified as severe, moderate, mild, or non-anemic according to hemoglobin-based criteria. Household wealth quintile was used to rank socioeconomic position. Weighted descriptive analysis and multinomial logistic regression were used to describe socioeconomic differences in anemia severity, and concentration-curve analysis with the concentration index (CI) was used to quantify wealth-related inequality.Results:           Overall, 56.4% of women were anemic: 25.8% had mild anemia, 28.5% had moderate anemia, and 2.1% had severe anemia. In the regression analysis, women in the poorest wealth quintile had higher odds of severe anemia than women in the richest quintile (AOR = 2.20, 95% CI: 1.09–4.45). Urban residence was associated with lower odds of severe anemia (AOR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.29–0.87). After additional adjustment for BMI, the wealth association was attenuated (AOR = 1.95, 95% CI: 0.95–3.98), while BMI remained associated with severe anemia (AOR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.93–0.99). The concentration curve indicated a pro-poor distribution of anemia, and the final concentration index was −0.0137.Conclusion:     Anemia among women in the Terai region shows a socioeconomic gradient, with a greater burden of severe anemia among women from poorer households. The negative concentration index indicates a pro-poor distribution of anemia burden. Policies addressing nutritional vulnerability together with socioeconomic disadvantage may help reduce these inequalities.

title: The Commensurability Problem in Kapp’s Theory of Social Costs: A Conceptual Response from Japanese Environmental Economics
affiliations: Momoyama Gakuin University

detail.title: The Commensurability Problem in Kapp’s Theory of Social Costs: A Conceptual Response from Japanese Environmental Economics
detail.abstract: K. W. Kapp’s theory of social costs holds that the firm’s money outlays do not measure the true total costs of production. But how to treat losses that resist monetary valuation — and whether any unit can render heterogeneous losses commensurable — is a problem Kapp left unfinished, and one that Sebastian Berger (2024) restates as a continuing task for a revolutionary social ecological economics: calculation in kind can exclude the absolutely inefficient but cannot, by itself, choose among incommensurable alternatives, which is left to social valuation. This paper asks how the Japanese reception of Kapp, and Miyamoto Ken’ichi in particular, addressed the problem. It argues that Miyamoto subjected Kapp’s single notion of social cost to a two-stage conceptual operation: first partitioning it into social loss (realized damage) and social cost (prevention expenditure); then dividing social loss into three — relative loss, which compensation can repair; absolute, irreversible loss, which it cannot; and an indeterminate zone between them. Absolute loss locates a domain of the incommensurable at the centre of the theory and grounds the priority of physical apprehension and of ex ante prevention in irreversibility rather than uncertainty; the indeterminate zone marks the contested boundary at which the line between the commensurable and the incommensurable is drawn. Developed largely without the mediation of the Anglophone Kapp literature, it offers — through damage analysis rather than calculation theory — not a solution at the level of calculation but a determinate location for the problem and a complementary illumination of it.

title: The Mandatory Pre-Trial Claims Procedure in Disputes with Railway Carriers under Russian Law

detail.title: The Mandatory Pre-Trial Claims Procedure in Disputes with Railway Carriers under Russian Law

keywords: Recognition and Enforcement of Arbitral Awards

detail.abstract: This article examines the mandatory pre-trial claims procedure governing disputes with railway carriers under Russian law. It considers the required content of a claim, the documentary record that must accompany it, permissible methods of service, the persons entitled to assert transport claims, and the legal consequences of missing the six-month and forty-five-day claim periods. The article argues that those periods are not peremptory and do not extinguish the claimant's substantive right where the statutory claims procedure is ultimately completed and the action is filed within the applicable limitation period. Particular attention is given to contemporaneous transport records, proof of the composition and amount of losses, an insurer's subrogation claim, the position of a cargo owner following Constitutional Court Resolution No. 45-P of December 16, 2023, and suspension of the limitation period while the carrier considers the claim. The final part explains why the same pre-trial materials may become important in international arbitration and at the stage of recognition and enforcement of an arbitral award.

title: Location Choice Modeling for the Hawaiʻi Deep-set Longline Fishery: Implications of Changing Ocean Conditions and Fluctuating Trip Costs
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Location Choice Modeling for the Hawaiʻi Deep-set Longline Fishery: Implications of Changing Ocean Conditions and Fluctuating Trip Costs
detail.abstract: To better understand how Hawaiʻi longline fishers choose fishing locations and how these choices may change under shifting tuna distributions and trip costs, we developed a fishing location choice model using a random utility framework and mixed logit specification. The model incorporates individualized trip costs and heterogeneous fisher preferences for bigeye and yellowfin tuna, and it correctly classifies 75.5% of in-sample location choices. Model results indicate substantial heterogeneity in fishers’ preferences for bigeye and yellowfin tuna, reflected in wide variation in willingness-to-pay for additional catch. Differences in willingness-to-pay are associated with vessel size, fishing effort, spatial footprint, and economic performance. Simulations of changes in expected catch based on projected 2050 changes in tuna biomass from Bell et al. (2021) suggest that the fleet may either concentrate effort closer to the main Hawaiian islands or expand farther into the eastern Pacific, depending on the magnitude and direction of biomass redistribution. Scenarios with higher and lower trip costs produce opposing but asymmetric spatial responses. Higher trip costs may lead some vessels to fish closer to port while others travel farther to productive fishing grounds to offset rising expenses. Lower trip costs reduce the marginal cost of travel and encourage expansion into more distant, historically productive areas. This study is among the first to integrate climate-driven tuna biomass projections into a location choice framework and it advances cost analyses by using individualized trip costs. The results provide a robust baseline for predicting fleet spatial distribution under changing ocean conditions and economic constraints.

title:
The Correction-Capacity Model 
Warrant-Responsive Rationality Under Self-Relevant Threat
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
The Correction-Capacity Model 
Warrant-Responsive Rationality Under Self-Relevant Threat
detail.abstract: This paper develops correction-capacity as a theoretical model of rationality under self-relevant threat. Human judgment depends on stable beliefs, identities, roles, and explanatory models, but those same structures can become difficult to revise when contradiction threatens personal worth, belonging, competence, legitimacy, or status. The model separates six events that are often compressed into the idea of being corrected: discrepancy, relevant constraint, correction claim, warrant, response, and durable revision. Warrant is treated as evidential, procedural, and proportional. A correction claim is stronger when it is supported by relevant and convergent evidence, can be meaningfully contested, and asks for no more change than the evidence justifies. Correction-capacity is defined as warrant-response calibration over time: the degree to which acceptance, resistance, or suspended judgment tracks the independently assessed strength of a correction claim and persists in later confidence, interpretation, behavior, repair, decision pathways, or evidential practice. This definition distinguishes calibrated revision from defensive non-revision, reasoned resistance, compliance, suspended judgment, and performative revision. The model also proposes that identity-belief fusion can impair calibration under self-relevant threat, while person-belief differentiation and noncontingent personal worth may make justified revision more survivable without increasing indiscriminate agreement. The framework is related to cognitive dissonance, motivated reasoning, identity-protective cognition, intellectual humility, feedback orientation, self-affirmation, self-compassion, cognitive flexibility, and belief revision. It then extends the same abstract logic, with domain-specific mechanisms, to organizational learning and AI corrigibility. For AI, the paper distinguishes persistent memory from trace-bearing correction that survives beyond the immediate exchange and transfers to structurally similar contexts. It also separates perceived social presence from system-level corrigibility and makes no claim that either property establishes machine consciousness. The theory is intentionally falsifiable. It would be weakened if correction-capacity adds no explanatory value beyond established neighboring constructs, if identity-belief fusion does not reduce warrantresponse calibration, if noncontingent-worth interventions merely increase compliance, if delivery conditions have no independent effect on durable uptake, or if the proposed distinctions cannot be measured reliably across time.

title: Assessing the EU Partner Countries' Legal Framework on Sustainable Development: What is the Role of the EU?
affiliations: and LUMSA University

detail.title: Assessing the EU Partner Countries' Legal Framework on Sustainable Development: What is the Role of the EU?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This Working Paper represents the result of the research carried out by the University of Cagliari Unit, in the context of the project ‘Make it Better (MiB): in search of a new normative model for the promotion of sustainable development in the EU external action’, during the quadrimester August-November 2024. Principal Investigator - Head of the Project: Prof. Luca Pantaleo, Associate Professor of EU Law at the University of Cagliari. Under His guidance and supervision, paragraphs 1 and 2 were written by Felipe Tomazini de Souza, Research fellow at the University of Cagliari; paragraphs 3 and 4 were written by Dr. Adriana Brusca, Research fellow at the University of Cagliari and Lecturer at LUMSA University.

detail.abstract:
This working paper examines whether, and by which mechanisms, the European Union influences the domestic legal frameworks governing sustainable development in its trade partners. Four jurisdictions are analysed, each selected to reflect a distinct legal instrument and a balanced geographical coverage: Bolivia (GSP+), Colombia (new-generation Free Trade Agreement with a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter), Cameroon (Interim Economic Partnership Agreement with the Central Africa Party, complemented by the FLEGT Voluntary Partnership Agreement) and The Bahamas (CARIFORUM–EU Economic Partnership Agreement). The study adopts a qualitative method, combining analysis of domestic constitutional and statutory law with treaty texts, the institutional output of the agreements, EU ex-post evaluations and GSP+ periodic reviews, ILO monitoring materials and independent NGO assessments.

The paper argues that the EU's influence is legally traceable in direct terms principally under unilateral conditionality: the ratification of ILO Convention No 29 by Bolivia and of ILO Convention No 182 by Colombia in 2005 is attributable to the eligibility requirements of the reformed GSP regime. Under bilateral instruments, by contrast, influence operates indirectly, through cooperation, technical assistance and capacity-building, institutional dialogue with civil society participation, the incentive of market access, and the latent leverage of non-execution clauses which, although seldom invoked, sustain a scheme of negative conditionality. Across all four cases, normative advancement is offset by a persistent implementation gap and by countervailing domestic legislation pursuing extractive and economic objectives. The paper concludes that attribution remains methodologically constrained by principles of non-interference, national ownership and the presence of competing external actors, and that the EU's impact is best characterised as a process of gradual, cross-sectoral transformation of protection standards and of progressive integration of partner States into the international legal framework on sustainability.

title: Caught in the Middle: A Review of Employee Trust, HR Credibility, and the Competing Expectations of Human Resource Management
affiliations: Bharathidasan Institute of Management (BIM)

detail.title: Caught in the Middle: A Review of Employee Trust, HR Credibility, and the Competing Expectations of Human Resource Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — no human participants or primary data collection involved.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: Human resource (HR) departments operate under a structural dual-loyalty dilemma, positioned between advancing organizational performance objectives and protecting workforce welfare. Although a substantial body of research addresses generalized organizational trust and trust in immediate leadership, comparatively little empirical work examines employee trust directed specifically at the HR function itself. This paper reviews the theoretical foundations relevant to this gap-organizational trust theory, organizational justice theory, psychological contract theory, and the employee voice literature-and integrates them with the human resource management literature on HR's strategic repositioning and role conflict. The review identifies a clear underexamined space at the intersection of these literatures: how competing stakeholder expectations placed on HR practitioners shape employee-perceived HR credibility, and how that credibility in turn influences employee voice and organizational trust. The paper concludes by outlining a proposed qualitative research agenda designed to address this gap.

title: Nature of the Factors: Value

detail.title: Nature of the Factors: Value
detail.abstract:
Two portfolios, both honestly called value, cut from the same universe on the same date and to the same size, hold seven names in ten differently. The reference book ranks a composite of four accounting ratios inside each company’s sector. The comparison book ranks book to market pooled. The three in ten they share carry 13.31 percent of the reference book’s market capitalization. Both shares are medians over 347 four week dates, 3 January 2000 to 13 July 2026. That is not a finding about markets. It is a finding about disclosure. 

Thirteen decisions stand between a set of financial statements and a value ranking. The profession publishes almost none of them. Each is taken with the argument on both sides, written down before any return was seen, and priced against the alternative afterward. Three of the thirteen measured worse than the alternative. All three are printed at full size. 

All results are gross. Two things are conceded before any evidence and neither is qualified later. The accounting component of market to book is unpriced. A value premium is earned where no book value exists. The claim left is narrower: accounting choices nobody publishes decide which companies a value rule holds. This paper publishes its own, including where its construction did not describe itself.

title: Policy Learning in Language-Mediated Stochastic Systems
affiliations: Peking University, City University of Hong Kong and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - School of Engineering

detail.title: Policy Learning in Language-Mediated Stochastic Systems
detail.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) makes the content of operational messages available to stochastic simulation, which enables the evaluation of communication policies that govern message timing, content, and subsequent receiver actions. Since repeated LLM calls are expensive, scalable simulation must group similar situations and reuse language outcomes collected for each group. This reuse creates an endogenous input problem, in which a stored language law changes simulated actions and future contexts, while those contexts define the law that the simulator should use. In this research, we formulate this relation through a policy-specific language input operator. We characterize exact reuse across policies and show that a precisely estimated shared input can create unavoidable error in operating values and reverse a dynamic policy ranking. Then, a decision-weighted analysis is developed, which studies representation, reference-to-policy context transport, and reference-to-stored adjustment components and measures their amplification through the operating system. We show that this amplification is generally unavoidable. We also construct a reusable empirical operator from one language sample and establish policy selection guarantees under a total call budget and an information lower bound for adaptive language collection. Numerical experiments on generated handoffs and code review conversations illustrate the practical importance of the proposed modeling and learning framework.

title: The Impact of Suicide Hotlines on Health: Evidence from 988 Implementation
affiliations: University of Oregon - Department of Economics, University of Toronto - Department of Economics and Duke University - Stanford School of Public Policy

detail.title: The Impact of Suicide Hotlines on Health: Evidence from 988 Implementation
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the impact of the National Suicide Hotline Designation Act, which introduced the universal 988 calling code and earmarked federal funding to suicide crisis call centers in July 2022. We use a difference-in-differences design that leverages pre-existing cross-state variation in crisis line capacity gaps, measured by the number of pre-988 calls routed to a state but not answered in-state. The rollout substantially improved crisis line operations in states with larger baseline capacity gaps: these states answered more calls in-state and increased their in-state answer rates. However, these operational gains did not translate into detectable reductions in suicide mortality. The mortality estimates are precise enough to rule out even modest short-run reductions. We also find no statistically significant improvements in broader population mental health outcomes. These findings suggest that expanding crisis line capacity alone may be insufficient to reduce suicide deaths.

title: Teen Suicide and the Outcomes of Surviving Peers
affiliations: Duke University, Yale University, Northwestern University and Northwestern University

detail.title: Teen Suicide and the Outcomes of Surviving Peers
detail.abstract:
By age 17, a quarter of U.S. students have experienced a peer suicide. Using linked administrative data from South Carolina and a matched difference-in-differences design, we find that exposure to a peer's self-harm death increases the probability of a self-harm diagnosis by nearly 50% and both the incidence and frequency of mental health visits. Effects on care use and criminal behavior are concentrated among white boys, and responses diverge by prior mental health history: students without a prior diagnosis increase felony offending rather than care-seeking. Deaths from assault and transportation accidents produce no comparable rise in self-harm, consistent with contagion.

title: Colleges, Assortative Mating, and Intergenerational Mobility in Twentieth-Century America
affiliations: Stanford University, University of California, Davis and Brigham Young University

detail.title: Colleges, Assortative Mating, and Intergenerational Mobility in Twentieth-Century America
detail.abstract:
We use newly digitized records for 1.2 million students at 60 co-educational U.S. colleges, 1915–1943, linked to enrollment records for their children through 1963, to study how colleges shape marital matching and the intergenerational transmission of educational advantage. About 6% of men and 9% of women marry someone from their own college. This homogamy is largely causal: within colleges, more different-sex classmates and longer campus overlap both raise same-college marriage. Same-college spouses are more educated, and this advantage persists across generations. Children of same-college couples more often attend selective colleges, with spousal education explaining a third of the gap.

title: Climate Status Report: Africa Synthesis: An Integrated Assessment of African Countries' Climate Position, Emissions Profile, and the Economic Effects of Adaptation and Mitigation Options to 2050

detail.title: Climate Status Report: Africa Synthesis: An Integrated Assessment of African Countries' Climate Position, Emissions Profile, and the Economic Effects of Adaptation and Mitigation Options to 2050

contentType.other: Climate Change Status Report for Africa

detail.abstract: This report synthesises the climate position, emissions profile and the economics of adaptation and mitigation across Africa to 2050, drawing on the individual AICTEM country assessments. It combines documentary climate and emissions evidence with the CSTATUS land-use carbon module and the CDCGE computable general equilibrium model coupled to a DICE-type climate module. The continent-wide findings are consistent: unmanaged warming damage falls hardest on rural livelihoods and food security; planned, water- and infrastructure-led adaptation recovers most of that loss; carbon pricing cuts energy emissions at a modest, revenue-recyclable cost along a convex abatement curve; and unilateral pricing leaks abroad, so border carbon adjustment helps sustain ambition. Computation of the least-cost way to attain the NDC targets is well grounded, using an optimisation methodology across the various adaptation and mitigation levers. Across economies, both agendas reduce to redirecting investment toward resilient, low-carbon capital; model results are structural and relative, not calendar-dated forecasts.

title: Search and Negotiation with Biased Beliefs in Consumer Credit Markets
affiliations: , Northwestern University, University of Virginia and Universidad Adolfo Ibañez

detail.title: Search and Negotiation with Biased Beliefs in Consumer Credit Markets
detail.abstract:
How do biased beliefs about the interest rate distribution affect search, negotiation, and loan terms in consumer credit markets? In collaboration with Chile's financial regulator, we conducted a randomized controlled trial with 112,063 loan seekers. Randomly eliciting beliefs about interest rates led participants to search more and obtain lower rates. Most participants underestimated both interest rate levels and dispersion. Showing them a price comparison tool we built using administrative data on the universe of consumer loans caused them to update their beliefs, negotiate more, obtain lower rates without searching more, and be more likely to take out a loan.

title: Algorithm-Driven SVARs: Navigating the Wilderness of Big Data
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt - University of Zurich and Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

detail.title: Algorithm-Driven SVARs: Navigating the Wilderness of Big Data
detail.abstract:
Every SVAR result is conditional on two choices: the restrictions that identify the shock and the variables on which they operate. The literature disciplines the first; the second is chosen by hand. We develop a Bayesian methodology that constructs information sets, uses an out-of-sample criterion, and retains the largest system it admits. Under recursive identification, output rises with housing production rather than household credit alone. For monetary policy, an anchor-free joint Bayesian proxy SVAR with multiple instruments strengthens the credit spread channel. A core system augmented with the selected corporate spread identifies expected default risk as a potent transmission margin.

title: Supplemental Medicare Insurance Coverage for Older Adults with Probable Dementia
affiliations: Tufts University, Tufts University and

detail.title: Supplemental Medicare Insurance Coverage for Older Adults with Probable Dementia
detail.abstract:
In this paper, we compare supplemental Medicare insurance coverage among people with probable dementia (PWPD) and matched controls, before and after onset. This retrospective secondary data analysis of insurance coverage changes using propensity score weights and the 2000-2016 Health and Retirement Study (HRS). The sample consists of 3,001 Medicare-enrolled adults age 65 and older with PWPD, and 14,055 controls. Probable dementia is assessed with the Langa-Weir approach and interviewer assessments for proxy interviews. Four years before onset, PWPD become more likely to have Medicare without supplemental coverage (2.97 percentage points; p=0.0016) than matched controls. This reflects the net effect of PWPD being less likely to have Medicare Advantage or traditional Medicare with supplemental coverage, and more likely to have Medicaid. Two years before onset, PWPD were more likely to be Medicaid-eligible (4.95 percentage points, p<0.001), but take-up rates were comparable. Enrollment assistance may improve supplemental coverage for PWPD around dementia onset, potentially increasing financial access to care.

title: Credit Card Banking
affiliations: Wharton School, Department of Finance, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, Columbia University and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Credit Card Banking
detail.abstract:
Credit card interest rates currently average 22%, an 18% spread over the short rate. This spread far exceeds that on any other loan or bond, yet nearly half of households are credit card borrowers. Why are credit card rates so high? To understand this, and the economics of credit card banking, we use regulatory account-level data to analyze the lifetime cash flows of 550 million monthly accounts, representing 90% of the US credit card market. While charge-off rates are comparatively high, averaging around 6%, they explain only a fraction of cards' spread. Reward payments and non-interest expenses are more than offset by interchange and non-interest income. Operating expenses, particularly marketing, are very large, and are used to generate pricing power. Yet, after deducting them, card lending still earns a 6.8% return on assets (ROA), more than four times the banking sector's ROA. Using the cross section of accounts, we estimate that credit card rates price in a 4.3% default risk premium, similar to high-yield bonds. Accounting for this, card lending earns an alpha of around 1.5% relative to the aggregate bank sector.

title: Monopsony Makes it Big
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, University of Massachusetts Amherst and Columbia University

detail.title: Monopsony Makes it Big
detail.abstract:
The literature on imperfect competition in labor markets has expanded rapidly in recent years. This article provides a guide to the field, focusing on the firm-specific ("residual") labor supply elasticity as the definition of a firm's labor market power. We present a general framework showing how this elasticity nests the three widely studied sources of monopsony power: search frictions, preference heterogeneity, and employer concentration. We summarize the empirical estimates of the elasticity of labor supply, highlighting sources of possible heterogeneity. We emphasize that it is difficult to infer elasticities from markdowns (and vice versa) due to the diversity of firm wage-setting practices, illustrating this point using the interaction between monopsony and efficiency wages. We discuss how policy issues in antitrust, labor market regulation, immigration, and macroeconomics interact with monopsony and conclude by listing several areas for future research.

title: Exchange Rates, Structural Change, and Productivity Growth
affiliations: University of California, Davis - Department of Economics, Korea University and Korea University Business School (KUBS)

detail.title: Exchange Rates, Structural Change, and Productivity Growth
detail.abstract:
Macroeconomics tends to view exchange rate movements as transitory. However, persistent exchange rate realignments and the associated capital flows can have long-run implications for structural change and productivity growth. We provide empirical evidence that policies of reserve accumulation and currency undervaluation have had significant effects on manufacturing productivity, as well as on manufacturing share, product varieties, and domestic orientation of production chains. We develop a dynamic two-country model with two sectors, firm dynamics, and trade hysteresis to demonstrate a novel mechanism by which exchange rate policy reorients global supply chains and industrial structure. The model identifies conditions under which such a policy raises productivity and welfare in the home country. It also identifies conditions under which the policy leads to either permanent or reversible deindustrialization in a trading partner. Findings have implications for the long-run relationship between China and the U.S.

title: Social Clubs and Political Office
affiliations: University of Oxford - Blavatnik School of Government, New York University (NYU) - Department of Politics, University of San Andres, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Political Science, New York University (NYU) - New York University and New York University (NYU) - Wilf Family Department of Politics

detail.title: Social Clubs and Political Office
detail.abstract:
Elites maintain disproportionate political power even in formally inclusive political systems, yet the institutions through which they coordinate and reproduce this advantage remain poorly understood. We study membership in the Buenos Aires Jockey Club—Argentina's most prominent elite social club—exploiting staggered variation in family entry. Using difference-in-differences techniques, we find that Jockey Club membership increased the probability of holding legislative office by approximately four percentage points—more than twice the control-group mean. Consistent with a network-based mechanism, membership also increased families' centrality in elite marriage networks—a resource that can facilitate political success through access to party nominations and voter mobilization. This electoral advantage declines substantially after the 1912 Sáenz Peña democratizing reforms, suggesting that the political returns to club membership are conditional on institutional contexts that make elite network connections valuable. Our findings shed light on how elite social institutions reproduce political inequality where personal connections are essential for accessing political office.

title: The Limits of Government Outsourcing: Property Tax Re-Assessments in India
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and Cornerstone Research

detail.title: The Limits of Government Outsourcing: Property Tax Re-Assessments in India
detail.abstract:
Theories of outsourcing often presume that private firms are more efficient producers of goods and services, but that contracting frictions mean that firms do not internalize the government's objective function. But perhaps, for some tasks, the government can actually be more productively efficient? We study this question through an experiment in Chennai, India, where the government randomly selected neighborhoods to have property tax assessments determined by private firms contracted by the government, rather than government tax inspectors. We show that inspections by government tax inspectors yielded almost double the increase in tax revenue as those done by private firms. They were also more accurate, as judged by comparing new assessments to independent assessments done by third-party surveyors we hired. Difficulties contracting with the government discouraged many competent firms from bidding. Perhaps as a result, government inspectors had higher skills and put in more effort than the workers at the private firms. Importantly, the government inspectors also had more authority to enter properties, which may be hard to transfer even to higher quality firms. The results suggest that the limits to government outsourcing may go beyond multitasking issues.

title: Revisiting The Keynesian Investment Demand Function
affiliations: University of Brasilia and University of Brasília (UnB)

detail.title: Revisiting The Keynesian Investment Demand Function
detail.abstract: This paper revisits the Keynesian investment demand function by critically examining whether money-centered, causal-sequential interpretations originating with Keynes, Lerner, and Davidson are theoretically equivalent to Tobin's q-theoretic, simultaneous-equations framework. After clarifying the distinction between the marginal efficiency of capital and the marginal efficiency of investment and restating the Keynesian causal ordering in which the money rate of interest conditions investment and income, the paper contrasts this approach with Tobin's Wicksellian model, where investment responds to asset valuations and long-run equilibrium is anchored by a natural marginal productivity compatible with full employment. We argue that Davidson's claimed precedence and equivalence with q-theory cannot be sustained: the two approaches rest on distinct causal architectures, imply different long-run equilibria, and assign different primacy to money, expectations, productivity, and employment. Incorporating recent theoretical advances on irreversibility, uncertainty, financial frictions, and the rise of intangible capital, the paper shows why valuation signals and low interest rates can coexist with muted investment and "investment-less growth." The analysis highlights the continuing relevance of Keynesian causal ordering and underscores policy levers-expectations management, balance-sheet strength, and institutional design-that are central to sustaining investment in contemporary economies.

title: Beliefs about Government Debt Valuation and Sustainability
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Beliefs about Government Debt Valuation and Sustainability
detail.abstract:
What ultimately supports the market value of U.S. government debt? We measure valuation frameworks: the perceived channels that back debt value. We survey bond investors, registered voters, and economics or finance graduate-degree holders, asking them to allocate debt value across six sources derived from open-ended answers and the literature. Global safe-asset demand and permanent rollover together account for almost half of perceived value in every group, so debt value heavily relies on investor absorption rather than on government resources. Future primary surpluses, the textbook debt backing, receive about 16% even among the graduate-trained; roughly one-third say they provide little or no support. Allocations concentrate within respondents but disperse across them, forming belief archetypes that vary little with fiscal knowledge. A model shows why belief elicitation matters: identical debt quantities and price schedules can conceal differences in saleable public backing and stress-resilient demand, and therefore in debt sustainability. Concern about debt sustainability is widespread, and all three groups put the ten-year crisis odds near 50%. However, among respondents expressing concern, 90% of voters report that it is not decisive in their voting decisions, and 72% of investors report no concrete portfolio change.

title: The Middle Corridor in 2026: Route Choice and U.S. Compliance Risk

detail.title: The Middle Corridor in 2026: Route Choice and U.S. Compliance Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Middle Corridor is not a route-wide compliance-risk category. This brief evaluates the corridor through commodity, transaction, control-point and U.S.-nexus analysis rather than assigning one risk level to a geography. Kazakhstan is used as the principal quantitative case. A cross-match of Kazakhstan-reported exports to Russia against the 50-code BIS Common High Priority List shows that, in January-June 2026, the constructed basket fell approximately 5.6 per cent year on year while HS 851762 (communication and network apparatus) rose 138.8 per cent and reached 45.4 per cent of the basket. Aggregate decline can therefore conceal product-level escalation. Kyrgyzstan provides a regulator-tested comparator: Council Regulation (EU) 2026/506 applied Article 12f to CN 8457 10 and 8517 62 after the EU reported sharp anomalies in first-ten-months 2025 trade. The comparison does not establish Kazakhstan circumvention. Import-side testing also rejects a uniform China→Kazakhstan→Russia explanation: sourcing patterns differ materially by commodity, and reported supplier country is not actual origin. Aggregate evidence is therefore an escalation signal, not transaction tracing. The most consequential control points arise when legal entity, custody, documentation, destination, product identity, origin or processing information, or the payment chain materially changes. U.S. exposure likewise differs by nexus: export control, sanctions, banking, customs and tariff, investment, policy and strategic supply are separate analytical variables. The practical implication is differentiated transaction controls, not generic corridor or country derisking.

title: Short-Run Impacts of SNAP Restriction Waivers on Beverage Purchases
affiliations: University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business - Department of Economics and University of Georgia - Department of Public Administration and Policy

detail.title: Short-Run Impacts of SNAP Restriction Waivers on Beverage Purchases
detail.abstract:
Ten states implemented Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Food Restriction Waivers to restrict purchases of sugary beverages with SNAP funds for the first time in program history in 2026. We estimate the short-run impact of these waivers using a new panel dataset of household beverage purchases. For the average SNAP household, these waivers decrease soda purchases by 13 percent with persistent effects for up to two months after implementation. For inframarginal SNAP households, these waivers decrease soda purchases by 18.5 percent. These findings are inconsistent with the predictions of traditional demand theory and suggest that behavioral models incorporating mental accounting and labeling better characterize consumer responses to SNAP purchase restrictions.

title: Identifying Policy Causal Effects from Rule Changes
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Identifying Policy Causal Effects from Rule Changes
detail.abstract:
Recent applied work has used interacted local projections to study how the propagation of macroeconomic shocks changes with the policy regime. We characterize the estimand of such strategies and relate it to the policy shock literature. Our main result is a set of conditions on the regressors and underlying data-generating process under which those two approaches are equivalent in the nature of their estimand, with both identifying slices of the same space of policy dynamic causal effects. Since policy is inherently high-dimensional, however, the two approaches generically recover different slices of that space. For example, for monetary policy, standard shocks tend to deliver the effects of transitory policy rate changes, while looking across policy regimes instead isolates gradual, more forward guidance-like policy treatments.

title: Declining Occupations and Career Outcomes in the United States
affiliations: Institute for Social Research, Norway, University of New Mexico - Institute for Social Research, Wellesley College and Harvard University - Entrepreneurial Management Unit

detail.title: Declining Occupations and Career Outcomes in the United States
detail.abstract:
We study long-run career consequences of initial employment in an occupation that subsequently declines. Linking the 2000 Decennial Census to US administrative employment and earnings records through 2020, we follow more than 2.4 million workers. Employment in an occupation that contracts by at least 25 percent is associated with about 5 percent lower cumulative earnings despite slightly more quarters worked. The earnings differential closely matches evidence from Sweden and Norway, although employment adjustment differs. Occupational mobility is substantial but incomplete, while children’s later occupational destinations are much less tied to their household heads’ 2000 occupational-growth categories.

title: Introduction to the Symposium on Measuring the Rule of Law: Contestation, Politics, and Policy
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley Law School and University of California, Berkeley - School of Law

detail.title: Introduction to the Symposium on Measuring the Rule of Law: Contestation, Politics, and Policy

publicationDetails.detailsText: American Journal of International Law Unbound (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract:
The demand for rule of law measurement is widespread and consequential. International organizations rank countries by their adherence to the rule of law, investors and firms price political risk around it, development agencies condition funding on it, and the European Union has tied billions of euros in disbursements to it. At the same time, data-manipulation scandals and political contestation have intensified longstanding concerns about how these measures are constructed and used. In 2021, following allegations of corruption and reviews documenting data irregularities, the World Bank discontinued its Doing Business report. The essays in this symposium examine other threats to rule of law measurement: conceptual slippage, directional bias, legal multiplicity, strategic responses by measured governments, and the omission of legally consequential practices that are difficult to observe. With rule of law decline widely documented across Western democracies, the need to examine, improve, and develop alternatives to standard measures has become urgent.

This symposium brings together scholars who have been thinking about measurement, existing rule of law indices, and their policy implications. The essays combine conceptual analysis, empirical critique, legal ethnography, and systematic interviewing. They connect measurement choices to development policy, investment decisions, treaty compliance, executive power, judicial independence, and the European Union’s response to democratic backsliding among its member states.

title: Do Children Derail Women from the CEO Track?
affiliations: and University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Do Children Derail Women from the CEO Track?
detail.abstract:
Gender disparities in becoming a CEO are pronounced, and women who become CEOs, especially of large firms, are less likely to have children or be married. We study the effects of children and marriage on becoming a CEO, using longitudinal administrative data covering the universe of tax-registered firms in Costa Rica, matched to universal civil registry records that provide the timing of childbirth and marriage. We find that first childbirth is followed by a persistent decline in women’s probability of becoming a CEO, but no comparable decline for men and some evidence that CEO attainment rises. Marriage displays a different but still divergent pattern: it is associated with higher subsequent CEO attainment for men, but little change for women. Changes around childbirth account for a substantial share of the overall gender difference in CEO rates. Finally, we find evidence consistent with household specialization as a potential mechanism. Around marriage and first childbirth, women’s formal employment, earnings, and share of household earnings decline, while men become more central to household earnings as their partners reduce formal employment.

title: The Cov-lite Liquidity Advantage, Regulatory Pressures, and the Evolution of the Leveraged Loan Market
affiliations: Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business and Ohio State University (OSU) - Fisher College of Business

detail.title: The Cov-lite Liquidity Advantage, Regulatory Pressures, and the Evolution of the Leveraged Loan Market
detail.abstract:
Following the global financial crisis (GFC), regulators made it harder for banks to retain leveraged loan exposure. We conjecture their actions increased the share of leveraged loan issuances with no maintenance covenants (cov-lite loans) because such loans are easier to sell. We find that, post-GFC, the share of cov-lite loan issuance increased more for banks facing stricter regulation, failing to pass a stress test outright, or exhibiting greater vulnerability to the severely adverse stress test scenario. We show that, as expected from theory, cov-lite loans have a liquidity advantage that lowers their credit spread and is higher for private firms.

title: "Beat the Market" Revisited An Independent Replication and Statistical Audit of an Intraday Momentum Strategy

detail.title: "Beat the Market" Revisited An Independent Replication and Statistical Audit of an Intraday Momentum Strategy

contentType.other: Revisited Independent Replication and Statistical Audit

detail.abstract: Zarattini, Aziz, and Barbon report that a simple intraday time-series momentum strategy applied to SPY produced a total return of 1,985%, an annualized return of 19.6%, and a Sharpe Ratio of 1.33 from May 2007 through April 2024. This paper performs an independent replication and a post-publication extension using approximately 2.6 million one-minute SPY observations from TradeStation spanning January 2000 through August 2026. After reconciling two material implementation details against the authors’ published Python reference code—the use of typical-price Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP) and VWAP confirmation at entry—the original result is reproduced almost exactly: 1,989% total return and a Sharpe Ratio of 1.317 on the paper window under the closest paper-matching convention. The independent update also closely reproduces the authors’ September 2025 FAQ update: 2024 returns are 31.8% versus their 32.2%, and January–August 2025 returns are 1.4% versus their 1.0%. The longer sample changes the interpretation, but not in the simple form suggested by the pooled May 2024–August 2026 Sharpe of 0.35. Disaggregating the post-publication path reveals two sharply different regimes. Under a Q24-comparable monthly convention, May 2024–29 August 2025 returns 19.3% with Sharpe 1.057; using the exact first trading day after the 10 May 2024 publication, the corresponding return is 23.3% with Sharpe 1.284. By contrast, the subsequent 2 September 2025–14 August 2026 stretch returns -8.1% with Sharpe -0.461. Thus the evidence does not support a narrative of immediate post-publication alpha decay; it supports a strong initial post-publication period followed by a materially weak recent regime. A systematic search then evaluates asymmetric short filters, relative-volume sizing, volatility overlays, persistence filters, profit locks, breakeven rules, trade caps, daily loss limits, VWAP-dominance rules, intraday decay, regime overlays, and performance-based overlays. Only a small subset survives the consistent multi-window standard applied during the extension stage. The final frozen selected specification reaches a valid-period Sharpe Ratio of 1.274, a -14.8% maximum drawdown, and a 2110.6% total return over 2000–2026, while deliberately sacrificing terminal wealth relative to the baseline. To address multiple testing, a research ledger of 129 trials is reconstructed and 80 SPY search alternatives are identified. Combinatorially Symmetric Cross-Validation yields a Probability of Backtest Overfitting of 38.49% under the historical convention and 40.87% on a common-valid sample. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio of the final candidate, using 𝑁 = 80 as the primary multiple-testing count, is 99.999986796%. These statistics support a strong retrospective edge but do not provide a genuine prospective validation because the search was adaptive and the 2024–2026 data were observed during model development. The correct next experiment is therefore not another retrospective optimization, but the passage of time with frozen parameters.

title: The Global Transition – The Impact of Demographics and AI on Economic Power
affiliations: Chapman University, Boston University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: The Global Transition – The Impact of Demographics and AI on Economic Power
detail.abstract:
This study deploys a multi-region, dynamic life-cycle, general equilibrium model to assess demography’s impact, through the course of this century, on global development. Our model’s 17 regions encompass more than 150 countries comprising 99% of the world’s population. Output is produced with three labor skill groups and internationally-mobile capital, with each country deciding annually whether to adopt its frontier automation technology. Our model features region-specific fiscal policy, TFP growth, and idiosyncratic mortality. Agents live for 100 years, first as children, then as workers, and then as retirees. Work and saving decisions are governed by CES preferences. Lifespan is uncertain, but there are no annuities apart from state pensions. Hence, bequests, while significant, are unintended. Our fertility, mortality, and net immigration rates are region- and age-specific and align fully with the UN’s projections. To illustrate demographics’ power to impact the global transition, we simulate our model under the UN’s markedly different demographic projections for 2017 and 2024. The 2024 forecast is particularly pessimistic about China’s fertility prospects. Both projections produce very substantial global aging, a major global capital glut producing very low long-run real capital returns. The latest forecast entails 10% lower global GDP in 2100 and far higher payroll tax rates to fund old-age benefits. Most important, it entails a major change in the course of economic hegemony with China’s 2100 global GDP share falling from 25.6% to 14.9% and the US share rising from 11.2% to 14.4%. Our results are sensitive. Should the US eliminate all future immigration, its 14.4% global 2100 GDP share would drop to 9.2%. And were global fertility to follow the UN’s low variant, 2100 world output would be one third, not one tenth lower. The level and division of global output is also highly sensitive to the speed at which AI expands frontier technologies. Accelerated AU/AI – 4x faster-than-recent growth in capital’s share through 2050 – or Transformative AU/AI – 10x faster capital-share growth – reinforce demographic forces, ensuring long-run US economic hegemony. Indeed, Transformative AI combined with 2024 demographics implies US and Chinese 2100 global GDP shares of 25.3% and 16.9%, respectively. And not withstanding its considerable technological catch up, the US retains, based on our calibration, a technological edge over China throughout the century.
