detail.abstract: The complexity of business environments in developing economies such as Nigeria has intensified demand for intelligent decisionsupport systems capable of interpreting dynamic economic conditions and assisting Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in strategic planning. This study presents the design and implementation of a Hybrid Economic Expert System that integrates rule-based reasoning with machine learning analytics to support decision-making in taxation, compliance, funding, pricing, forecasting, and policy evaluation. The system was designed against three stated objectives: at least 85% accuracy in economic forecasting within a simulated environment, coverage of at least five distinct economic decision scenarios, and a user satisfaction rate of at least 80% in usability testing. Development followed a hybrid of Object-Oriented Analysis and Design Methodology (OOADM) and Agile methodology, decomposing the system into input, inference, output, and user interface components. The inference engine combines deterministic rule-based models for policy and tax computation with predictive machine learning models for trend forecasting. The system was implemented using Django, ReactJS, and SQLite, employing the Gemini and Hugging Face APIs for natural-language explanation of analytical outputs. A functional prototype covering nine advisory modules was completed and deployed for local testing. Scope of results reported. This report documents the design, architecture, and implementation of the prototype. The formal evaluation against the stated accuracy and satisfaction objectives has not yet been conducted; the test plan and instruments are specified in Chapter Four, and results will be reported on completion. No performance figures are claimed in advance of that evaluation.

title: Libertarian Realism and the Management of Hydroelectric Rents: Lessons from Norway
affiliations: University of Tromsø - The Arctic University of Norway - School of Business and Economics and Western Norway University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Libertarian Realism and the Management of Hydroelectric Rents: Lessons from Norway

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: This paper develops libertarian realism: a form of libertarianism that takes seriously the constraints of human nature and the practical burdens of maintaining even a minimal state. Freedom from regulation is itself a good, yet high moral motivation is scarce, so the state should remain as small as possible. Its proper role is limited to narrow rules that favor the creation of wealth over zero-sum contests for control. We apply the framework to Norwegian hydroelectric potential, a large publicly owned natural resource. We argue that unregulated private extraction simply transfers a non-produced scarcity rent into private hands and encourages control-seeking rather than creation. The resulting rent is better managed through carefully designed, ownership-anchored market rules than through tax-and-transfer schemes that enlarge an already extensive state. The argument draws on Nozick's entitlement theory and the resource-curse literature, with concrete application to Norwegian electricity markets.

title: Parliament, Sovereignty, and the Lobbies: A Comparative Study of How Pakistan's Pharmaceutical Industry Influences Government Regulation

detail.title: Parliament, Sovereignty, and the Lobbies: A Comparative Study of How Pakistan's Pharmaceutical Industry Influences Government Regulation
detail.abstract: At the heart of parliamentary democracy lies the idea of representation-of the electorate, and therefore of the people. The core claim of that idea is that the legislature works for the benefit of those whom it represents. This paper contends, however, that the sovereignty the people have delegated to Parliament is routinely subverted by covert and overt lobby groups that operate as de facto mafias over the regulatory framework. I use the case of "Big Pharma" in Pakistan as empirical evidence that corporations, among many other actors, exercise coercive control over legislation. Unlike the institutionally recognised lobbying of Western democracies such as the United States, the system of lobbying in Pakistan rests on opaque networks of clientelism, patronage, political financing, and market control. This system prioritises elite interests and diverts legislative intent towards private profit rather than towards regulation in the interest of the majority whom legislators represent. Drawing on political theory, the 2022 Panadol scandal, and a broader analysis of market politics in Pakistan, I conclude that the covert mechanisms of influence at work in Pakistan's legislative politics-distinct from those of Western models-have a catastrophic effect on democratic accountability and public service. The paper integrates a comparative political approach with a legal analysis of the law-making process and a socio-anthropological account of how the Panadol Crisis unfolded, in order to expose the covert system that controls the assemblies from behind the veil.

title: The Structural Rate of Interest
affiliations: University of Turku - Turku School of Economics

detail.title: The Structural Rate of Interest
detail.abstract: This paper introduces and examines a single object: the structural rate of interest, 𝑖 * = 𝐾 𝑀 / [s + 𝑘 𝐴 •(1-s)]. It is the rate at which the economy's total transaction flow capitalises its total wealth, written in terms of three measurable quantities: the velocity of money 𝐾 𝑀 , the share s of money that finances production, and the valuation 𝑘 𝐴 of non-productive wealth relative to the money that circulates it. The rate is derived in four steps from the dual-sector monetary framework of The Economic Wheel, and its properties are established: it is bounded between 𝐾 𝑀 /𝑘 𝐴 and 𝐾 𝑀 , it rises with the productive share and falls with asset valuation, it is invariant to the level of the money stock and of the monetary base-it is a rate of the economy's balance sheet, not of the central bank's-and it is the money-weighted harmonic mean of two sectoral capitalisation rates. Because the productive share obeys a law of motion, the structural rate has dynamics of its own: it drifts toward a long-run value fixed by where the marginal unit of money goes, and it is path-dependent in the two sources of money, so that an easing followed by an equal tightening does not return it to its starting value. The paper then places 𝑖 * among the interest-rate concepts economists already use-Wicksell's natural rate, the filtered r* of Laubach and Williams, the finance-neutral and convenience-yield variants, Keynes's marginal efficiency of capital and Tobin's q, the growth-theoretic rates of Ramsey and the golden rule, and the operational policy, shadow and Taylor-intercept rates-organised by the question each was built to answer, and states precisely where it differs: it is nominal, it is built from stocks rather than from an output gap, it is observable up to one scale parameter, and it is not invariant to monetary policy. Its uses as a stance measure, as a moving anchor in a policy rule, and as an organising concept for balance-sheet statistics are assessed, and a programme of theoretical and empirical research is laid out. The paper contains no estimation; its purpose is to launch the concept in a form that can be tested.

title: Governance Without Peace: How Prosperity Party Rule Deepened Ethiopia's Crisis
affiliations: Bule Hora University

detail.title: Governance Without Peace: How Prosperity Party Rule Deepened Ethiopia's Crisis

declarations.funderStatement: The study didn't get any fund anyone.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the compounding political, institutional, and security crises in Ethiopia under the administration of the Prosperity Party, led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. While the 2018 political transition initially raised hopes for democratic reform and national reconciliation, the administration's consolidation of power has instead coincided with severe state fragility, widespread civil conflict, and institutional decay. This paper analyzes how centralized governance models, the instrumentalization of ethnic federal structures, and aggressive military strategies have deepened polarization rather than resolved historical grievances. By examining key conflict theaters-most notably the devastating conflicts in Tigray and the Amhara region-the study demonstrates how contemporary governance practices prioritize executive dominance at the expense of sustainable peace, human security, and constitutional stability.

title: The Relative Value of Theory and Data
affiliations: Cornell University, Cornell University and Columbia University in the City of New York

detail.title: The Relative Value of Theory and Data
detail.abstract: We develop a framework to study the relative value of theory and data. A decision maker can improve predictions either by acquiring an additional observation or by using reasoning to eliminate competing hypotheses. We characterize the expected marginal value of these two activities and study how their relative importance depends on the amount of available data, prior beliefs, and the statistical distance between competing hypotheses. Our findings suggest that the relationship between the value of theory and the value of data can be quite complex, even in simple settings. In particular, we present a simple example in which the relative value of theory in data-rich environments can be higher than when data are scarce. The relative value of theory can also be nonmonotonic in the amount of available data.

title: State-Sponsored Violence, Structural Marginalization, and the Quest for Survival: Analyzing the Crisis of the Amhara People Under the Administration of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed
affiliations: Bule Hora University

detail.title: State-Sponsored Violence, Structural Marginalization, and the Quest for Survival: Analyzing the Crisis of the Amhara People Under the Administration of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed

declarations.funderStatement: Didn't have any fund partner.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the escalation of state-sponsored violence and structural marginalization targeting the Amhara community in Ethiopia under Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Initially aligned with federal authorities during the northern conflict, the Amhara population has increasingly faced systemic exclusion, targeted extrajudicial operations, and demographic displacement. By examining the institutional mechanics of Ethiopia's ethnic federal structure alongside the Abiy administration's security strategies, this study highlights the transition from localized grievances to a broader humanitarian and political crisis. The analysis assesses how military operations, emergency decrees, and civic disenfranchisement have given rise to popular armed resistance.

title: 2024 Heatwave Exposure and Labour-Market Vulnerability in India: A State-Level Comparative Analysis

detail.title: 2024 Heatwave Exposure and Labour-Market Vulnerability in India: A State-Level Comparative Analysis
detail.abstract: Extreme heat is increasingly becoming an economic and public-health concern in India. Heatwaves can affect workers through physiological stress, reduced work capacity, illness and premature mortality. The consequences may be particularly important in states with large populations employed in heat-exposed activities. This study examines the association between 2024 heatwave exposure, heat-related deaths and the worker population ratio across Indian states and union territories. The study constructs a cross-sectional state-level dataset by combining 2024 heatwave-day and heatrelated mortality information with the 2023-24 Worker Population Ratio (WPR) reported by the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). The final analytical sample consists of 25 states and union territories for which comparable observations were available. Descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation analysis are used. The analysis finds substantial geographical variation in heatwave exposure: heatwave days range from 1 to 39 across the sample. Odisha records the highest number of heatwave days (39), followed by Rajasthan (35), Uttar Pradesh (33) and Bihar (32). Heat-related deaths also vary considerably, with Odisha, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh among the states reporting the highest numbers. The correlation between heatwave days and WPR is negative (r =-0.228), while the correlation between heat-related deaths and WPR is-0.192. These associations are descriptive and do not establish causality. The findings indicate that heat exposure and labour-market vulnerability should be considered jointly in India's climate-adaptation policy. The results support greater integration of heat action plans, occupational health measures, labour-market policies and state-level climate adaptation.

title: Journal of a Dissenter: On History, Philosophy, and Politics, 1996-2025

detail.title: Journal of a Dissenter: On History, Philosophy, and Politics, 1996-2025
detail.abstract: This is a lengthy intellectual journal by a political radical that ranges over a variety of subjects, such as Marxism, capitalism, history, many schools of modern philosophy, psychology, economics, and contemporary American politics. It also includes quite a few 'personal' passages, but I've kept those only because they express common experiences and youthful psychological tendencies. They constitute a 'primary source,' as it were: the perspectives of a fairly characteristic young person in the early 2000s. The journal's most useful content for students might be its many summaries of good historical and philosophical scholarship, especially in its second half. Ultimately, it is a wide-ranging expression of a particular society as refracted through an inquisitive and critical mind, from the ages of 15 to 44.

title: A National Plan for Addressing Alzheimer's Disease
affiliations: The SPRING Institute, , , The Perrin Research Institution and

detail.title: A National Plan for Addressing Alzheimer's Disease
detail.abstract: Alzheimer's research has reached an inflection point. For the first time, disease-modifying therapies exist that can slow cognitive decline, and blood tests can now confirm the disease's underlying pathology in a primary care office rather than a specialty imaging suite. These new innovations have already paved the way for a new future within Alzheimer’s treatment. However, there are still shortcomings within the system. We identify gaps in Alzheimer's research in this paper and provide a comprehensive set of recommendations for the Federal Government to take to address these gaps.

title: The Coordination Wedge: Why Task-Level AI Productivity Does Not Aggregate and What This Means for Artificial Superintelligence

detail.title: The Coordination Wedge: Why Task-Level AI Productivity Does Not Aggregate and What This Means for Artificial Superintelligence
detail.abstract: Controlled studies report task-level productivity gains of approximately 15 to 56 per cent, yet the leading task-based aggregation places the cumulative ten-year total factor productivity effect of artificial intelligence at only 0.55 to 0.71 per cent. This paper argues that the contrast contains two analytically distinct objects. Most of the headline gap is the mechanical consequence of cost-share weighting and task selection. The economically important remainder is an organisational conversion failure: the share of a technically feasible task saving that firms do not realise in production. I formalise that remainder as a coordination wedge. Extending the task-based automation framework, I treat organisational capital as an essential, rival and slowly accumulated complement to non-rival AI capability. The resulting first-order identity separates exposure, technical saving and integration, while a distinct measurement equation explains why true and measured productivity may diverge during an investment cycle. Under an explicit capability-saturation path condition, the direct contribution of further capability improvement converges to zero. The remaining growth contributions arise from expansion of the exposed task space and accumulation of organisational capital. This conditional result is weaker than an unconditional technological limit, but stronger empirically because its assumptions are stated and falsifiable. The framework yields three practical implications. First, integration should be estimated rather than assumed, and the paper proposes an absorption-ratio statistic for that purpose. Secondly, a coordination account and a capital-misallocation account make different predictions for within-industry productivity dispersion. Thirdly, where capability supply is contestable, durable rents migrate towards scarce complements such as organisational capital, proprietary process data, energy interconnection and regulatory access. The policy priority is therefore not capability governance alone, but an integrated programme of measurement, interoperability and absorptive capacity.

title: "Differences Between Constitutional Law and Administrative Law": A Comparative Analysis

detail.title: "Differences Between Constitutional Law and Administrative Law": A Comparative Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, professional, financial, or other relationships with individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently by the author and received no financial support or external funding from any individual, organization, institution, or funding agency.

contentType.other: It is unpublish research paper which i have written during seventh semesters of BALLB

detail.abstract: The present paper is an attempt at a thorough study of the difference between constitutional law and administrative law, both of which are important branches of public law that constitute the core of any modern legal system. Although both of these fields of law aim at regulating the relations between the state and the individual, they differ greatly in terms of their scope, purposes, and methods of functioning. Constitutional law defines the basic legal framework of the state and the system of separation of powers, as well as the fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens, thus being the supreme source of law that all others derive from. On the contrary, administrative law concerns itself with the structure, competences, and activities of administrative bodies and deals primarily with bureaucratic governance. The paper will explore the historical background, juristic theories, and institutions of both branches of law, paying special attention to the way in which constitutional law serves as the basis for legitimation and accountability, while administrative law takes care of the efficiency of state activities and the rule of procedure. It ends with the claim that comprehension of their relationship is necessary for ensuring the rule of law, democratic accountability, and the maintenance of a proper balance between state power and individual rights in a constitutional democracy.

title: IP Rights in the Metaverse: Emerging Challenges for Copyright and Trademark Law

detail.title: IP Rights in the Metaverse: Emerging Challenges for Copyright and Trademark Law
detail.abstract: The metaverse is a changing virtual ecosystem that has changed how people interact online by creating a strong economy for virtual goods including art, clothes, and real estate. This change makes it hard for intellectual property (IP) rights to keep up, especially under India's Copyright Act of 1957 and Trade Marks Act of 1999, which were established for physical commodities. It's easy to copy digital works like avatars or virtual designs, but copyright difficulties can come up because it's not always apparent who owns them due to platform conditions or blockchain-based non-fungible tokens (NFTs). When fake virtual items with real-world brand logos confuse customers, trademark issues might happen, such in the case of Hermès International v. Rothschild. It is hard to enforce because users are anonymous, platforms work across borders, and licensing is not clear. In India, there are laws that exist, but they haven't been tried in virtual environments yet. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, makes it hard to figure out whose jurisdiction applies, and the Information Technology Act, 2000, doesn't stretch outside India's borders very far. Platforms that are protected by safe harbour laws often put expansion ahead of IP protection, which makes creators vulnerable. This paper talks about these problems, compares Indian laws to laws from other countries, and shows how important it is to change the legislation. It suggests broadening the definitions of intellectual property (IP) to cover virtual goods, setting up digital courts, and requiring platforms to put in place strong IP protection systems. India can protect creators and brands in the metaverse by filling in gaps in ownership, jurisdiction, and enforcement. This will encourage innovation and trust in this new digital frontier.

title: Generativity Governance of Open Knowledge Propagation: A Preliminary Discussion of Events, Relations, and Conditions under Nonlinear and Multi-Entity Causation

detail.title: Generativity Governance of Open Knowledge Propagation: A Preliminary Discussion of Events, Relations, and Conditions under Nonlinear and Multi-Entity Causation
detail.abstract: Once a body of knowledge enters an open commons it propagates through a system of many heterogeneous participants, in which copies are modified, recombined, implemented, automated, commercialised and redeployed, and in which the conditions of further propagation are altered by the propagation itself. Where harm eventually appears in such a system, the reconstruction of a complete causal history is frequently unavailable, and the legal apparatus of attribution, which requires an antecedent subject, an acyclic chain, a datable injury and a proportionate contribution, is correspondingly difficult to apply. This paper asks what governance remains possible when complete causal reconstruction is unavailable, and what form it should take so that it neither waits for a proof it cannot obtain nor suppresses the propagation it exists to protect. The answer developed here places three objects under governance in place of one. Events supply observable points at which duties may attach, records may be created and interventions may occur. Relations supply the structure through which a local disturbance is amplified or damped, and which determines whether an event has consequences at all. Conditions supply the settings, defaults, terms and incentives under which further generation proceeds, and they operate on whole populations at once where an event duty operates on a single act. The paper defines generativity governance as the governance of these three, and states at the outset that the term names an object of governance and never an objective of maximisation. The framework's instruments are matched to its objects. Event duties take the form of requirement sets attaching to classes of consequential transformation, with capability transformation identified as the class that existing law, whose triggers are largely transactional, does not reach. Relational duties are supervisory and bound amplification in place of adjudicating contributions. Condition duties are structural and operate through defaults, terms and infrastructure. A provenance ledger is examined as evidence infrastructure, together with the two limits that govern its use: the schema of recordable events is itself chosen by an interested party, and the population a voluntary ledger reaches is correlated with willingness to comply. Post-hoc attribution is retained as a backstop for deliberate misconduct and clear negligence, and is shown to be admissible at an event only as compliance with the requirements in force there, never as a share of a distant outcome.

title: The Geography of Green Capital: Why Clean Investment Concentrates in Some Economies and Bypasses Others

detail.title: The Geography of Green Capital: Why Clean Investment Concentrates in Some Economies and Bypasses Others
detail.abstract:
The report argues that the global clean‑energy transition is shaped less by technology and more by the structural realities of international finance. Although renewable technologies have achieved dramatic cost declines, green investment remains overwhelmingly concentrated in advanced economies. Emerging markets—despite strong resource endowments and rising energy demand—face systematically higher costs of capital, driven by sovereign risk premiums, currency volatility, shallow financial markets, and institutional constraints. As the document states, “the green transition in emerging markets is not bottlenecked by a lack of natural resources or viable technology, but by the gravitational pull of advanced‑economy bond yields and the frictions of global capital markets.”

The report uses a quantitative macro‑systems framework to model how monetary policy, risk pricing, technological diffusion, and grid infrastructure interact to shape the geography of green capital. It shows that while learning rates and cost‑curve compressions have made solar and wind globally competitive, localized supply‑chain frictions and underfunded grid systems prevent many emerging economies from reaching system‑level parity.

Regional case studies—including Brazil, Chile, South Africa, India, Vietnam, Indonesia, Mexico, Kenya, the Philippines, and Colombia—demonstrate recurring structural bottlenecks: currency mismatch between PPAs and debt, curtailment risks from weak transmission networks, and elevated WACC levels that erase the natural cost advantages of renewables. As one repeated section notes, “institutional investors must navigate these localized frictions, which often inflate the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) to levels that challenge grid parity.”

The report concludes that closing the global green‑investment gap requires aggressive de‑risking architectures, large‑scale blended finance, sovereign guarantees, FX‑hedging facilities, and reforms to multilateral development banks. Without compressing risk premiums for emerging markets, capital will continue to pool in the Global North, undermining both climate goals and long‑term development trajectories.

title: The Quiet Power of Culture Corners
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Quiet Power of Culture Corners
detail.abstract: How, dedicated spaces and micro activities shape high performing workplaces A POV (3 pages) By: Soumyadeep Nag If you've worked through a stretch of back to back meetings, you know the feeling, your brain is technically on, but your attention is scattered, and the small task feels heavier than it should. Now imagine that, between two intense calls, you step into a small room where a colleague is softly strumming a guitar, someone else is trying a five minute shuffle step, and a few people are simply laughing. Nothing mandatory. Just a brief, human pause. You return to your desk and almost surprisingly you're clearer, kinder, and faster. That's the premise of what I call a culture corner: a deliberate space (and permission) for low stakes cultural activities, music, micro dance breaks, games, creative prompts, community Rituals. In many organizations, these are treated as optional nice to haves. But the evidence Suggests they can be quiet performance tools because they change how people think, connect, And recover. Below is a research grounded argument for why cultural micro activities and dedicated creative rooms can meaningfully influence workplace outcomes without turning the office into a carnival.

title: Collective Mental Health Intelligence: A Behavioral Theory of Institutional Knowledge Production
affiliations: Duke Kunshan University and Duke Kunshan University

detail.title: Collective Mental Health Intelligence: A Behavioral Theory of Institutional Knowledge Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: Universities and other institutions are increasingly expected to address the mental health of their populations, yet they possess remarkably little reliable knowledge about it. Higher education constitutes a strategic setting for confronting this gap: universities combine bounded, digitally reachable populations and explicit dutyof-care expectations with the same knowledge deficit that afflicts institutions generally. Existing routes to visibility-help-seeking records, episodic surveys, and, more recently, passive digital sensing-fail in characteristic ways: the first observes only those who overcome barriers to disclosure, the second trades temporal resolution for representativeness, and the third acquires information without the cooperation that renders institutional knowledge legitimate. This paper argues that these failures share a common root: population mental health is a hidden institutional reality, a condition that is consequential for institutional action but knowable only through the voluntary cooperation of the individuals who experience it. Knowledge about such conditions is not collected; it must first be behaviorally produced. We develop the concept of collective mental health intelligence (CMHI): an institution's capacity to generate reliable, timely, and actionable population-level knowledge of mental well-being through sustained voluntary contributions of sensitive personal information. Drawing on collective action theory, stigma research, privacy theory, institutional trust research, and research on psychological safety, we specify three behavioral conditions-participation, authentic disclosure, and sustained engagementresting on a foundation of institutional legitimacy, and derive falsifiable propositions about their antecedents. We then analyze the governance tensions internal to the construct, including the trade-off between anonymity and longitudinal insight, the limits of aggregate-only knowledge under a duty of care, and selection bias as an equity problem. The framework repositions population mental health monitoring as a problem of knowledge production and governance rather than measurement alone.

title: Book Review: Unsettling Data Mapping Labour and Land against the Representationalist Legal Form
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Book Review: Unsettling Data Mapping Labour and Land against the Representationalist Legal Form
detail.abstract: This review examines Dilan Dagaz's Unsettling Data Mapping Labour and Land against the Representationalist Legal Form. It focuses on the book's critique of the representationalist legal form through which law constructs data as a distinct and governable object. The review considers three related interventions: how representationalism obscures data's relation to land, how it depoliticises land by rendering it passive, and how data governance constructs land as a resource for extraction. Drawing attention to the book's engagement with Indigenous Place-Thought, the review highlights its reconceptualisation of data through relations among human and unhuman agencies, labour and land. It argues that the book's significance for socio-legal scholarship lies in showing how the legal construction of data can conceal the material and political relations that make contemporary data economies possible.

title: The Architecture of Climate Finance

detail.title: The Architecture of Climate Finance
detail.abstract:
The report argues that the global net‑zero transition is fundamentally a macro‑systems challenge rather than a problem of capital scarcity. Although global financial assets exceed $400 trillion, climate finance remains under‑deployed by more than $3 trillion per year, largely due to structural, institutional, and risk‑pricing failures. The document identifies three systemic bottlenecks: (1) over‑reliance on constrained public balance sheets, (2) severe mispricing of sovereign and FX risk in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs), and (3) inefficient financing pathways for early‑stage climate technologies.

Climate finance must evolve from fragmented project‑level funding into a coordinated global asset class. The report shows—using examples such as solar PV, wind, and lithium‑ion batteries—that targeted public investment can trigger cost‑curve compression and self‑sustaining private‑sector adoption. However, replicating this success in harder‑to‑abate sectors and high‑risk geographies requires blended finance, sovereign guarantees, and MDB balance‑sheet reform.

Key mechanisms include first‑loss tranches, FX‑risk mitigation facilities, Article 6 carbon trading, and aggressive public procurement for deep‑tech commercialization. The report concludes that the climate transition is an architectural challenge: only by restructuring MDB capital adequacy frameworks, standardizing carbon markets, and mobilizing private institutional capital at scale can the world close the multi‑trillion‑dollar climate finance gap.

“Mobilizing the capital required to re‑engineer global energy, transport, and agricultural architectures is not fundamentally a challenge of absolute capital scarcity; global financial assets exceed $400 trillion.”

“Blended finance—the strategic use of development finance and philanthropic funds to mobilize private capital flows to emerging markets—emerges as the critical lever for global progress.”

title:
Structural Support in Distributed Human Systems

A Relational Theory Of Warrant Preservation Across Transformation, Authority, and Continuation

detail.title:
Structural Support in Distributed Human Systems

A Relational Theory Of Warrant Preservation Across Transformation, Authority, and Continuation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, professional, or financial interests that could have influenced this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Human systems routinely distribute observation, interpretation, documentation, authority, decision, action, consequence, and correction across different people, roles, records, and institutional locations. This distribution creates a problem that is not reducible to information loss, individual error, invalid inference, or missing provenance. A downstream claim or action can remain locally defensible while the relation that once warranted its use has changed, narrowed, or disappeared. Building on the relational support condition developed in The Architecture of Human Systems, this paper refines structural support as a claim-and use-relative construct for analyzing that problem. Structural support is the set of warrant-relevant relations and distinctions that must remain sufficiently preserved for a downstream claim, decision, authority, or continuation to remain proportionate to what supports it. The framework identifies support-bearing dimensions including source, epistemic status, scope, provenance, uncertainty, reference, level, and return path. It develops structural overextension as the central failure condition: downstream consequential use continues as if required support were intact even when one or more warrant-relevant conditions have not survived passage. The paper distinguishes structural support from factual accuracy, formal validity, information quantity, provenance alone, procedural legitimacy, and organizational coherence. It then develops authority-support alignment, revalidation, correction, and inherited continuation as consequences of the same construct. A minimal formal representation defines a claim-and userelative support envelope: the set of consequential uses still warranted by the support conditions that remain preserved. It further distinguishes the mechanisms of support loss from the locations at which loss can occurduring formation, passage, or continuation-and proposes experimental and field designs capable of discriminating structural support from generic information loss, perceived coherence, local correctness, and ordinary provenance awareness. The resulting theory is intentionally narrow: it does not claim that all organizational failure is structural-support failure. Its distinctive contribution is the particular claim-and userelative support-envelope model developed here: an account of which consequential uses remain warranted, how recurrent mechanisms of support loss differ from the locations at which loss occurs, and how authority can be asymmetrically repaired by narrowing use without pretending that missing support has been restored.

title: African Personhood in a Digital Age: Ethics, Identity and Human Flourishing

detail.title: African Personhood in a Digital Age: Ethics, Identity and Human Flourishing
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technology across Africa has restructured communication, identity formation, social interaction, and moral life. Social media platforms, artificial intelligence systems, and digital economies now fundamentally shape how individuals understand themselves and relate to others. While these modern technological developments have created new opportunities for expression, education, and social mobility, they have also produced moral fragmentation, online aggression, performative identity, and the decline of communal bonds that have historically been central to African ethical life. The aim of this paper is to examine the contemporary crisis of identity and dignity in Africa through the framework of African personhood. This article uses a conceptual-philosophical methodology. The paper argues that African conceptions of personhoodspecifically, personhood as moral achievement, dignity as relational and identity as communally constituted-provide substantive ethical resources for responding to four specific crises produced by digital modernity: performative identity, online dehumanization, algorithmic injustice, and digital colonialism. The study further engages emerging scholarship on African AI ethics, particularly the relational ethics framework developed by Abeba Birhane, and situates the argument within postcolonial critiques of digital power advanced by Sabelo Ndlovu-Gatsheni and Nick Couldry. In response to these crises, the paper recommends a renewed African humanism, grounded in relational ethics, communal responsibility, and moral recognition, as a framework for human flourishing in a digital age. It also recommends that religious communities, families, and cultural institutions develop strategies for using digital technologies in ways that strengthen, rather than dissolve, the relational bonds through which persons are formed.

title: Managing Online Content Platforms with AI-Generated Content: Content Amplification and Disclosure Enforcement
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics,  and University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) - School of Management

detail.title: Managing Online Content Platforms with AI-Generated Content: Content Amplification and Disclosure Enforcement
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Online content platforms face a growing governance challenge when creators use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) without disclosure. We study how the platform's content amplification, which expands content reach, interacts with creators' manual effort, GenAI use, and disclosure choices. We compare two enforcement approaches: relabeling, which attaches a label of AI-generated content (AIGC) when nondisclosure is detected, and penalizing, which removes verified noncompliant content and truncates its remaining circulation and lifetime revenue. 

Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretic model of a content platform and a representative creator. The platform decides whether to amplify the content, while the creator chooses manual effort, GenAI effort, and whether to disclose GenAI use. Undisclosed AIGC that escapes the platform's detection exposes the platform to external regulatory sanctions. We find that more effective amplification encourages hybrid human-AI production when AIGC aversion is mild but can induce a switch to manual production when aversion becomes stronger. Consequently, the platform's amplification incentive can be non-monotonic in AIGC aversion. In addition, better detection of AIGC can either help or hurt the platform, depending on regulatory pressure, and stricter external regulation may reduce both platform and creator profits by inducing the platform to withdraw amplification. Comparing the two enforcement approaches, we find penalizing can induce truthful disclosure and may improve outcomes for the platform, creator, and users simultaneously when AIGC aversion is mild and amplification e!ectiveness is intermediate, although neither approach dominates uniformly.  

Managerial implications: Platforms should jointly design content amplification, AIGC detection, and disclosure enforcement. The preferred enforcement approach depends on user attitudes toward AIGC, amplification effectiveness, and regulatory pressure. Regulators should also account for platforms' endogenous responses, because stricter regulation may suppress amplification without eliminating undisclosed AIGC and can thereby reduce both platform and creator payoffs.

title: Riemann Hypothesis: Loop-Theoretic Approach

detail.title: Riemann Hypothesis: Loop-Theoretic Approach
detail.abstract: This proposes a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) in the operator language of Loop Theory (Isong, 2026). Working inside the completed integer-prime archive, primes are identified as transverse-silent fundamentals, composite integers as recombinant states with nonzero dependency depth, and the critical line Re(s)=1/2 is derived as the Identity-Reflection locus of the archive's Balance REFLECT operator, rather than assumed. A quaternionic spectral signature is then used to classify every possible spectral event-ordinary points, false alarms on the critical line, trivial zeros, off-balance candidates, and genuine non-trivial zeros-and Loop Theory's Exclusion Principles dictates that a genuine non-trivial zero is transverse-silent and balance-admissible, and therefore lies on the critical line.

title: A Reproducible Geospatial Framework for Equity-Focused Transit Service Gap Analysis
affiliations: , Syracuse University - School of Information Studies and George Mason University - Environmental and Infrastructure Engineering

detail.title: A Reproducible Geospatial Framework for Equity-Focused Transit Service Gap Analysis
detail.abstract: Public transit serves as critical infrastructure for urban equity, yet service is often weakest where transit-dependent populations are most concentrated. This study develops a reproducible geospatial framework for transit desert identification integrating: (1) a Composite Public Transit Accessibility (CPTA) score synthesizing nine supply-side metrics; (2) a Transit Dependency Index (TDI) estimating demand through equityweighted demographic factors aligned with Title VI requirements in the US; and (3) Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) clustering to identify statistically significant service gaps. We validate the framework across four U.S. metropolitan areas (Baltimore, Philadelphia, Nashville, and Dallas) representing diverse transit systems and urban forms. Results reveal 18-20% of Census tracts in each city qualify as transit deserts with pronounced demographic disparities: minority population concentrations are 14.7 to 35.2 percentage points higher in transit deserts. The open-source pipeline enables practitioners to apply this framework to other metropolitan areas, supporting evidencebased transit planning that centers equity in service allocation decisions.

title:
Expansive Public Service Delivery: 
Advancing Public Value Governance
affiliations: , Northern Illinois University and Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Public Affairs

detail.title:
Expansive Public Service Delivery: 
Advancing Public Value Governance

declarations.ethicsApproval: Human Subjects Approval: All interview participants provided informed consent (Protocol #18358, Indiana University).

detail.abstract:
Public administration has traditionally emphasized the normative ideal that public
agencies have a responsibility to improve the lives of communities through public service delivery.
We turn to public libraries to explore possibilities for what we call Expansive Public Service
Delivery. Expansive Public Service Delivery is defined by a mission to serve all, professional and
ethical responsibilities, and proactive responsiveness through outreach and (re)assessment. Public
libraries have long aimed to improve communities and advance democracy by providing open,
free information access to all. Today, they also proactively seek to expand their services to
underserved groups ensuring their relevance and mission achievement. This research draws from
25 in-depth qualitative interviews to explore librarian narratives to identify four core
responsibilities that constitute Expansive Public Service Delivery. We conclude with a discussion
of how service for all, professionalism, ethical responsibility, and reflexive decision-making
around community needs can result in more vibrant, sustainable public organizations.

title: ANCORA Flow: A Conceptual Model for Change Management and AI Adoption with Psychological Safety, Sensemaking, and Sociotechnical Governance

detail.title: ANCORA Flow: A Conceptual Model for Change Management and AI Adoption with Psychological Safety, Sensemaking, and Sociotechnical Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares a conflict of interest: the ANCORA Flow is also the basis for commercial services offered by her. This document includes its limitations (Section 10) explicitly to mitigate promotional bias. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: This white paper introduces the ANCORA Flow, a proprietary conceptual model for guiding artificial intelligence adoption and organizational change with explicit focus on combined maturity diagnosis, psychological safety, and sociotechnical governance. The model organizes transformation as a continuous six-phase cycle — Assess, Name, Cultivate, Orchestrate, Reinforce, and Anchor — built through integrative synthesis of established change management literature (Lewin, Bridges, Kotter, Hiatt), organizational maturity and readiness models (MIT CISR, MITRE, Gartner, Weiner, Blumberg and Pringle), the social neuroscience of behavior (Rock), psychological safety (Edmondson), organizational sensemaking (Weick), leadership storytelling (Denning), organizational culture (Schein; Cameron and Quinn), and AI governance frameworks (NIST, OECD, UNESCO, ISO/IEC 42001). The model's central contribution is repositioning psychological safety and combined organizational-individual diagnosis as structural preconditions for sustainable generative AI adoption, rather than desirable byproducts. Although developed in the context of generative AI adoption — the most urgent technological transformation currently underway — the ANCORA Flow's architecture derives largely from general change-management and human-behavior theory, not AI-specific literature, suggesting applicability to any technological or structural change process involving people. The model is presented as a conceptual contribution: it has not yet undergone systematic empirical validation, a limitation stated explicitly in this document as a future research agenda rather than a concealed gap.

title: The Shareholding Rights Shift from India to Delaware and Texas
affiliations: Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law and National Law University, Jodhpur

detail.title: The Shareholding Rights Shift from India to Delaware and Texas

publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Corporate law is quietly changing what a share entitles its owner to do. The governance rights that matter are being converted from shareholder rights, which a person holds because she owns stock, into shareholding rights, which she holds only if she owns enough stock. The difference is not one of degree. Below the threshold, there is no diminished version of the right. Instead, there is no right at all. And the threshold may be drawn in dollars, in percentages, in head counts, or in years of uninterrupted ownership. This is why the conversion from shareholder rights to shareholding rights has been so easy to accomplish one piece at a time. This Article names that conversion and traces it through the statutes of the past two years in Delaware and Texas. It reads those statutes against a system that has already made the shift: India.

 

India has lived with this design for a generation. Its Companies Act grants minority shareholders an unusually generous array of rights and then conditions each entry on capital or coordination that dispersed holders cannot assemble. The result is that the most potent remedies are the least used. For example, the class action, available for over a decade, has yet to produce a decided victory. American scholarship has treated that pattern as a symptom of concentrated ownership and therefore as someone else’s problem. It is not. Reading the two systems against each other across voice, representation, enforcement, and information, this Article finds that the statutes passed during the recent competition for corporate charters, Delaware’s Senate Bill 21 and the Texas provisions on shareholder proposals, derivative standing, the business judgment rule, and inspection, have carried American law to the Indian position and in some places past it.

 

The comparison also yields two cautions that neither system’s domestic literature supplies. The first is about reform. The obvious answer to a threshold written in capital is to write it in people instead, and India has already run that experiment: its small shareholder director provision counts members rather than shares and has remained largely theoretical, because a law that counts heads while supplying no means for the heads to find one another has written a right nobody can trigger. The means American law would have to supply is the inspection right these statutes have just narrowed. The second is about substitutes. Where a right has been priced beyond reach, both systems offer the independent director in its place. Both define independence by the absence of enumerated ties rather than the presence of demonstrated autonomy, a definition that cannot see the capture it exists to prevent. What makes the timing acute is that retail shareholders are entering both markets at scale at the precise moment the entitlements attached to their shares are being drained of content. The Article closes with the discipline neither system imposes: that a legislature drawing a governance line should say which kind of rule it is writing and defend it accordingly.

title: Method Identity and the Limits of Formalism

detail.title: Method Identity and the Limits of Formalism
detail.abstract:
This essay is an extension of method models described in The Science of Methods by Eric Cafritz, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18733134 (referred to below as the "Register"), and in particular in the companion paper A Sheaf-Theoretic Model of Methods, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20312085 (the "Sheaf-Theoretic Model"). The essay is intended to be readable on a standalone basis.

Parts I and II of the Register supply the foundations and grammar for the execution model in this essay. To the extent required, defined terms from the Register and the Sheaf-Theoretic Model are recapitulated below.

Much of the Register, as well as the Sheaf-Theoretic Model, concerns the retrospective examination of established or crystallized methods, whose configurations have been fixed by design or practice. This essay describes methods in application in formal terms. It presents executions as sampled runs, from which patterns in a method can be read, together with the records of completed applications.

This execution model investigates which characteristics carry or preserve method identity, so that a method remains distinctively recognizable despite variation among the steps taken in its applications. The essay also focuses on the limits of formalization, examining the points at which an agent's determination is required in application. At each such point, the ensuing formal consequences depend upon the determination supplied by the agent.

title: The Clean Transition Imperative: How Decarbonization, Electrification, and Circular Systems Jointly Reduce Climate and Pollution Risks

detail.title: The Clean Transition Imperative: How Decarbonization, Electrification, and Circular Systems Jointly Reduce Climate and Pollution Risks
detail.abstract:
The report argues that the global economy is undergoing a structural transformation driven by three mutually reinforcing systems: decarbonization, electrification, and circularity. Together, these pillars form what the document calls the Triad of Resilience, a macro‑systems framework for reducing climate and pollution risks while strengthening economic stability. As stated in the Executive Summary, “Decarbonization cleans the primary energy inputs; electrification dramatically increases system efficiency… and circularity mitigates the immense material footprint required to build this new infrastructure.”

The report demonstrates that rapid cost declines in renewables, batteries, and electrified technologies are fundamentally reshaping capital allocation, enabling non‑linear adoption curves across regions. Electrification improves thermodynamic efficiency and shifts pollution away from population centers, while circular systems reduce dependence on virgin minerals and alleviate supply‑chain vulnerabilities. Sectoral deep dives—power generation, transportation, heavy industry, built environment, and agriculture—show how each domain experiences similar transition mechanics driven by policy alignment, technology diffusion, and capital market dynamics.

A central thesis is that these systems, when modeled concurrently, multiply resilience rather than merely add to it. The report introduces a Multi‑System Resilience Index (MSRI) to quantify how integrated clean‑transition systems dampen exogenous shocks such as commodity volatility and geopolitical risk. Emerging markets, in particular, benefit from decentralized clean technologies that accelerate poverty reduction and enable leapfrogging of legacy fossil infrastructure.

Ultimately, the document concludes that the clean transition is not a cost burden but “the most significant deflationary and stabilizing macroeconomic project of the 21st century.” It frames the transition as a macroeconomic reorganization whose success depends primarily on deployment velocity, policy alignment, and capital flow optimization.

title: Introducing Trimmed Imports and Exports *
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City and Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City

detail.title: Introducing Trimmed Imports and Exports *
detail.abstract: Trade flows are volatile and notoriously difficult to predict. This paper introduces trimmed import and export growth rates for the United States to help improve trade forecasts. We calculate the growth rates as a trimmed mean that strips out subcomponents with less predictive power. By separating the signal from the noise, our trimmed growth rates provide a better perspective on where aggregate imports or exports are heading, particularly at horizons four to 12 months ahead. Consequently, out-of-sample forecasts based on our trimmed growth rates reduce forecast errors by up to 15 percent relative to forecasts from aggregate import or export growth. These trimmed forecasts are simple to compute, outperform both naive forecasts and models that rely on a richer information set, and are particularly useful during episodes with heightened volatility. We update the trimmed growth rates monthly and make them publicly available.

title: Intelligism and Collective Cognitive Sovereignty: Institutionalised AI as a New Axis of Political Economy

detail.title: Intelligism and Collective Cognitive Sovereignty: Institutionalised AI as a New Axis of Political Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This article is a a conceptual research article in political philosophy and political economy using comparative conceptual analysis, conceptual engineering and ideal-type construction, which did not involve human participants, animals, identifiable personal data, or primary data collection. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence becomes politically significant not only when it automates labour, but when institutions depend on it to produce actionable knowledge, coordinate activity and revise their own procedures. Existing accounts of AI capitalism, computational socialism, technocracy, algocracy and machine-based value production explain major parts of this transformation. This article argues that a residual political-economic problem emerges when institutionalised AI becomes a durable, cross-domain and recursively influential infrastructure of production, social coordination and institutional learning. It develops Intelligism as an order-organising axis for analysing this condition. Its defining conflict is who determines the purposes of intelligent infrastructures, constructs their epistemic categories and possesses the effective power to revise, suspend or replace them. The article develops collective cognitive sovereignty as the capacity of political communities and materially affected groups to govern these powers. It then contrasts two institutional outcomes: the AI Republic, where intelligent infrastructures remain subordinate to democratic purposes, separated powers, contestation, revisability and public cognitive capacity; and AI Empire, defined by dependency without effective authorship. Intelligist relations can coexist with or transform capitalist, socialist and mixed political economies. The central political struggle of the AI age is whether societies remain authors of the intelligence through which they understand, organise and transform themselves.

title: Substance Without a Directive: Residence, Permanent Establishment and the Withdrawal of ATAD 3 as They Apply to Owner-Managed Companies

detail.title: Substance Without a Directive: Residence, Permanent Establishment and the Withdrawal of ATAD 3 as They Apply to Owner-Managed Companies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author notes that several of the paper's conclusions run against that commercial interest. The paper argues that a Bulgarian company managed from abroad holds its tax rate contingently rather than securely; that the corporate-parent structure frequently does not repay the cost of the second entity it requires; and that advisory material in this market systematically under-reports residence risk because the honest answer reduces the size of the addressable market. These are stated because the analysis supports them, not despite the interest declared above. The paper cites a companion working paper by the same author (SSRN abstract 7313658). No other self-citation is present.
declarations.ethicsApproval: he paper is a doctrinal analysis of published legislation, official statements and decided case law. Parties named in the cited judgments are corporate litigants in published decisions, cited as legal authority rather than as research subjects.

detail.abstract: A companion paper showed that the effective tax burden on an owner-managed Bulgarian company is governed less by the headline rate than by a fixed cost floor, and noted that the arithmetic excludes the question of whether the arrangement is respected at all. This paper takes up that question. It argues that the exposure of a small owner-managed company is systematically misperceived, and that the misperception has a specific structure. The controlled foreign company regime under Article 7 of the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive, which owners most often ask about, carries a de minimis threshold of €750,000 in accounting profits and €75,000 in non-trading income, and therefore does not reach most of this population. Corporate residence and permanent establishment, which owners rarely ask about, carry no such threshold and apply in full at any size. The paper further argues that Bulgaria's incorporation-based residence rule, generally presented as a simplifying feature, guarantees rather than avoids a residence conflict where the company is managed from abroad, because Bulgaria does not release a company it has registered. The 2017 replacement of the place-of-effective-management tie-breaker in Article 4(3) of the OECD Model with a mutual agreement procedure, adopted by roughly 35 per cent of signatories to the Multilateral Instrument, leaves the resulting conflict to a procedure that is not realistically available at this scale. Finally, the paper examines the withdrawal of the Unshell proposal (ATAD 3) after ECOFIN discontinued work in June 2025, and the absence of substance-based hallmarks from the recast of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation published on 24 June 2026. It concludes that the withdrawal, widely reported as a relief for small structures, removed the prospect of a common and knowable substance test and returned the question to twenty-seven national administrations and a body of treaty practice, which is the less favourable outcome for the smallest taxpayers. The paper is doctrinal and reports no new empirical data.

title: Whose Rate Is It? Licensor Identity and the Limits of Comparability Analysis in Royalty Pricing: Evidence from 6,050 Disclosed Licences in Seven Jurisdictions
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Whose Rate Is It? Licensor Identity and the Limits of Comparability Analysis in Royalty Pricing: Evidence from 6,050 Disclosed Licences in Seven Jurisdictions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no competing interests to declare. The author is not employed by, retained by or otherwise engaged with any provider of licensing-terms data, valuation services or transfer-pricing advisory work, and holds no financial interest in any such provider. This statement names the class of counterparties rather than being made in general terms, because the article evaluates the reproducibility of commercial royalty databases.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study analyses corporate regulatory disclosures that issuers are required to make public. No human participants, no personal data and no animals were involved, so no institutional review board approval was sought or required.
