Cloud inference costs of approximately USD 22 for the extraction of the English-language subset were paid by the author. There were no external funders, and no funder had any role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript. The author's institution provided no financial support for this work.

detail.abstract:
Transfer pricing, impairment testing and patent damages all price a licence by selecting comparable transactions on observable attributes — industry, technology field, territory, date, royalty base — and reading a rate off the survivors. The selection step carries much of the analysis, and external comparable searches commonly proceed on the assumption that those coarse observable attributes carry enough information to narrow the set of plausible rates. That assumption is rarely stated and still more rarely tested. This paper measures how much information those attributes carry. The evidence is 6,050 licence contracts disclosed by 2,007 identified licensors in seven jurisdictions — the United States, Korea, Japan, China, India, Brazil and twenty-eight European countries filing under ESEF — for fiscal years 2016 to 2025, reconstructed from the public record with a released extraction specification. The observation is the contract rather than the disclosure, because firms re-file the same agreement in successive annual reports, and the industry variable is harmonised across the seven regimes before use.
In this dataset the coarse observable transaction attributes available in a public comparable search explain a limited share of the observed variance. A harmonised industry screen yields an adjusted R-squared of 0.067 and narrows the interquartile range of centred rates by 2.7%; adding the contract year raises it to 0.072. Licensor identity, on the same estimator, gives 0.264 — about four times as much, bounded by 0.234 and 0.427 across three ways of counting a contract, with an intraclass correlation that agrees to within a thousandth. Estimated separately in ten source streams that share no filings, no language and no extraction path, it exceeds the industry screen in nine. The exception is the stream of separately filed material agreements, where the disclosure rule selects individually negotiated deals rather than a routine licensing programme — so the finding is conditional and the condition is legible. The consequence for comparability analysis is practical rather than sceptical. The paper does not reject comparability analysis as such; it measures the limited informational content of the coarse observable screens available in a public external search, and disclosed industry classifications map the licensed subject matter only imperfectly, so the estimates test the screens practice can actually apply rather than the full set of theoretically relevant factors. Within those bounds, the dimension with the greatest explanatory power is one external searches will often be less able to hold constant than an internal comparable. The results therefore supply an empirical magnitude for the practical preference for internal comparables, and suggest that where no internal comparable exists, public external comparables are often more informative as range-bounding evidence than as the sole basis for a tightly specified point estimate.

title: The Digital Lower Bound
affiliations: University of the West of England - Bristol Business School

detail.title: The Digital Lower Bound
detail.abstract: Can the central bank utilize the interest on retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) as an independent monetary policy instrument? This paper shows that the answer is yes, provided that the interest on CBDC is set below the target money market rate. If the rate on CBDC is higher than the central bank's target money market rate, then the latter becomes irrelevant, because the money market rate equals the CBDC rate. This finding implies that the CBDC rate acts as a "digital lower bound" for the short-term rate. The paper also explains why the central bank cannot utilize the quantity of CBDC as a policy instrument.

title: Culturally Safe Care in Adult Day Programs for Ethnoculturally Diverse Older Adults with Dementia: A Critical Review
affiliations: York University, York University, York University, York University, York University, York University, York University, York University and

detail.title: Culturally Safe Care in Adult Day Programs for Ethnoculturally Diverse Older Adults with Dementia: A Critical Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this review used data from previously published studies and did not involve human participants directly.
declarations.funderStatement: The realist review that this research is based on was funded by three research grants, all held by MH (senior author of this paper and overall project lead): a CIHR Knowledge Synthesis and Mobilization Grant (funding reference number BK8 - 191190), a research grant from the Carswell Family Foundation (no funding number available), and a trainee support grant from the Carswell Family Foundation (no funding number available). BZB (corresponding author of this paper) received a Carswell Graduate Fellowship in Dementia Care, awarded by the Helen Carswell Chair in Dementia Care, Faculty of Health, York University (no funding number available).

detail.abstract: Adult day programs (ADPs) are essential for dementia care. Ethnoculturally diverse older adults often benefit less due to culturally misaligned care and systemic inequities. Cultural safety addresses disparities by challenging provider biases and structural barriers, but it is underexplored in ADPs. This critical review examined how culturally safe ADP care for persons living with dementia is conceptualized, experienced, and implemented. We selected 20 studies from references included in a broader realist review by our team. Cultural safety and intersectionality guided study appraisal, data extraction, and thematic synthesis. Five themes emerged: first, definitions of culturally safe care in ADPs; second, experiences of ethnoculturally diverse older adults and their caregivers, including belonging alongside challenges (exclusion, language barriers, environmental incongruence); third, contexts and mechanisms shaping culturally safe care (organizational rigidity, provider-centered routines, workforce constraints); fourth, implementation of culturally safe care, (superficial adaptations vs relational change); fifth, gaps/future directions (absence of operational models, insufficient outcome evaluation, limited participant and caregiver voices). Culturally safe ADP care can advance equity for ethnoculturally diverse older adults living with dementia and their caregivers, yet current approaches remain largely symbolic. Achieving culturally safe care will require structural reforms, organizational accountability, participatory design, and policies that support flexibility, relational practice, and system-level responsiveness.

title: The Fall and Rise of a Global Village
affiliations: Bar Ilan University, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) and

detail.title: The Fall and Rise of a Global Village
detail.abstract: We study repeated local competition for economic opportunities. In each period, a random group of agents participates in an all-pay contest for a prize, and accumulated prizes determine wealth. We call an opportunity structure a global village if expected wealth dispersion remains uniformly bounded over time. We show that global integration is governed by the interaction between the exposure of every group to economic opportunities and the competitive advantage of poorer agents generated by concavity of their utility function. When the agents' absolute risk aversion remains bounded away from zero at high wealth levels, poorer agents retain a strong competitive advantage. In graph-based opportunity structures, global integration is then equivalent to connectivity. When absolute risk aversion vanishes sufficiently fast, this balancing force becomes asymptotically weaker, and stronger cross-group exposure is required. We illustrate this distinction in the Erdős-Rényi random graph process. With high probability, in the first regime the global village emerges exactly when the last isolated vertex disappears. In the second regime, it emerges exactly when the last leaf falls. Thus, in the latter regime, the fall of the last leaf marks the rise of the global village.

title: Purely Hedonic Image Concerns and Audience Size: Evidence from a Charity Dictator Game
affiliations: and Prague University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Purely Hedonic Image Concerns and Audience Size: Evidence from a Charity Dictator Game
detail.abstract: We study whether image preferences in isolation from strategic considerations, namely purely hedonic image concerns, can motivate prosocial behavior and whether this audience effect is mediated by the number of observers. Answers to related questions from the extant experimental literature are often mixed or influenced by multiple mechanisms evoked by the context at hand or design employed. We employ an experiment involving a dictator game with a charity receiver and a binary choice with unambiguous social valence. Choices are observed by an anonymous, passive, and external audience whose size varies across treatments. Our simple experimental design allows us to isolate purely hedonic image concerns about appearing altruistic from strategic considerations and other confounding features of alternative designs. We find that donations rise by 10.2 percentage points on average when audiences are present, with every observer increasing the probability of donating by an estimated 2.12 percentage points. We provide evidence that the size of the audience also matters.

title: The Dynamics of 'Geopolitical Migration' by Russians to the United Arab Emirates

detail.title: The Dynamics of 'Geopolitical Migration' by Russians to the United Arab Emirates
detail.abstract: This article examines Russian migration to the UAE amid the backdrop of the Russia-Ukraine war and western sanctions. It explores the economic, political and social dynamics that underpin this migration trend. The UAE emerges as a particularly compelling case in the study of Russian migration patterns to the Gulf region, underscored by its strategic neutrality and the unique socio-economic opportunities it presents. Unlike its geopolitical counterparts, the UAE has not imposed sanctions on Russia, thereby positioning itself as a geopolitical outlier and a sanctuary for Russian capital and migrants.

title: A Property Rights Theory of Monetary Issuance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Property Rights Theory of Monetary Issuance
detail.abstract: Can the right to create money be defined as a property right? Under modern fiat monetary systems, the authority to issue base money has been administratively centralized, with public institutions responsible for maintaining a unified monetary system and pursuing macroeconomic stability objectives. However, as an institutional right capable of creating new purchasing power and generating seigniorage revenue, this right has not yet been systematically examined from the perspective of property-rights theory. Given an established monetary regime and an aggregate issuance constraint, the issuance space for base money can be defined as a standardized institutional right with specified quantity, exercise conditions, and contractual obligations. This framework reveals that monetary issuance rights contain key elements of a property-rights bundle, including exclusivity, allocation, entitlement to returns, and enforceable obligations associated with their exercise. Building on this property-rights framework, this paper proposes the Auctioned Issuance Rights (AIR) mechanism. Under this mechanism, the public sector retains authority over the monetary unit, legal tender rules, aggregate issuance constraints, and monetary stability objectives, while market competition determines the allocation of limited issuance space and reveals its market value through competitive bidding.

title: Separating Decodability, Readout Accessibility, and Procedure-Relative Learnability in Evolving Spiking Networks

detail.title: Separating Decodability, Readout Accessibility, and Procedure-Relative Learnability in Evolving Spiking Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The research was conducted independently, without external influence. The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or animal subjects; therefore, institutional review board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding

detail.abstract: Decodability is often treated as evidence that task-relevant information is available to a neural system. Yet availability to an external decoder need not imply availability to the system's operative readout, and a useful readout need not be reliably discovered by a finite learning procedure. We distinguish decodability, readout accessibility, and procedure-relative learnability in evolving recurrent spiking networks performing delayed match-to-sample. Under corrected edge-specific dynamics, an all-neuron ridge decoder achieved mean held-out balanced accuracy of 0.758, compared with 0.443 for the designated neuronal output. Neural dynamical-state reset before cue two reduced ridge accuracy to 0.525. Designated outputs remained nearly silent, and alternative rules remained at chance. Direct supervised access to recurrent activity increased held-out balanced accuracy to 0.688, but recovery was class-asymmetric: match sensitivity was 0.86-0.98 and nonmatch specificity was 0.36-0.52. The specified evolutionary procedure did not meet its frozen developmental criterion: ten-block mean reward was 0.628 against a threshold of 0.75. At zero delay, held-out balanced accuracy increased descriptively to 0.768 and reward to 0.740, weakening any categorical interpretation of that threshold while leaving the protocol verdict unchanged. A post hoc analysis found direct output connections from neurons with nonzero decoder coefficients in every seed, arguing against simple disconnection without establishing functional access. Thus, task information can be decodable from recurrent dynamics without being accessible to a designated neuronal output, and improved readout accessibility does not guarantee criterion-level performance under a specified optimization procedure. Information availability is therefore mechanismdependent, and these three computational properties should be evaluated separately.

title: The Transfer Gap: Is US Fiscal Policy Out of Line in 2026?
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Transfer Gap: Is US Fiscal Policy Out of Line in 2026?
detail.abstract: In 2032 the United States is scheduled to cut Social Security benefits by 22 percent. This is not a forecast. It is current law, and it is the mechanism by which the federal government resolves a promise it has made and not funded. This paper measures that promise and asks whether fiscal policy is out of line. It reaches two conclusions. First, not all deficits have the same dynamics. Deficits arising from sources other than transfer promises are short lived and are followed by sharp consolidations. Deficits arising from transfer shocks, that is from increases in the present value of promised benefits given the tax base, are longer lasting and are followed by weaker consolidations, because the promise is a stock rather than a flow and because the stock is indexed to demography rather than to legislation. Second, the fiscal position of 2026 is driven primarily by a transfer shock. Stabilising debt at its current 101 percent of GDP requires a permanent primary adjustment of 2.2 to 3.2 percent of GDP a year, depending on how much of today's yield curve passes through to the average cost of the debt. Of the 2.87 percent required in the central case, a Shapley decomposition assigns 2.03 points to the growth of the transfer block, 0.66 points to the interest rate regime, and 0.19 points to everything else the federal government does. Current law closes about a third of the gap, but it closes it by cutting transfer payments 17 to 22 percent in 2032 to 2034, which is to say by administering exactly the kind of shock that has the most persistent output effects. The gap is worth $912 billion a year, roughly the entire national defense budget, or $6,843 per household per year, permanently. Whether households have discounted a cut whose date is already written in statute is an open question; a personal saving rate of 2.7 percent suggests they have not.

title: Drowning in Debt? Mortgage Defaults in European Flood Zones
affiliations: University of Venice - Department of Economics, ICMA Centre, Henley Business School, University of Reading, University of Reading - ICMA Centre and ICMA Centre - Henley Business School, University of Reading

detail.title: Drowning in Debt? Mortgage Defaults in European Flood Zones
detail.abstract: We estimate the association between flood exposure and mortgage default in Europe and find marked crosscountry heterogeneity. Flood exposure raises default risk in some countries, reduces it in others, and has mixed or no detectable effect elsewhere. Counterintuitive reductions in observed defaults are consistent with disaster response mechanisms, including insurance payouts, payment holidays and public support, whose short-run cash-flow benefits may more than offset the underlying shock. Default responses are concentrated in four-quarter windows with one flooded quarter, whereas repeated flooding within the same window has weaker effects, consistent with borrower adaptation to flood risk or survivorship selection. Moderately severe floods are more likely to yield positive estimated changes in mortgage default probability than extreme events, which can prompt stronger public intervention and help stabilise mortgage performance.

title: Funding Discontinuities and Arbitrage-Free Pricing of Perpetual Futures
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and University of Pennsylvania - Finance Department

detail.title: Funding Discontinuities and Arbitrage-Free Pricing of Perpetual Futures
detail.abstract: Kalshi's recent perpetual futures design introduces a discontinuous funding rule with zero funding inside an inaction region and a discrete jump outside it. This note shows that such a specification can eliminate stationary arbitrage-free futures-to-spot ratios when the net cost of carry is moderate but nonzero. In this region, funding is either too low or too high to rule out arbitrage. The resulting trades and price pressure are illustrated.

title: Housing-Market Equilibrium, Resident Selection, and the Endogeneity of Local Income

detail.title: Housing-Market Equilibrium, Resident Selection, and the Endogeneity of Local Income

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this theoretical research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A local housing market is also a spatial allocation mechanism: the equilibrium housing cost affects not only the price of occupying a location but also the composition of households able to occupy it. This paper studies the information consequence of that equilibrium selection. In a constrained local housing market with heterogeneous resident demand and positive turnover, an outward housing-demand shock raises the clearing price. When lower purchasing-capacity resident demand is more price-sensitive than higher-purchasing-capacity resident demand, current resident allocation shifts toward the latter group; turnover then carries that allocation difference into the resident stock, raising observed resident income even when within-group incomes do not change. The model therefore characterizes observed resident income as partly an equilibrium outcome. The main result shows that the selection induced response of observed resident income and structural housing-price responsiveness to locally anchored purchasing capacity depend on different combinations of demand primitives. Consequently, the same post-selection price–resident-income relationship can coexist with different structural local-income responsiveness. Observed local price–income comovement therefore need not identify structural price anchoring to the purchasing capacity of a compositionally stable resident population. Non-local housing demand provides a transparent initiating shock, while an affordability implication follows as a secondary corollary.

title: Outside Options and Collective Bargaining Spillovers
affiliations: and

detail.title: Outside Options and Collective Bargaining Spillovers
detail.abstract: This paper studies how stronger unions generate spillovers through labor market competition. We exploit a Brazilian reform that strengthened union bargaining at a subset of firms and identify competing employers from workers' job mobility networks. Directly affected firms raise wages and union-bargained amenities. Competing employers raise wages by one-quarter as much, while amenities are unchanged. We find no evidence that unions actively mediate these spillovers. Employers instead respond to competition, raising wages most where they compete for costlier-to-replace workers, and leaving workforce size and composition largely unaffected. Within firms, pay does not respond to outside-option heterogeneity, suggesting internal wage-setting constraints.

title: Problem, Solution and Policy Credibility in Low Carbon Innovation Acceleration
affiliations: University of Edinburgh Business School and Manchester Institute of Innovation Research at Manchester Business School

detail.title: Problem, Solution and Policy Credibility in Low Carbon Innovation Acceleration
detail.abstract: This paper aims to explore the role of credibility in low-carbon innovation acceleration. We develop a conceptual framework that treats credibility as a dynamic and multidimensional phenomenon, where problem, technology and policy credibility are all important, and where credibility is built through interactions and feedback loops between firms, users, policymakers and civil society and polity as they interact around problem framings, proposed solutions, technological choices and policy choices. These interactions co-construct or erode credibility across its three dimensions, leading to acceleration or slowdown in low carbon innovation diffusion. We apply our framework to the cases of offshore wind and solarPV in the UK. These two technological choices were introduced as aspects of the solution to the problems of climate change and energy security. Both technological choices have benefited from problem and technical credibility, but only offshore wind saw the construction of a credible policy mix.

title: A Spatial Mathematical Model of Human--Cattle Overlap and Insecticide-Treated Cattle for Residual Malaria Control
affiliations: University of Dar es Salaam

detail.title: A Spatial Mathematical Model of Human--Cattle Overlap and Insecticide-Treated Cattle for Residual Malaria Control
detail.abstract: Residual malaria transmission by Anopheles arabiensis, a behaviourally flexible and opportunistic malaria vector that readily feeds on both humans and livestock continues to undermine malaria elimination despite widespread use of long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and indoor residual sprays (IRS). Although insecticide-treated cattle (ITC) have been proposed as a complementary intervention, existing mathematical models largely neglect the influence of host spatial organization on mosquito host selection and intervention effectiveness. Here, we develop a spatially explicit deterministic malaria transmission model that integrates continuous human, cattle, and mosquito density surfaces with mosquito host-seeking behaviour, feeding-cycle dynamics, LLINs, and ITC to quantify how human--cattle spatial overlap influences malaria transmission across heterogeneous landscapes.The model demonstrates that intervention effectiveness depends jointly on LLIN coverage, ITC coverage, and the spatial organization of hosts. Increasing human--cattle spatial overlap consistently reduced human blood index (HBI), feeding-cycle survival and entomological inoculation rate (EIR). Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated that these conclusions were robust across plausible variations in host abundance, spatial dispersion, and ITC efficacy parameters, with cattle spatial spread and ITC mortality emerging as the most influential determinants of intervention performance.​These findings identify spatial host organization as a previously underappreciated ecological driver of malaria transmission and integrated vector-control effectiveness. More broadly, the study demonstrates that spatial host organization can substantially enhance malaria-control outcomes beyond those achievable through increasing intervention coverage alone. The proposed model provides new insights for designing integrated interventions against residual malaria transmission by a behaviourally flexible and opportunistic vector.

title: From Occupation to Optimization: AI, Military Language, and the Administrative Translation of Force
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: From Occupation to Optimization: AI, Military Language, and the Administrative Translation of Force
detail.abstract: This article introduces administrative translation of force as a formal effect of AImediated military and security discourse. The concept describes a transformation in which violence, occupation, surveillance, targeting, or coercive control remains semantically present but is re-expressed through the operational vocabulary of risk management, target validation, collateral estimation, proportionality assessment, escalation control, security response, or optimization. The claim is not that these categories are inherently illegitimate. Modern armed forces require procedures for target development, legal review, civilian-harm mitigation, and decision support, and international governance frameworks increasingly insist that human responsibility and judgment remain traceable when artificial intelligence is used in military decisionmaking. The analytical problem begins when procedural language changes the grammatical architecture through which force is recognized: actors become systems, decisions become thresholds, attacks become operations, civilian harm becomes an estimate, and responsibility becomes distributed across models, scores, intelligence pipelines, and authorization chains. The article uses Gaza-related reporting on the reported military use of AI-enabled decision-support systems as its principal empirical anchor, while Iran-Israel and United States security discourse function as comparative environments for examining the language of precision, pre-emption, targets, threat, escalation, and operational necessity. It does not infer undisclosed technical use from political language, and it treats contested claims about specific systems as reported claims rather than established technical facts. Building on prior work on responsibility loss, asymmetric visibility, and politicalsubjecthood reduction, the paper argues that operational syntax can preserve factual description while weakening the linguistic traceability of force, decision, civilian consequence, and institutional agency (Startari, 2025a, 2026a, 2026b, 2026e). Methodologically, the paper proposes Operationalization Density (OD) and a Force Optimization Index (FOI). OD measures how frequently clauses about force are structured through administrative, predictive, proportionality-based, or optimizationoriented categories. FOI measures the combined degree of action nominalization, system- mediated responsibility, civilian-harm compression, operational-necessity framing, and decision-chain opacity. The framework is explicitly falsifiable: if operationalization occurs at comparable rates across actors, source genres, and power positions, or if source texts already contain the same structure, the stronger geopolitical interpretation must be narrowed. AI ethics and military-AI governance should therefore ask not only whether systems are accurate, explainable, or lawful, but whether the language surrounding their outputs preserves the chain through which force is chosen, applied, experienced, and attributed.

title: Migrant Protection by Education in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC): Lessons and Recommendations on the Philippine Post-Arrival Orientation Service (PAOS) in Qatar
affiliations: and Unaffiliated Authors

detail.title: Migrant Protection by Education in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC): Lessons and Recommendations on the Philippine Post-Arrival Orientation Service (PAOS) in Qatar
detail.abstract: This paper examines the Philippine PAOS program in Qatar (2010-2015) and explores its challenges and practices in delivering services to OFWs, particularly to domestic workers.5 Using existing government data and secondary policy materials, we argue that the PAOS program is not only a vital migrant protection mechanism in upholding migrant workers’ rights and welfare but also the least implemented program across the Gulf countries, which, to an extent, may contribute to the growing vulnerability of some low-skilled migrant workers. The paper is composed of three sections. First, we examine the Philippine migration to Qatar and more specifically, the domestic work migration to Qatar and of the Gulf countries. Second, we provide a background on the PAOS program in Qatar and identify broader challenges and practices in program implementation. Third and lastly, we highlight the implications of the Qatar PAOS program and offer recommendations to protect migrant workers and mitigate asymmetric information through the PAOS program.

title: From Funding to Delivery: A Framework for Implementation Readiness and Decision Support in Publicly Funded Clean-energy Programs

detail.title: From Funding to Delivery: A Framework for Implementation Readiness and Decision Support in Publicly Funded Clean-energy Programs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable private information. It develops a practitioner framework based on published literature and publicly available documentary sources; the applications presented are illustrative constructions rather than accounts of institutional engagements.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Public investment in clean-energy programs in the United States has expanded substantially, but the institutions responsible for converting that funding into delivered projects may not be assessed for delivery capability until after implementation problems have become visible. Federal oversight findings show that important implementation-capacity deficiencies may become apparent only after delivery has begun. Federal oversight bodies have repeatedly documented delays, staffing shortfalls, weak contractor oversight, and incomplete reporting among recipient and subrecipient institutions, yet the federal-award management architecture prescribes no single government-wide instrument for assessing implementation readiness before funds are obligated. This paper develops a diagnostic framework for assessing implementation readiness in publicly funded clean-energy programs. The framework organizes assessment around eight readiness dimensions, applies a four-level rating scale with an explicit "evidence unavailable" outcome, and links readiness findings to a defined set of management decisions through a six-step workflow. Three design commitments distinguish it from adjacent instruments: findings are designed to support comparison across institutions assessed with the same instrument; critical deficiencies are flagged rather than averaged into a composite score; and the absence of documentation is recorded as an assessment outcome rather than resolved in favor of readiness. Two illustrative applications are presented, one at the level of a single state energy office and one at the portfolio level, where a pass-through entity applies the instrument across multiple subrecipients. The portfolio application illustrates the framework's principal claim: repeated application of a common instrument makes patterns across institutions visible, locating diagnostic questions at the level of the delivery system rather than the individual recipient. The framework is presented as a proposed instrument requiring external validation. No claim is made that readiness ratings predict implementation outcomes, and a validation agenda is set out.

title: Certified Low-Rank Gaussian Processes via the Noise-Floor Rule

detail.title: Certified Low-Rank Gaussian Processes via the Noise-Floor Rule

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical and computational study involving no human participants, animals, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Low-rank approximations scale Gaussian-process regression, but they are typically judged by kernel accuracy rather than posterior-solve safety; this paper introduces a noise-floor rule for certified low-rank GP linear solves. Given strictly positive observation-noise variance σ², a low-rank kernel replacement K_r is accepted only when its residual satisfies ||K-K_r||_F ≤ εσ² and the resulting rank provides a cost advantage. For a nonzero response vector, a resolvent perturbation argument then guarantees ||α-α̂||₂/||α||₂ ≤ ||K-K_r||₂/σ² ≤ ||K-K_r||_F/σ² ≤ ε, where α=(K+σ²I)⁻¹y and α̂=(K_r+σ²I)⁻¹y. An accompanying absolute bound covers y=0. The accepted replacement is evaluated via Woodbury solves and the matrix determinant lemma. On a smooth RBF kernel with n=4000, the certified method selects rank 239, delivers an 855× speedup for the recorded fresh factorization-and-log-determinant invocation, and produces a posterior mean relative error of 2.1×10⁻⁵, using the exact test–training cross-covariance vector, under a certified 5% posterior-solve bound. A rough near-full-rank control is correctly rejected; timings are hardware-dependent, discovery is much slower than one exact solve in this implementation, and cached repeated-right-hand-side performance was not benchmarked.

title: What Does It Take to Protect Capital in the Age of AI? The Four Conditions of Protected Capital

detail.abstract: This paper examines the accountability gap emerging as artificial intelligence becomes embedded in institutional investment decision-making, and proposes a framework for closing it. Drawing on a 2026 survey finding that ninety-two percent of directors have personally used AI for board-related work while sixty percent of their boards have no formal governing policy, the paper argues that most current AI governance amounts to what it terms vibe governance, the appearance of oversight without the capacity to demonstrate it under scrutiny. In response, the paper introduces the Four Conditions of Protected Capital: Independence, Persistence, Specificity, and Consequence, a framework independently converged upon in 2026 by a national AI regulator, a major technology company's internal engineering practice, and a leading investment professional body, despite no coordination between them. The paper applies this framework to three distinct institutional settings, family office succession planning, the General Partner-Limited Partner relationship in investment funds, including a newly identified risk termed cognitive convergence, and private equity Investment Committee diligence, drawing on documented cases and current regulatory developments in each. The paper concludes with a practical action matrix and policy checklist, and a discussion of the boundary between what AI-assisted governance can achieve and where human judgment and accountability remain irreducible.

title: Deserter State: A Genealogy of an Analytical Framework of State Transformation

detail.title: Deserter State: A Genealogy of an Analytical Framework of State Transformation

keywords: Selective State Decomposition under Democratic Continuity

detail.abstract: This article reconstructs the genealogy of the category "Deserter State" and analyzes its conceptual evolution toward the contemporary notions of State decomposition, Selective State decomposition under Democratic Continuity, and Gradual Civic Capitulation. The work traces the emergence of the term at the turn of the century as a tool for interpreting the consequences of structural reforms, privatizations, and the retreat of state functions. It subsequently examines its reformulation toward a characterization of the functional asymmetry of state capacities, as well as its reception in academic production at the Universidad Nacional de La Plata (UNLP) and the Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA). Finally, it proposes an expansion of the framework toward the categories of State decomposition, Selective State Decomposition under Democratic Continuity, and Gradual Civic Capitulation.

title: Doors and Engines: A Theory of Selection and Treatment Effects in European Integration, with Evidence from Greece and Türkiye

detail.title: Doors and Engines: A Theory of Selection and Treatment Effects in European Integration, with Evidence from Greece and Türkiye
detail.abstract: This mixed-methods study examines whether economic development preceded or was strengthened by European Economic Community (EEC) membership through a comparative analysis of Greece and Türkiye. Drawing on economic growth, transformation, and institutional theories, it uses comparative, qualitative, and quantitative evidence to assess European integration's determinants and consequences. The findings indicate that Greece's accession depended mainly on democratic consolidation, institutional quality, and macroeconomic stability, not economic development, with long-term economic benefits emerging gradually after accession. Although full European Union (EU) membership offers larger economic gains than Türkiye's partial integration, these benefits depend on domestic institutional capacity and reform. Overall, the study concludes that accession was a political and institutional selection process, while membership acted as a conditional driver of long-term economic growth.

title: When a Few Misfits Trigger Digital Adoption Cascades Network Reach, Threshold Heterogeneity, and Performance-conditioned Complex Contagion in an Agent-based Model of Firms
affiliations: ESADE Business School, Safe Intelligence and Barcelona Supercomputing Center

detail.title: When a Few Misfits Trigger Digital Adoption Cascades Network Reach, Threshold Heterogeneity, and Performance-conditioned Complex Contagion in an Agent-based Model of Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Why does a superior technology sometimes sweep through a population of firms and sometimes stall, even when its expected returns are an order of magnitude higher? We build an explanatory agent-based model-not a forecasting model-in which firms adopt a digital technology by imitating their successful neighbours, a fast-and-frugal social-comparison heuristic in the tradition of Gigerenzer. We contrast frequency-based (bandwagon) imitation, where a firm adopts when enough of all its neighbours are digital, with performance-conditioned imitation, where it adopts when enough of the neighbours that outperform it are digital. Defining a cascade dynamically-high final adoption reached through a rapid, accelerating takeoff rather than slow accumulation-we find, in the calibrated regime studied here, that: (i) dynamic cascades are produced by performance-conditioned imitation but not by an exogenous hazard or by frequency-based imitation; (ii) on degree-controlled networks, adoption tips sharply once the network supplies enough reach (small-world rewiring β* ≈ 0.41, 95% bootstrap CI [0.39, 0.43]), a condition jointly carried by short paths, low clustering, and high-reach nodes rather than any single graph statistic; (iii) at a fixed mean threshold, concentrating receptiveness in the lower tail can trigger cascades that homogeneous thresholds cannot; and (iv) the network position of both initial adopters and low-threshold pioneers strongly conditions cascade probability. At a realistic, human-scale observation degree the mechanism is genuine complex contagion: adoptions are triggered by reinforcement from many successful exemplars, the cascade survives an explicit requirement of two or more successful digital neighbours once ignition is given an adequate, clustered seed (the Centola-Watts critical-mass signature), and-consistent with bounded cognition and the Dunbar limit-it operates within human-scale neighbourhoods and weakens beyond them. The mechanism holds over a bounded region of parameter space and the model suggests where interventions may have leverage rather than forecasting any industry. The central, carefully bounded lesson is that broad cultural change is not required for systemwide adoption: a small minority of receptive firms, placed where the network can carry their success, is enough. In short, a few misfits can change the world.

title: The Unmeasured Gap: A Swedish Study of Non-academic Absorption of Doctoral Graduates, 1973-2025, in International Context

detail.title: The Unmeasured Gap: A Swedish Study of Non-academic Absorption of Doctoral Graduates, 1973-2025, in International Context

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only publicly available, aggregated, de-identified administrative statistics (SCB, UKÄ) and previously published secondary sources; no individual-level or personally identifiable data were accessed, and no ethics review was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Across OECD countries, doctoral training has expanded faster than the supply of academic positions, and most doctorate holders now build careers outside the university sector. This paper is a register-based case study of Sweden, benchmarked against the United States, Canada, and Australia. Combining Statistics Sweden's time series on doctoral degrees (1973-2025) with its labour market establishment statistics (2017-2024), we find that national establishment rates for Swedish doctoral graduates, measured one year after graduation in SCB's Tema434 register table, rose from 84.1 to 87.5 percent between the 2017 and 2024 cohorts, with large, stable field differences: humanities and arts graduates trail medicine and health graduates by roughly 17 percentage points. Citing UKÄ's own cohort study directly (Vogiazides, Viberg, & Bergenfeldt, 2024), 56 percent of established 2013-2018 graduates worked outside the higher education sector three years on. This fits the wider international pattern: Australia alone shows an absolute imbalance (PhD numbers up 37 percent, academic posts down 13 percent, 2016-2021), and Canadian policy literature most explicitly frames the trend as a possible waste of capacity. Neither in Sweden nor across a properly powered 20-country European test do we find faster-growing fields showing weaker labour-market outcomes, evidence against a simple oversupply story. Whether this reallocation is a loss of research capacity or its redistribution remains unresolved: no register or survey we could find measures whether non-academically employed doctorate holders retain unmet interest in research. We examine why Swedish universities may resist expanding the one formal re-engagement channel we identified (adjunct research appointments) and propose five targeted institutional reforms. We propose a five-level model of research involvement, from consuming research to leading funded projects, as a concrete basis for measuring that gap in future survey work.

title: A Dual-Attention Hybrid Model for Head and Neck Lesion Segmentation from PET Images
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Turku - Turku PET Centre, University of Turku - Turku PET Centre, University of Turku - Turku PET Centre, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Turku - Turku PET Centre, University of Turku - Turku PET Centre, University of Tabriz, University of Turku - Turku PET Centre and University of Turku - Turku PET Centre

detail.title: A Dual-Attention Hybrid Model for Head and Neck Lesion Segmentation from PET Images
detail.abstract:
Background. In this paper, we propose a new dual-attention hybrid model using Adjacent Cross Attention Module (ACAM), Cross Scale Channel Attention Module (CSCAM), and bottom-up attention flow with deep supervision for head and neck cancer segmentation in positron emission tomography (PET) images.
ewline Materials and methods. Using a PET dataset of 100 patients with expert drawn tumor segmentations as the ground truth, we cross-compared our proposed method with U-Net, U-Net++, Swin UNETR, SegFormer, MBSNet and AHF-U-Net models. The ability to detect the cancerous pixels was evaluated in terms of Dice score, Jaccard index, sensitivity, and specificity. In addition, the model architecture designs were evaluated with specifically planned ablation study. Finally, the differences between the models were evaluated by detailed inspection of the effect of lesion size to the model performance. The statistical differences were determined using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
ewline Results. Our proposed method achieved the best overall segmentation performance, with the highest mean Dice score (0.51±0.06), mean sensitivity (0.603) and mean specificity (0.998) of the evaluated models. The model has relatively few parameters, only 3.1 million, requiring 2.66 G-FLOPS (one billion floating-point operations per second) performance. The ablation study showed that the unique design of our model including ACAM, CSCAM, and bottom-up attention flow are necessary to facilitate top performance. Our approach also showed improved performance with different lesion sizes.
ewline Conclusions. With novel and unique architecture designs, our model outperforms the state-of-the-art models. The performance gains are largely attributed to improved multi-scale encoder-decoder feature transfer via the ACAM and CSCAM.

title: Corruption in Nepal's Local Governments: A Case Study of Institutional Weaknesses and Citizen Outcomes

detail.title: Corruption in Nepal's Local Governments: A Case Study of Institutional Weaknesses and Citizen Outcomes
detail.abstract: This case study deals with corruption in public procurement at the local government level in Nepal. Nepal established 753 local governments with substantial responsibility for public spending, including procurement of goods, works and services, following the adoption of the Constitution in 2015. Mostly today, public spending is the responsibility of local governments, especially on capital investment in infrastructure, such as roads, schools, health facilities and water supply systems. But the speed of devolution of responsibilities has not been matched by adequate systems of transparency, accountability and integrity. This paper explores the nature and extent of corruption in local government procurement in Nepal, drawing on publicly available data from the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority, Transparency International, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and government audit reports. The analysis shows that procurement is a high-risk area for  corruption at the local level. Corrupt practices are many and include bid-rigging, inflated costs, shoddy work, kickbacks, collusion among bidders, political interference with contract awards, etc. The data show that many local governments do not follow procurement rules well, publish limited information and have weak oversight. Audit reports frequently find irregularities in procurement by local government. The paper investigates factors leading to procurement corruption including weak institutional capacity, political interference, lack of transparency, limited oversight by citizens and poor enforcement. The report ends with recommendations for improving procurement integrity, including better procurement rules, more transparency, capacity building, stronger oversight, more citizen participation, and accountability enforcement.

title: FDM-Net: Frequency-domain Decoupling and Multi-scale-aware network for medical image segmentation
affiliations: Nanchang Hangkong University and Nanchang Hangkong University

detail.title: FDM-Net: Frequency-domain Decoupling and Multi-scale-aware network for medical image segmentation
detail.abstract: To address limitations in existing medical image segmentation methods, including insufficient multi-scale feature perception, susceptibility of skip-connection feature fusion to noise and artifacts, and the inability of conventional channel attention to balance feature enhancement and noise suppression, we propose a Frequency-domain Decoupled and Multi-scale-aware network (FDM-Net). First, the encoder incorporates a Dynamic Multi-window Feature Extraction (DMFE) module. Equipped with multi-window gMLP branches and an adaptive gating mechanism, the module fuses multi-scale features to balance global contextual information and fine-grained local details, thus boosting the model’s multi-scale feature perception capability. Second, we design a Frequency-domain Decoupled Fusion (FDF) module to mitigate interference caused by noise and artifacts in skip-connection fusion. It adaptively decouples input features into high- and low-frequency components via the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). Guided by deep semantic priors derived from the decoder, the module leverages two dedicated attention branches that work collaboratively to achieve simultaneous image denoising and lesion boundary enhancement. Finally, a Differential Channel Attention (DCA) module is embedded within the bottleneck layer. Featuring an excitation-suppression dual-path architecture, it adaptively enhances lesion-relevant features while suppressing undesired background noise, achieving synergistic optimization between feature enhancement and noise suppression. Extensive comparative experiments on three public datasets (ISIC 2018, Synapse, and ACDC) demonstrate that FDM-Net achieves DSC improvements of 0.13%, 0.44%, and 0.32%, respectively, relative to state-of-the-art baselines. Such performance validates the generalizability of FDM-Net in medical image segmentation scenarios with large lesion scale variations and complex noise environments.

title: The Distributional Misery Index (DMI) Making the Five Economies Visible

detail.title: The Distributional Misery Index (DMI) Making the Five Economies Visible

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research received no external financial or non-financial support.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable to this research as no patients or participants were involved in this work.
declarations.funderStatement: The author funded this research. There are no additional relationships to disclose.

detail.abstract:
The Distributional Misery Index (DMI) is a distribution-aware extension of the classic Misery Index, commonly defined as the sum of inflation and unemployment. The classic measure provides a compact gauge of macroeconomic discomfort but treats national averages as though they describe a common household experience. The DMI adds the question the aggregate leaves unanswered: for whom?

The DMI applies the Five Economies framework, which is the proposition that one national economy can produce materially different lived conditions across the income distribution, and operationalizes it through By Fifths analysis. It combines income-quintile-weighted consumer-price inflation with a transparent measure of labor-market slack. Recurring public releases are currently national; geographic differentiation remains a planned extension.

The operational family has two specifications. Baseline combines quintile-weighted headline CPI inflation with U-3 unemployment. Slack-Plus substitutes U-6 labor underutilization where comparable data are available. Core is an intended third specification that would exclude food and energy, but it has not been implemented or validated and is not part of the operational public family. The current eight-category CPI–Consumer Expenditure mapping cannot isolate all relevant energy components. A manifest-driven monthly process separates reference periods, data vintages, methodological versions, specifications, and quality-assurance results.

The canonical result is a five-quintile profile. Four summaries describe distinct features of that profile: DMI Median reports its middle value; DMI Stress its maximum; Income Pressure Spread the nonnegative maximum-minus-minimum distance; and Income Pressure Tilt the signed Q1-minus-Q5 contrast. Because the current method applies the same labor-slack rate to every quintile, cross-quintile differences arise from the distributional inflation component. Quintile-specific labor slack remains a research extension.

The note also distinguishes the CPI-based DMI from the Bureau of Economic Analysis income-stratified Personal Consumption Expenditures price index. The two systems differ in scope, weighting, and purpose and provide a useful comparison and validation track. Evidence that income-group inflation gaps may be modest or regime-dependent reinforces the project’s central discipline: distributional heterogeneity should be measured rather than presumed.

The DMI is descriptive, not prescriptive. It is intended to improve visibility, comparison, and empirical inquiry, not to serve as a comprehensive welfare index, causal model, or mechanical policy rule.

reference: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Working Paper No. RWP26-09
title: Cautious Careers: Job Mobility under Incomplete Markets
affiliations: Paris School of Economics (PSE), University of Leicester - Department of Economics, Finance and Accounting, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Cautious Careers: Job Mobility under Incomplete Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Working Paper No. RWP26-09
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Job mobility is risky, workers are risk averse, and insurance markets are incomplete. This paper studies how these features curb and distort job-to-job transitions by making workers excessively cautious, placing too much weight on job safety over wage and productivity gains. We demonstrate this tradeoff by eliciting employed workers' wage-safety indifference curves in a custom, representative survey. On average, employed U.S. workers require a 1.63 percent pay raise to accept each additional percentage point of annual unemployment risk in a new job. We assess the macroeconomic consequences of our mechanism by embedding it into a general equilibrium search model. Jobs differ in both wages (productivity) and unemployment risk, and risk-averse workers self-insure against unemployment risk through a non-state-contingent bond while searching on and off the job. We find that a complete markets counterfactual would boost job mobility by 12 percent and productivity by 0.19 percent. We also highlight a new role for unemployment insurance-encouraging employed workers to accept risky but highproductivity offers, thereby increasing productivity (by 1.3 percent) and job creation, as well as job loss and unemployment.

title: Housing-Market Equilibrium, Resident Selection, and the Endogeneity of Local Income

detail.title: Housing-Market Equilibrium, Resident Selection, and the Endogeneity of Local Income

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
A local housing market is also a spatial allocation mechanism: the equilibrium housing cost affects not only the price of occupying a location but also the composition of households able to occupy it. This paper studies the information consequence of that equilibrium selection. In a constrained local housing market with heterogeneous resident demand and positive turnover, an outward housing-demand shock raises the clearing price. When lower-purchasing-capacity resident demand is more price-sensitive than higher-purchasing-capacity resident demand, current resident allocation shifts toward the latter group; turnover then carries that allocation difference into the resident stock, raising observed resident income even when within-group incomes do not change.

The model therefore characterizes observed resident income as partly an equilibrium outcome. The main result shows that the selection-induced response of observed resident income and structural housing-price responsiveness to locally anchored purchasing capacity depend on different combinations of demand primitives. Consequently, the same post-selection price–resident-income relationship can coexist with different structural local-income responsiveness. Observed local price–income comovement therefore need not identify structural price anchoring to the purchasing capacity of a compositionally stable resident population. Non-local housing demand provides a transparent initiating shock, while an affordability implication follows as a secondary corollary.

title:
Quantifying Maturity of Complex System of Humankind [Series Paper #12]: 
The Super-invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Quantifying Maturity of Complex System of Humankind [Series Paper #12]: 
The Super-invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind

declarations.ethicsApproval: There were no patients/participants in this study. No ethics approval is needed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was not funded by anybody.

detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the macro-historical trajectory of humankind by conceptualizing it as a single complex system spanning from 50,200 BCE to 2026 CE. By applying complex systems methodologies, the Super-Invention (SI) Taxonomy, and quantitative metrics-specifically the System Maturity Index (SMI) and the SMI Ceiling (SMIC)-the study models the evolution of systemic complexity over millennia. Through comparative testing of linear and Rogers-based diffusion distribution models, the research demonstrates structural invariance across accumulation curves. 
       The findings reveal five distinct evolutionary phases, highlighting a contemporary convergence in which humankind has transitioned into tight structural coupling, exhausting historical diffusion buffers and binding future evolution to the immediate generation rate of new super-inventions.

title: Misreading Social Identity Theory: Why Affective Polarization Research Got It Wrong
affiliations: University of Kansas - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Misreading Social Identity Theory: Why Affective Polarization Research Got It Wrong
detail.abstract: This paper challenges the theoretical foundation on which contemporary research on affective polarisation rests. Since Iyengar et al. (2012), scholars have largely attributed partisan hostility to social identity theory, assuming that group membership automatically produces both in-group favouritism and out-group dislike. I argue that this interpretation is based on a fundamental misreading of Tajfel (1972)'s original theory. The minimal-group experiments that gave rise to social identity theory examined behavioural discrimination in resource allocation, not emotional hostility toward out-groups. By conflating discrimination with dislike, subsequent research has overstated the emotional consequences of partisan identity while neglecting the role of intergroup conflict. Drawing on Realistic Conflict Theory, this article develops a conflict-centred framework that distinguishes identity, discriminatory behaviour, and negative affect. It shows that hostile emotions towards out-groups arise from conflict rather than from social categorisation itself. This reinterpretation clarifies a long-standing conceptual error and situates affective polarisation within a broader theory of group conflict and political emotion.

title: The AI Judge: Algorithmic Decision-Making, Due Process and the Future of Judicial Power

detail.title: The AI Judge: Algorithmic Decision-Making, Due Process and the Future of Judicial Power

keywords: The AI Judge: Algorithmic Decision-Making and Due Process 2 Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: Judicial systems across multiple jurisdictions are integrating artificial intelligence into adjudicative workflows, ranging from decision-support tools that summarize evidence to systems that generate sentencing recommendations and draft judgments. This article asks whether the due-process requirement that a court give reasons for its decision imposes a structural limit on how far that integration may go before it changes the legal character of the act itself. Using doctrinal and comparative analysis across Brazil, the United States, the European Union, and China, together with the Council of Europe's ethical framework for judicial artificial intelligence, the article argues that the reason-giving requirement is not merely an evidentiary or transparency safeguard but a constitutive element of judicial power: a court's authority to bind the parties depends on the availability of a reviewable, case-specific justification that a human judge has authored and can defend. Statistical and pattern-matching systems, however accurate in the aggregate, cannot supply that justification because their outputs are correlational rather than case-specific reasons. The article develops this distinction through State v. Loomis, Brazil's evolving judicial artificial intelligence regulation, the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, and China's Shanghai "206 System," and proposes the Motivated Adjudication Continuity Standard, a governance framework that distinguishes lawful decision-support functions from unlawful decision-substitution functions and ties the permissible scope of judicial artificial intelligence to whether human-authored reasoning remains the operative legal act. The article concludes that the central regulatory task is not to prohibit or license artificial intelligence in courts as such, but to preserve the specific institutional practice-giving reasons that a losing party can contest-on which judicial legitimacy depends.

title: The Cost of Commitment: What Standard Diligence Does Not Measure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Cost of Commitment: What Standard Diligence Does Not Measure
detail.abstract:
When a mid-market company signs its first or second major vendor commitment (an ERP, a CRM, an AI platform), the contract price is not the real number. On a $7.5 million deal, the costs that arrive after signature typically run another $1.9 to $3.1 million. Standard diligence is not built to see them, and the moment to act on them is before signing, while leverage still exists. 

The Cost of Commitment introduces a five-component model for estimating those costs deal by deal, before the agreement is signed. Two of the components (what a vendor's ownership change costs a buyer and what an underused bundle costs), have not been priced anywhere else. The model grounds the switching-cost, incomplete-contract and lock-in literature in two decades of implementation evidence, and applies it through a worked example run as a base case and a high-cost case. It is built for the operating leaders and investors around companies in the $40 to $70 million range, where one of these commitments lands against thin margins and a small pool of leadership attention.

title:
The Future of Quantitative Finance: 
Simulating People, Simulating the World

detail.title:
The Future of Quantitative Finance: 
Simulating People, Simulating the World
detail.abstract: This paper proposes two objects for the next generation of quantitative research: simulate people, simulate the world. It begins with a failed trader-distillation experiment. A model learned portions of the author's trading behavior but did not reproduce his out-of-sample advantage; its short sub-strategy lost money. The failure suggests that executions are lossy projections of intuition. What must be learned is how an expert selects information, comprehends regimes, revises beliefs, allocates risk, and abstains. Yet even a successful human twin cannot generate prices alone. Prices emerge from heterogeneous participants, institutions, information diffusion, liquidity, and order matching. We therefore propose a human-world dual-distillation framework: identify an expert's market situation awareness and control process; embed agents with different horizons, roles, and constraints in a runnable virtual market; inject earnings or policy shocks under strict point-in-time locks; and accelerate many possible worlds. The framework survives only if it explains beliefs, orders, liquidity, and prices on unseen events and adds value beyond mature same-information benchmarks.

title: Does Director Tenure Erode Board Monitoring Effectiveness? Evidence from India
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Does Director Tenure Erode Board Monitoring Effectiveness? Evidence from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency.

detail.abstract: In September 2018, IL&FS defaulted on more than ₹91,000 crore of debt, despite having independent directors, external auditors, and 169 subsidiaries that each filed their own regulatory returns. Every formal governance requirement was satisfied. The monitoring failed anyway. This paper argues that formal independence is not what predicts when boards stop working. Tenure is. Among India's largest listed companies by market capitalisation, sixty-six per cent are promoter-controlled (OECD, 2020), and in firms like these, directors who stay long enough alongside a dominant shareholder tend to stop challenging them. The Companies Act 2013 introduced the first statutory tenure cap on independent directors in Indian corporate law, which created the exogenous variation this question needs. Because pre-existing tenure was reset rather than carried forward, the main displacement wave under the reform is concentrated around 2024, once the first cohort of directors completed two fresh five-year terms. I use a difference-indifferences design across approximately 1,500 to 2,000 listed firms from 2010 to 2025, with treatment measured by the share of directors displaced by the cap. Primary outcomes are earnings quality, related-party transaction intensity, and audit quality. If tenure, not independence, is the binding constraint, then a decade of governance reform built around formal independence may have been solving the wrong problem.

title:
Refundable Stake does not Expand Deterrent Capacity in Long-lived Delegation: 
Collateral, Premia, and Pseudonymous Markets
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title:
Refundable Stake does not Expand Deterrent Capacity in Long-lived Delegation: 
Collateral, Premia, and Pseudonymous Markets
detail.abstract: Practitioners of delegated pseudonymous markets, from proof-of-stake validation to agent economies, commonly assume that a slashable, refundable bond deters misconduct: the operator who cheats loses the stake, so a larger stake buys more honesty. This draft reports the central result of a formal project testing that assumption: in the strict long-match limit, increasing refundable escrow does not expand the credible capacity frontier. In a model where identities can be discarded and re-minted at negligible cost, a refundable bond released at exit pads the operator's walk-away value by the full release-discounted principal; custody carry is an additional tax. In the strict long-match limit, refundable escrowed principal weakly contracts the credible capacity frontier in all four cells of a two-by-two regime map spanning exit versus in-place misconduct and leaky versus captive stake: the contraction is strict in both exit cells and strict in both stay cells if and only if the adjudication probability is positive. The relationship premium supplies the continuation-value component of deterrence. The capacity frontier is identically $\theta X \le P + \varphi (d_h - R) F$ against exit misconduct and, at the baseline with no clawback and no continuation damage, $\theta X \le p P + p [d_h - (1-s) \delta_E] F$ against in-place misconduct. Those displays are accounting identities at a given $(P, F)$; the envelope derivatives in $F$ are the slopes reported below, which already include the decline of $P$ in $F$. Away from the limit, escrow has a positive marginal effect only under turnover-funded admission conditions derived in closed form; at the ideal leaky-exit corner this requires timely filing coverage above a floor that exceeds one in the strict long-match limit with positive carry. The result yields a regime-general capacity prediction; deriving predictions for observed misconduct rates requires an additional behavioral model, offered here as a conjecture. A second, conditional result endogenizes the market outside option and bounds admissible entry fees; whether a small fee also selects among formation equilibria remains open pending an extensive-form formation game.

reference: American Journal of International Law Unbound (forthcoming 2026)
title: Interviews as a Method for Rule of Law Measurement
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley Law School, University of California, Berkeley - School of Law  and Temple University - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Interviews as a Method for Rule of Law Measurement

keywords: Court of Justice of the European Union

publicationDetails.detailsText: American Journal of International Law Unbound (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract: The rule of law is measured in many ways: through surveys of expert opinions and public perceptions, institutional proxies, and assessment of political, legislative, and judicial events bearing on the rule of law. This essay argues that systematic interviewing of judges and other legal elites belongs in the empirical toolkit of rule-of-law scholarship. The methodological literature in political science has solidified best practices for interviewing and has demonstrated that interviews can be a rigorous method for eliciting information when designed with care around selection, design, and reporting. Interviews also draw on comparative advantages that legal scholars possess, including access, shared professional vocabulary about substance and procedure, and the capacity to read silence. Interviews offer empirical access to the inside view of the actors whose decisions other measurement approaches capture only at a distance. We share these insights and apply them to rule of law measurement. To motivate these claims with empirical evidence, and illustrate best practices, we draw on 24 on-the-record interviews conducted in 2024 with sitting members of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU).

title: Condemning Monopoly
affiliations: Delaware Law School

detail.title: Condemning Monopoly
detail.abstract: Monopoly is harmful. But under U.S. antitrust law, only monopoly acquired or maintained by exclusionary conduct is unlawful. At the same time, the U.S. Constitution permits property to be taken for "public use" as long as the property owner receives just compensation. "Public use" is a fairly low bar, as it merely means that the property must be used for a "public purpose." The Supreme Court's decision in Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff holds that one such valid public purpose is the correction of an "oligopoly" in land. This article tests the limits of that holding. It does so by contemplating the use of the eminent domain power to correct monopolistic markets. In undertaking this analysis, this article is a thought experiment that assesses whether the eminent domain power is a sleeper pro-competition tool that is outside of the antitrust laws.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium in the Financing of State Contracts: Analytical Resolution of an Intertemporal Signaling Game to Determine Equilibrium Interest Rates

detail.title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium in the Financing of State Contracts: Analytical Resolution of an Intertemporal Signaling Game to Determine Equilibrium Interest Rates
detail.abstract: In Colombian public procurement, contractors who win a state contract often require private financing for working capital, especially when the contract does not include a sufficient advance payment. Private lenders face information asymmetry: they do not know with certainty the contractor's true execution capacity or default risk. The SECOP system (Public Procurement Electronic System) provides an observable track record of past performance that can serve as an intertemporal signal about the contractor's type. We formalize a dynamic game with three players: the State (principal), the contractor (informed agent), and the private lender (financial principal). The relevant equilibrium is a Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium (PBE), which extends the Bayesian Nash Equilibrium concept to sequential games with beliefs updated by Bayes' rule.

title: The Role of E-Governance in Reducing Corruption in Local Government: A Case Study of Pakistan
affiliations: Hazara University Mansehra, University of Haripur, Hazara University, University of Genoa, University of the Punjab and Xi’an Jiaotong University

detail.title: The Role of E-Governance in Reducing Corruption in Local Government: A Case Study of Pakistan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based entirely on secondary data (published literature, government documents, and publicly available reports) and does not involve human participants or primary data collection. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Corruption in local government remains one of the more persistent obstacles to effective public service delivery in Pakistan, particularly in routine transactions where citizens must repeatedly approach officials to get ordinary work done. This qualitative study asks a fairly simple question: can e-governance actually narrow the space in which this kind of everyday corruption occurs, and if so, how? Using Pakistan as a bounded case, the paper draws on secondary sourcesacademic literature, government documents, and assessments from international bodies published mainly between 2010 and 2026and analyses them thematically, guided by a Principal-Agent framework of corruption. The services examined include police clearance certificates, digital land records, vehicle and tax services, digital payments, online complaint systems, and e-procurement. What emerges from this analysis is that digitalization tends to reduce face-to-face interaction, improve transparency, and strengthen the traceability of records, while also giving citizens a more direct channel to raise complaints. At the same time, none of this happens automatically; institutional capacity, digital literacy, and basic infrastructure all shape how far these gains actually go. In my view, the more useful way to think about e-governance is not as a cure for corruption but as a mechanism that narrows its opportunities, one that only works fully alongside institutional reform. This paper also tries to close a specific gap in the literature by defining Pakistan clearly as the case under study, separating local-government relevance from provincial and federal examples, and situating the discussion within a qualitative, mechanism-level lens that much of the existing e-governance literature does not adopt.

title: Asymptotic Limits of Macro-Fx Fragility: A Mathematical Demonstration on The Limiting Behavior of Colombian International Reserves as Exchange Rate Volatility Tends to Infinity

detail.title: Asymptotic Limits of Macro-Fx Fragility: A Mathematical Demonstration on The Limiting Behavior of Colombian International Reserves as Exchange Rate Volatility Tends to Infinity
detail.abstract: We construct a continuous-time stochastic model showing that if the exchange rate volatility tends to infinity and the central bank defends a fixed exchange rate barrier using finite international reserves, then the reserves are exhausted almost surely in the limit. The proof uses continuous martingale theory, local time, and Fatou's lemma.

title: Closed-Form Formulas for Volatility Surfaces Under Affine Jump-Diffusion: Derivation of an Analytical Solution Via Characteristic Functions and Fourier Transforms for Option Pricing

detail.title: Closed-Form Formulas for Volatility Surfaces Under Affine Jump-Diffusion: Derivation of an Analytical Solution Via Characteristic Functions and Fourier Transforms for Option Pricing
detail.abstract: The model integrates historical derivatives chains and formulates an affine stochastic process that captures implied volatility without resorting to numerical simulations. A detailed methodological derivation is presented for constructing implied volatility surfaces using affine jump-diffusion models, characteristic functions, and Fourier transforms.
