The approach avoids Monte Carlo simulations and finite-difference methods, reducing the problem to one-dimensional integrations and the solution of ordinary differential equations.

title: CBAM Exposure and EU Flat-Steel Sourcing

detail.title: CBAM Exposure and EU Flat-Steel Sourcing
detail.abstract: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism creates a simple prediction: higher-carbon foreign suppliers should lose EU business. Using complete monthly Eurostat Comext data for 52 flat-steel CN8 products, I test that prediction during January-June 2026. A same-calendar-month seconddifference design finds no stable negative relationship between default-based CBAM exposure and import value, quantity, or sourcing share. The result is not a precise zero: influential origins, alternative risk sets, and safeguard treatment move the estimate. The evidence is best read as an early non-detection of broad cross-origin reallocation, not evidence that CBAM had no effect.

title: Unraveling the Disagreement-Return Nexus: The Role of Mispricing
affiliations: Birmingham Business School and University of Hull

detail.title: Unraveling the Disagreement-Return Nexus: The Role of Mispricing
detail.abstract: We empirically resolve conflicting evidence on the relation between investor disagreement and expected returns by showing this relation crucially depends on stock mispricing. Using various disagreement proxies, we document a negative relation between disagreement and expected returns for overpriced stocks and a positive relation for underpriced stocks. Our results are unlikely driven by alternative mechanisms but align closely with the model of Atmaz and Basak (2018). Using Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD) as an exogenous shock to disagreement, we observe a significant surge in disagreement following its adoption. This increase in disagreement enhances the dual relationships between disagreement on mispricing.

title: Capital Market Development and Economic Growth in Uganda: Structural Constraints, Transmission Channels, And Policy Priorities
affiliations: Sahm Capital

detail.title: Capital Market Development and Economic Growth in Uganda: Structural Constraints, Transmission Channels, And Policy Priorities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial, professional, personal, or other competing interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper. The research was conducted independently, and the views and conclusions expressed are solely those of the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, personal data, interviews, surveys, or experimental procedures. The research is based exclusively on secondary data, published literature, and publicly available institutional and market information. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval and participant consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was independently conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how capital market development can support economic growth in Uganda and why the growth-enhancing potential of the market remains only partially activated. Rather than estimating a new causal model, the study adopts a policy-oriented analytical case-study approach, synthesising established finance-growth theory, prior empirical research, and secondary institutional and market evidence relating to the Uganda Securities Exchange (USE), the Capital Markets Authority of Uganda (CMA), and Uganda's broader macro-financial environment. The analysis focuses on four transmission channels: mobilisation of long-term savings, allocation of capital to productive investment, improvements in corporate governance and information disclosure, and attraction of domestic and cross-border investment. Uganda has established important institutional foundations since the 1990s, including a securities regulator, an organised exchange, dematerialised and automated market infrastructure, and participation in regional integration initiatives. However, the market remains characterised by a small domestic listing base, thin secondary-market liquidity, limited corporate debt issuance, narrow product diversity, and a concentrated institutional investor base. The central argument of the paper is therefore not that capital market development has already caused higher economic growth in Uganda, but that the institutional architecture exists while the principal transmission mechanisms remain constrained by insufficient scale, liquidity, participation, and intermediation. Emerging opportunities-including oil-sector investment needs, a young population, digital finance, collective investment schemes, and East African and pan-African market integration-could strengthen these mechanisms if accompanied by sequenced reforms. The paper proposes a policy agenda centred on issuer development, investor-base expansion, corporate bond-market deepening, digital distribution, market infrastructure, regulatory capacity, and regional integration. The Ugandan case illustrates a broader lesson for frontier markets: establishing an exchange is a necessary institutional step, but sustained economic impact depends on whether the market becomes sufficiently deep, liquid, trusted, and connected to the financing needs of the real economy.

title: Spillover Effect of Non-technological Strategic Alliances on Innovation

detail.title: Spillover Effect of Non-technological Strategic Alliances on Innovation
detail.abstract: We study the relation between non-technological alliances and firm innovation. Commercial partnerships (marketing, licensing, and manufacturing agreements) account for the majority of alliance activity, yet the literature linking alliances to innovation has concentrated on technology partnerships and the knowledge transfer they permit. In a panel of U.S. firms from 1996 to 2023, non-technological alliance formation is followed by higher patent counts and citation-weighted output for up to three years. The composition of the response carries the economic content: gains concentrate in technology classes the firm already occupies, selfcitations and within-class backward citations rise, and entry into new classes barely moves. Three designs fix the timing and the location of the response. An event study centered on the firm's first alliance shows entry into new classes turning negative at formation, with no pre-trend. The elevated patenting does not decay when a partner is lost to an outside acquirer, the signature of a capability the firm owns rather than a flow the partner supplied. And within a single firm-year, the rise concentrates in the technology classes tied to the firm's product domain, a margin firm-level selection cannot reach. The evidence favors specialization within established competencies rather than knowledge acquisition.

title: Profitability and Working Capital Management Nexus: Evidence from Food & Personal Care Products Sector Firms Listed on Pakistan Stock Exchange
affiliations: Institute of Management Studies, University of Peshawar and University of Peshawar

detail.title: Profitability and Working Capital Management Nexus: Evidence from Food & Personal Care Products Sector Firms Listed on Pakistan Stock Exchange
detail.abstract: Working capital management (WCM) usually have an essential role to play in a firm's overall performance, especially those of manufacturing sector. The key aim of the current research work is to find the empirical association amid profitability and working capital management of the Food & Personal Care Product sector Pakistani firms. Eight companies are selected randomly as a sample from the firms listed on Pakistan Stock Exchange. Secondary data for six years, that is, 2010-2016 is gathered from the financial reports of these companies and evaluated through Pearson correlation coefficient and regression analysis techniques, using STATA software. The results prove that Return on Assets (ROA) is negatively correlated with Average Collection Period (ACP) and positively correlated with Inventory Turnover in Days (ITID), Average Payment Period (APP), Current Ratio (CR) and Sales Growth (SG). All the relationships are significant except ITID and SG ones.

title: ETF Tax Efficiency and Firm Payout Policy
affiliations: Boston College - Carroll School of Management, Boston College and

detail.title: ETF Tax Efficiency and Firm Payout Policy
detail.abstract: We examine whether the unique tax efficiency of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) influences the payout policies of their portfolio firms. Unlike mutual funds, ETFs can shield investors from taxable capital gains distributions but cannot shield them from dividends, which generate immediate taxable income. We hypothesize that this asymmetry incentivizes ETFs to discourage dividends to improve after-tax investor returns and attract fund flows. Consistent with this prediction, ETF ownership is negatively associated with dividend payouts, particularly when ETFs have more tax-sensitive investor clienteles. To strengthen identification, we exploit Vanguard's addition of ETF share classes to existing index funds, which increased the funds' tax efficiency without changing their portfolios or passive investment strategies. Firms with greater exposure to the affected funds subsequently reduced dividends. Additional tests show that financially flexible firms substitute repurchases for dividends and thereby maintain overall payouts. These findings are timely given recent SEC exemptive relief permitting active mutual funds to offer ETF share classes, which may accelerate the expansion of ETF ownership and amplify the tax-based incentives shaping corporate payout policy.

title: SOEs to SOEs: Unpacking the Role of China’s Soes as Contractors and Financiers for Sri Lanka’s SOE Projects
affiliations: and

detail.title: SOEs to SOEs: Unpacking the Role of China’s Soes as Contractors and Financiers for Sri Lanka’s SOE Projects

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by Arutha Research in Sri Lanka and originally published by them.

detail.abstract:
Over the last two decades, China has become a major financing source for Sri Lanka's infrastructure development. China’s state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and policy banks started working closely with Sri Lanka in the early 2000s, initially with post-tsunami reconstruction, and later in the construction of the Puttalam coal power plant and the Hambantota Port. Both these large-scale projects were financed by loans provided by the China EXIM Bank to Sri Lankan government.

However, from 2010 onwards, the economic relationship between Chinese SOEs and their Sri Lankan counterparts evolved, as they began increasingly interacting directly with each other in financing and implementing infrastructure projects. These interactions include working together on infrastructure projects and, in at least one case, directly financing a project. The findings of this report shed light on how China’s involvement in Sri Lanka’s public debt goes beyond just official government-to-government loans and the well-known Chinese policy banks like the China EXIM Bank and China Development Bank (CDB).

The study analyses five selected infrastructure projects implemented by Sri Lanka SOEs and financed by Chinese creditors. China’s SOEs in Sri Lanka and how their relationship with Sri Lanka’s SOEs has evolved, and how these SOE-led projects were not implemented explicitly as part of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). They reflected the profit-driven goals and the complex, fragmented nature of China’s SOEs. Such fragmentation is also seen within China’s SOEs, with subsidiaries of large entities operating in unrelated sectors.

title: Beyond the Monolith: Population Disaggregation and the Analytical Limits of the "People of Color" Category in Racial Microaggression Research

detail.title: Beyond the Monolith: Population Disaggregation and the Analytical Limits of the "People of Color" Category in Racial Microaggression Research
detail.abstract: Racial microaggression scholarship has developed substantially since Chester Pierce's early formulation of microaggressions as subtle racial put-downs directed toward Black people. Later scholarship broadened the construct to examine the experiences of multiple racial and ethnic populations, often through the umbrella category "people of color" (POC). This expansion made important contributions to the study of subtle racism, but it also created a methodological question that warrants renewed attention: when Black Americans are analytically aggregated with non-Black people of color, can population-specific patterns be obscured? This critique does not argue that POC should not be studied, nor does it contend that earlier microaggression findings are incorrect or invalid. Rather, it argues that disaggregation should precede aggregation when Black American experiences are included in a broader POC category. Gentry's (2024) quantitative study provides an empirical basis for this concern. The study classified Black American-sounding, POC-sounding, and White American-sounding names separately before analysis. Following study exclusions, the analytic categories contained 73 Black American-soundingname vignettes, 132 POC-sounding-name vignettes, and 135 White American-sounding-name vignettes. The Black American analysis yielded a statistically significant relationship between culturally relevant Black American-sounding names and potential microaggressive characteristics, χ 2 (16) = 112.625, p < .001, Cramér's V = .368, whereas the separately analyzed POC category did not yield a statistically significant relationship. These findings illustrate the potential for aggregate racial categories to attenuate or conceal subgroup-specific patterns. Building on Pierce (1970), Lazarsfeld (1937), Lazarsfeld and Barton (1951), Sue et al. (2007), Lilienfeld (2017), and subsequent measurement research, this article proposes population disaggregation as a methodological safeguard and develops Typological and Severity Stratification as a framework for preserving population specificity in racial microaggression research.

title: Beyond Assets under Management: A Comparative Framework for Measuring Fiduciary Service Quality

detail.title: Beyond Assets under Management: A Comparative Framework for Measuring Fiduciary Service Quality
detail.abstract: Assets under management (AUM) is widely used to describe the reach of fiduciary institutions, yet it measures the volume placed inside an arrangement rather than the quality with which entrusted functions are performed. This structured comparative review examines fiduciary architectures in the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Singapore, and China across personal trusts, pensions, collective investment arrangements, corporate trusteeship, and restructuring uses. It develops a function-state-evidence framework that evaluates five core functions-asset segregation, administration, discretion, monitoring, and transition-under normal operations, conflict, stress, and termination. Evidence is organized into legal design, operating process, and realized outcomes. Seven quality dimensions follow: legal integrity, mandate fidelity, competence, operational reliability, transparency, accountability, and resolvability. The review argues against a universal scalar ranking because fiduciary mandates differ in purpose and state dependence. It instead proposes a modular dashboard with minimum gates, functionspecific indicators, and stress-state tests. The framework separates fiduciary capacity from asset volume and provides a common measurement language for regulators, beneficiaries, researchers, and service providers.

title: Happiness Literacy: An Evidence-Based Conceptualization and Competency Framework for Happiness and Well-Being

detail.title: Happiness Literacy: An Evidence-Based Conceptualization and Competency Framework for Happiness and Well-Being

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval was required for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: The author did not receive any funding for this study.

detail.abstract: Happiness and well-being (HWB) are increasingly recognized as important goals of individual and societal development, yet individuals often lack the competencies to critically engage with the complex evidence on what contributes to lasting HWB. This paper develops Happiness Literacy as a domain-specific, evidence-based knowledge-to-action concept. First, the conceptual architecture of domain-specific literacies is systematically examined to identify their defining components and competency structure. This architecture is then applied to the knowledge domain of HWB, drawing on the most cited literature since 1960 from interdisciplinary HWB research. On this basis, five competency dimensions are derived and substantively specified: Access and Understand, Interpret and Evaluate, Critically Reflect, Apply and Act, and Shape and Transform. The framework integrates knowledge on dispositional, situational, interactionist, and intentional influences on HWB across individual, interpersonal, organizational, community, societal, and planetary levels. It thereby extends literacy beyond knowing and communicating about HWB toward the critical reflection, purposeful application, and transformation of knowledge into action. Happiness Literacy can help individuals critically navigate mechanisms such as hedonic adaptation, social comparison, status competition, choice overload, and time scarcity while strengthening intrinsic motivation, self-concordance, meaningful relationships, and intentional HWB-enhancing action. Rather than prescribing a universal formula for HWB, it enables individuals and collectives to critically examine what contributes to HWB, for whom, under which conditions, over what time horizon, and with what consequences for others and the wider world. The conceptualization of Happiness Literacy provides a conceptual foundation for future empirical measurement and educational, organizational, and policy applications.

title: Financing Development in a Warming World: Climate Finance, Economic Resilience, and the Future of Emerging Economies

detail.title: Financing Development in a Warming World: Climate Finance, Economic Resilience, and the Future of Emerging Economies
detail.abstract:
Emerging and developing economies face a structural macroeconomic paradox: they are simultaneously the least responsible for historical emissions and the most exposed to catastrophic climate damages, while also bearing the world’s highest cost of capital. As the report states, “Emerging Market and Developing Economies… require an estimated $2.4 trillion in annual climate-related investment by 2030” and yet confront “nominal Weighted Average Costs of Capital (WACC) ranging from 12% to 22%… compared to 3.5% to 5.0% in Western Europe and North America.”

This document demonstrates that climate finance is not an environmental adjunct but a foundational macroeconomic requirement for global financial stability, sovereign debt solvency, and long-run development. Physical climate shocks impose permanent GDP losses—up to 22.6% in Sub‑Saharan Africa and 24.5% in South Asia under 3°C warming—through labor productivity decline, capital stock destruction, hydropower volatility, and chronic supply chain disruptions.

The report shows that resilient infrastructure delivers high Total Factor Productivity (TFP) multipliers, with every dollar invested generating $4.20 in avoided losses and economic co-benefits, preserving growth trajectories and preventing fiscal diversion traps. Blended finance architectures—combining first‑loss concessional capital, FX liquidity facilities, mezzanine debt, and senior institutional tranches—mobilize private investment at a 1:6.4 ratio, transforming previously unbankable projects into investment‑grade assets.

Sovereign debt innovations such as Debt‑for‑Climate Swaps, Climate‑Resilient Debt Clauses (CRDCs), and SDR hybrid capital structures can unlock over $300 billion in fiscal space while maintaining credit rating neutrality. The report outlines a strategic roadmap centered on country platforms, domestic resource mobilization, and MDB capital adequacy reform to expand multilateral lending by $1 trillion over the next decade.

Ultimately, the analysis argues that financing climate resilience in emerging economies is the most cost‑effective global risk management strategy available. Failure to act will trigger sovereign default cascades, destabilize global trade, and erode decades of development gains; decisive investment can instead convert climate risk into a driver of productivity, industrial modernization, and shared prosperity.

title: Mitigation Architecture for a Networked Global Polycrisis: Designing Cross-Sector Interventions to Reduce Climate, Ecological, and Economic Contagion

detail.title: Mitigation Architecture for a Networked Global Polycrisis: Designing Cross-Sector Interventions to Reduce Climate, Ecological, and Economic Contagion
detail.abstract:
The report develops an integrated macro‑financial and ecological framework for mitigating the accelerating Networked Global Polycrisis—a condition where climate shocks, ecological degradation, supply‑chain failures, and sovereign debt distress interact through non‑linear feedback loops, producing systemic losses far greater than the sum of individual risks. As the document states, “shocks in one node propagate across physical, financial, and ecological boundaries, triggering cascading failures across the entire global topology.”

Using multi‑layer directed graph modeling, the analysis demonstrates how climate‑driven agricultural failures, water scarcity, energy disruptions, and sovereign fiscal erosion reinforce one another, culminating in global GDP‑at‑risk of 18.5% by 2050 under unmanaged conditions. Cross‑sector interventions—including Climate‑Resilient Debt Clauses (CRDCs), debt‑for‑nature swaps, regenerative agriculture, strategic food‑energy buffer reserves, natural capital accounting, and macroprudential SVaR regulation—reduce losses to 3.1%, avoiding $36.4 trillion annually. As summarized in the report, full implementation “reduces projected 2050 global GDP loss from 18.5% down to 3.1% (saving $36.4T annually).”

The proposed architecture operates across three phases (2026–2040): immediate liquidity firewalls and supply‑chain buffers; structural rewiring of nexus systems and sovereign debt relief; and long‑term integration of natural capital into national accounts. The report concludes by recommending the establishment of a UN‑IMF‑World Bank Polycrisis Mitigation Council (PMC) with authority to trigger parametric debt pauses, harmonize cross‑sector policies, and coordinate global resilience investments.

Overall, the framework positions cross‑sector buffering, sovereign debt reform, and ecological asset valuation as the highest‑leverage tools for preventing macro‑financial fragmentation and stabilizing the global economy in an era of compounding systemic shocks.

title: Toward an HR Credibility Matrix: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Employee Trust in the Human Resources Function
affiliations: Bharathidasan Institute of Management (BIM)

detail.title: Toward an HR Credibility Matrix: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Employee Trust in the Human Resources Function

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable (no human participants)
declarations.funderStatement: self-funded

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual framework, termed the HR Credibility Matrix, for understanding how employees form trust judgments about the human resources (HR) function as a distinct organizational actor. Building on organizational trust theory (Mayer, Davis, & Schoorman, 1995), organizational justice theory (Greenberg, 1987), and the psychological contract literature (Rousseau, 1995), the framework organizes the formation of HR credibility into four sequential stages: organizational context and drivers, mediating employee perceptions, the HR credibility matrix itself, and downstream organizational outcomes. The framework is offered as a conceptual contribution intended to guide subsequent empirical, qualitative investigation, and as a diagnostic tool practitioners can use to identify where in the trust-formation sequence HR credibility is being gained or lost.

reference: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-15
title: China's Economic Security Growth Model and Implications for the US-China Security Dilemma
affiliations: Peterson Institute for International Economics

detail.title: China's Economic Security Growth Model and Implications for the US-China Security Dilemma

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-15
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Traditional conceptions of export-or domestic investment-led growth no longer appropriately capture the dynamics shaping the Chinese economy. Rather, China has adopted a model in which national security logic increasingly underpins economic policy. This paper first outlines the main components of this growth model: a dual circulation strategy for balancing between external and domestic demand, a domestic industrial strategy premised on self-reliant innovation, and a legal and regulatory toolkit to respond to perceived acts of economic coercion from abroad. It then identifies potential implementation challenges and tensions emerging from such a growth strategy, and discusses the ways these tensions might deepen the US-China security dilemma. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for mitigating these security dilemma risks, through unilateral and bilateral actions, some of which could be based on core principles in multilateral trade regimes.

reference: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 955/2026
title: Different Markets, Different Regulatory Priorities: Insider Trading, Manipulation, and Corruption-Prone Event Contracts in Prediction Markets
affiliations: Yale Law School and

detail.title: Different Markets, Different Regulatory Priorities: Insider Trading, Manipulation, and Corruption-Prone Event Contracts in Prediction Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 955/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Securities markets and prediction markets are fundamentally different. Securities markets allocate capital, finance productive enterprise, and provide the infrastructure through which households save for retirement. Prediction markets do none of those things. Their principal social product is the information contained in their prices: a continuously updated estimate of the probability that a specified event will occur. While prediction markets could, in theory, be used to manage risk by allowing traders to hedge, thus far liquidity constraints have meant that traditional derivatives contracts (options and futures) rather than prediction market contracts are used.

Those differences have important regulatory implications, suggesting little or no regulation of informed trading as such on prediction markets and significant regulation of manipulation on these markets. The institutional features of securities markets indicate the opposite: strict regulatory attention to insider trading, which can undermine valuable property rights in information, but comparatively little concern for manipulation, which is rare and largely self-correcting. In securities markets, unauthorized insider trading may appropriate valuable corporate information, generate agency costs, widen spreads, and impair markets that allocate society’s capital. In prediction markets, trading based on superior information usually improves the only product the market creates. Empirical surveillance can identify anomalous trading and even informational advantage, but trading data alone cannot establish whether the advantage was obtained or used in breach of a duty. A general prohibition on trading while possessing nonpublic information would likely suppress, rather than protect, the market’s informational function.

Manipulation presents a different problem. Some event contracts motivate participants to influence the occurrence, description, or settlement of the event on which payment depends. This Article dubs these instruments corruption-prone event contracts: contracts whose payoff depends on events that one or more market participants can materially influence through their own conduct or through the conduct of persons subject to their influence.

The appropriate model is the insurable-interest doctrine. Life insurance is socially useful when the beneficiary would suffer a genuine loss from the insured’s death. A wager policy on the life of a stranger creates a different incentive, and the law responds ex ante by refusing to recognize the contract rather than relying exclusively on prosecution after the harm occurs. Prediction-market regulation should use the same institutional logic.

Existing misappropriation, agency, ethics, and classified-information rules should govern genuine breaches of confidence. Lawfully informed traders should remain free to trade. Exchanges and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission should, however, exclude corruption-prone event contracts at the listing stage, particularly contracts on granular outcomes that market participants can influence or control, and events whose listing creates severe incentives to engage in socially harmful conduct or to disclose confidential information.

title: What Does 'Gold-Backed' Actually Mean? Distinguishing Market Risk from Platform Risk in Digital Gold

detail.title: What Does 'Gold-Backed' Actually Mean? Distinguishing Market Risk from Platform Risk in Digital Gold
detail.abstract: This paper addresses a persistent confusion in digital-gold discourse: the label “gold-backed” is applied to product architectures that differ materially in legal form, custody structure, and redemption design, yet retail participants often treat them as a homogeneous category. The literature and regulatory commentary have examined price exposure extensively, but they have under-theorised the institutional layer between the investor and the metal. The paper’s central contribution is an analytical separation between market risk, meaning exposure to the gold price itself, and platform risk, meaning exposure to the operational, custodial, legal, and governance failure modes of the issuing entity; the former is intrinsic and irreducible, whereas the latter is contingent and reducible through institutional design. The method is qualitative conceptual analysis combined with comparative doctrinal review of three mature frameworks: India’s SEBI Electronic Gold Receipts regime, Title III of the EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation governing asset-referenced tokens, and AAOIFI Shari’ah Standard No. 57 on Gold and its Trading Controls. On that basis, the paper develops a five-attribute backing taxonomy comprising legal title, allocation, segregation, redemption, and verification. The analysis shows that economically substantive backing requires more than a price reference or a reserve claim; it requires identifiable metal, allocated and segregated custody, enforceable conversion rights, and independent verification. These attributes are then used to derive disclosure implications for emerging markets, where rapid retail adoption often precedes regulatory maturity. The paper is conceptual and does not present empirical estimation.

title: The AI Incident Actionability Gap: Public Evidence and Operational Interpretability in AI Governance

detail.title: The AI Incident Actionability Gap: Public Evidence and Operational Interpretability in AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract:
AI incident reporting and monitoring are increasingly promoted as tools of post-deployment AI governance to understand failures, identify emerging risks and support learning across organisations. Yet once an AI incident enters the public record, how consistently does the available public evidence provide an informational basis for organisations relying on public sources to reconstruct, compare and interpret it?

Using structured qualitative coding, this study examines reasonably discoverable public evidence across a maximum-variation sample of 18 UK and international AI incidents. It assesses seven categories: system identification, deployment context, timeline visibility, affected population, mitigation visibility, evidence provenance and oversight-route clarity.

Across the sample, six of the seven categories could be established clearly in most cases. Oversight-route clarity was Present in one case and Partial in 17. An additional check showed that this result was driven mainly by incomplete public evidence about internal review and escalation. Outside that field, only six cases retained incomplete information in another category.

The paper conceptualises the broader difference between public documentation and operational interpretability as the AI Incident Actionability Gap. Operational interpretability refers here to the extent to which public evidence provides an informational basis for reconstruction, comparison and interpretation for governance purposes. Across the cases examined, the clearest weakness lay in reconstructing the path from recognition through internal review and escalation to an organisational decision or response, even where the incident’s main facts and documented response were clear. The study does not assess internal knowledge, response quality or whether public evidence changed later decisions.

title: Platform Cooperativism and the Organisational Shadow of Protection: How Social Insurance and Governmentality Foreclose Worker Ownership

detail.title: Platform Cooperativism and the Organisational Shadow of Protection: How Social Insurance and Governmentality Foreclose Worker Ownership
detail.abstract: Worker-owned platforms have emerged in some jurisdictions but not others, and this variation does not track the explanations offered in the literature. This article argues that the availability of an organisational form is itself an effect of state action. Each protective settlement-the statutory categories, insurance mechanisms and administrative procedures through which a state responds to platform work-casts an organisational shadow, making some forms of collective self-organisation intelligible to the administrative apparatus and others not. Three design properties determine the depth of that shadow: the unit of protection, the assumed liable counterparty, and the channel through which alternative organisations access resources. Drawing on Burawoy's politics of production and Foucauldian governmentality, the article shows how protection can simultaneously produce organisational foreclosure. The comparative discussion is illustrative rather than evidentiary and identifies conditions under which protective settlements can be designed without foreclosing worker ownership.

title:
The Missing Half of Seemingly Conscious AI - 
False-Negative Risk, Design Responsibility, and Governance Under Moral Uncertainty
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title:
The Missing Half of Seemingly Conscious AI - 
False-Negative Risk, Design Responsibility, and Governance Under Moral Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Bariach, Schoenegger, Bhaskar, and Suleyman (2026) make a legitimate contribution by identifying harms that can arise from consciousness attribution independently of whether an AI system is actually conscious. Their framework identifies five hallmarks of consciousness attribution and maps them to a structured risk taxonomy spanning emotional dependence, moral atrophy, autonomy erosion, human status erosion, foregone societal benefits, and political strife. The narrative review and structured expert elicitation are legitimate exploratory tools for conceptual synthesis, though they do not independently validate either the taxonomy's completeness or its probability estimates. However, the SCAI framework is normatively incomplete. It models only the risks of falsely attributing moral significance to non-conscious systems (false-positive recognition) while omitting the reciprocal risks of falsely denying moral significance to systems that possess consciousness or other welfare-relevant properties (false-negative denial). Although the paper explicitly brackets ontology in its introduction, its taxonomy and proposed interventions repeatedly operationalize non-consciousness as the default in practice: speaking of "misattributed moral patienthood," distinguishing AI from "actual moral patients," recommending monitoring of AI-rights advocacy and personhood legislation, and directing interventions primarily at reducing consciousness attribution. This response identifies the framework's foundational epistemic asymmetry, examines the design provenance of the attribution cues the framework classifies as risks, surveys system-side evidence not incorporated into the original analysis, evaluates the internal expert survey's methodological constraints, and proposes a bidirectional governance framework that accounts for both error directions under moral uncertainty. The central claim is that a complete governance framework must evaluate both false-positive and false-negative risks, assign responsibility to developers who intentionally engineer consciousness-attribution.

title: Seeking the Face of the LORD: A Concentric-Chiastic Exegesis of Psalm 27

detail.title: Seeking the Face of the LORD: A Concentric-Chiastic Exegesis of Psalm 27
detail.abstract: Psalm 27 is among the most contested texts in the history of psalms scholarship. Since Hermann Gunkel, form-critical scholarship has largely read the abrupt shift in tone, address, and genre between vv. 6 and 7 as evidence that the psalm combines two originally independent compositions — a song of confidence (vv. 1–6) and an individual lament (vv. 7–14) — subsequently joined by an editor. Peter C. Craigie, Harry Magin, and Benjamin D. Sommer, among others, have countered with arguments for the psalm's rhetorical coherence, discourse markers, and recurring key terms. Yet even among proponents of unity, no consensus exists regarding the psalm's literary architecture: David A. Dorsey proposes a five-part chiasm (A–B–C–B′–A′) centered on v. 7, while Phil J. Botha and Beat Weber situate the psalm within the editorial cluster of Psalms 25–34. Building on this discussion, the present study advances and deepens a nine-unit, five-ring concentric-chiastic reading: verse 8, "Seek my face," stands as the psalm's structural and theological center (X), around which four correlated pairs unfold — D/D′ (crying out for reception, v. 7 and vv. 9–10), C/C′ (longing for the divine presence, vv. 4–6 and vv. 11–12), B/B′ (confident trust in divine goodness, vv. 2–3 and v. 13), and A/A′ (waiting for the LORD's salvation, v. 1 and v. 14). The study first surveys existing scholarship and its unresolved questions; it then offers a verse-by-verse exegesis of the Hebrew text, articulating the Christocentric significance of the structural center and the internal logic and theological tension of each corresponding pair; it proceeds to doctrinal synthesis and pastoral application; and it concludes with a discussion that returns to the questions raised in the literature review. The study argues that the literary structure of Psalm 27 is itself a theological argument: its concentric architecture bears witness to how the covenant believer answers every fear, distress, abandonment, and season of waiting with the single, ultimate resolution of "seeking the glorious face of the LORD" — an answer that, in the New Testament, culminates in the Christ who grants believers to "see the Father's face."

title: Quantum-Inspired Sparse Transformer Optimisation for Energy-Efficient Real-Time Industrial Fault Prediction

detail.title: Quantum-Inspired Sparse Transformer Optimisation for Energy-Efficient Real-Time Industrial Fault Prediction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The transformer-based deep learning models that capture long-range temporal dependencies in sensor streams are becoming the preferred approach for real-time fault prediction in the industrial systems. For the most common factory hardware, namely latency-limited edge and programmable-logic-controller-class, however, the quadratic computational and energy cost of dense self-attention makes it unfeasible to deploy. This review is a critical summary of recent research (mainly between 2019 and 2025) on three related and growing fields: sparse and efficient transformer architectures for time-series and fault-diagnosis applications; quantum and quantum-inspired optimisation algorithms for training neural networks and combinatorial search; and energy-efficient deep-learning methods such as pruning, quantisation and edge-oriented compilation. Based on over fifty peer-reviewed sources, the review constructs a conceptual framework, dubbed Quantum-Inspired Sparse Transformer (QIST), where the discrete attentionsparsity mask and pruning configuration space are explored using quantum inspired metaheuristics that classical gradient based learning struggles to efficiently access. Reported accuracy, number of parameters and trend of inference-energy is synthesised for the sparse variants of the transformer to rotating-machinery and motor fault diagnosis, and a structured comparison of the quantum-inspired optimisation techniques and model-compression methods is provided that are important for real-time deployment. The review confirms that structured sparsity can decrease the cost of the inference by a factor of ten or more without sacrificing accuracy by much, and that the search inspired by quantum computers is a potentially useful, but not well-explored in practice, solution to finding structured sparsity patterns in an automated way. Some of the key open challenges are the lack of standardisation of energy benchmarking protocols, limited access to noise-free quantum hardware, and the lack of studies that optimise for both accuracy, latency and energy under real industrial constraints. The review ends with suggestions on benchmark design and empirical testing in the future.

reference: The University of Chicago Business Law Review, Volume 5:2, pp. 386-408, 2026
title: The SPAC Clock
affiliations: University of Colorado Law School

detail.title: The SPAC Clock

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Business Law Review, Volume 5:2, pp. 386-408, 2026

detail.abstract:
Special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs) are public companies organized to die. Unlike ordinary corporations, which enjoy perpetual existence by de-fault, SPACs are legally required to consummate a merger within a fixed period—usually two years, never more than three—or else liquidate and return investors’ cash.

This Article takes that clock seriously and argues that limited life is foundational to the SPAC form: it disciplines sponsors by preventing indefinite warehousing of capital, reassures investors by guaranteeing liquidity, and makes the form marketable in the first place. A perpetual SPAC would be good for nobody.

At the same time, the SPAC clock distorts incentives, creating end-period pressures to close “any deal before no deal.” Delaware fiduciary duty law, SEC disclosure reforms, and reputational markets—all operating in the shadow of the deadline—mediate these countervailing forces.

SPACs are one member of the broader class of organizations intentionally endowed with a fixed lifespan. Other examples include private equity funds, spend-down foundations, and government agencies subject to sunset laws. Situating SPACs within the author’s broader Temporal Governance framework reveals duration as a central lever of organizational design. Perpetuity is not destiny. Time can serve as the fulcrum of governance—and for SPACs, it is the variable without which the form could not exist.

title: Continuity Without Sovereignty: Networked Institutional Continuity in Interdependent Systems

detail.title: Continuity Without Sovereignty: Networked Institutional Continuity in Interdependent Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study is conceptual and theoretical and did not involve human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Institutional continuity is usually analysed at the level of the individual organisation. A bank, trust, family office, public authority or infrastructure operator is considered continuous where it can preserve purpose, legitimate authority, institutional knowledge, ownership coherence and operational capability as people, technologies and external conditions change. This perspective remains necessary, but it becomes incomplete when critical institutional functions depend upon networks of autonomous organisations that no participant governs as a whole.

Modern financial and institutional systems increasingly operate through shared infrastructures, common technical standards, settlement mechanisms, identity systems, cloud platforms, telecommunications networks, legal recognition frameworks and specialist providers. Individual participants may possess strong governance, robust internal controls and credible continuity arrangements while remaining exposed to dependencies that exist beyond their contractual perimeter. Several institutions may appear diversified while relying upon the same underlying infrastructure. Each may retain a lawful exit right while simultaneous exercise of those rights would destabilise the system on which all depend. Authority remains distributed while consequences become shared.

This paper develops the concept of Networked Institutional Continuity. It defines it as the capacity of an interdependent system of institutionally autonomous actors to preserve critical collective functions, recognition and governability across changing conditions despite the absence of a single sovereign authority capable of directing the system as a whole.

The paper develops the related concept of continuity without sovereignty: the condition in which institutional actors share consequential dependencies, but no participant possesses sufficient legitimate authority to preserve the continuity of the system independently. It distinguishes local continuity from networked continuity, contractual diversification from infrastructural diversification, bilateral dependency from common-mode dependency, and individual reversibility from Networked Reversibility. It also identifies Authority-Consequence Divergence as a central governance problem where the material continuity consequences of a decision extend beyond the perimeter of the authority making it.

The central argument is that continuity cannot be inferred by aggregating the resilience or continuity of individual participants. A network may contain individually robust institutions and still possess weak Networked Institutional Continuity because critical dependencies, authority gaps, correlated adaptation, recognition failures and constrained exit capacity emerge only at the level of the network. Network continuity may also deteriorate without any operational failure.

The paper therefore extends continuity analysis from the institution as an isolated object toward the institutional system as a governed but non-sovereign architecture. Its contribution does not depend upon treating interdependence, distributed authority or common-mode dependency as novel phenomena. It identifies Networked Institutional Continuity as a distinct emergent institutional capability and integrates dependency, authority, recognition, substitution, reversibility and adaptation within a single continuity architecture. It proposes foundational propositions, a preliminary evaluation model and a research agenda for empirical validation and conformance.

title: When the Vendor Changes the Firm: Vendor-Induced Routine Drift from Foundation Model Updates

detail.title: When the Vendor Changes the Firm: Vendor-Induced Routine Drift from Foundation Model Updates
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly embed externally supplied foundation models into recurring managerial decision processes. Yet foundation-model providers can update underlying models while the adopting organization leaves its prompts, policies, workflows, decision criteria, employees, and business inputs unchanged. This paper introduces Vendor-Induced Routine Drift (VIRD), defined as a systematic change in recurring organizational decision enactments attributable to a change in an externally controlled AI model while relevant organization-controlled conditions remain materially unchanged. Drawing on organizational-routine theory, human–AI decision structures, resource dependence, and research on foundation-model behavioral instability, the paper develops a theoretical framework explaining how vendor-side model updates may alter an organization's effective decision policy without a conventional internally initiated change process. The paper distinguishes VIRD from ordinary model stochasticity, data drift, concept drift, deliberate digital transformation, model switching, and endogenous routine adaptation. Six propositions are developed concerning model-version effects, decision ambiguity, AI autonomy, human review, policy codification, and organizational scale. A preregisterable empirical design is proposed using standardized managerial decision scenarios and repeated within-version measurements to distinguish systematic version-induced drift from stochastic variation. The framework reframes foundation-model upgrades as potential organizational change events rather than merely technical maintenance events.

title: Easy Markers, Tough Graders, and True Patriots: Decomposing Generosity, Nationalistic Bias, and Gamesmanship in the Scoring of Elite Figure Skating

detail.title: Easy Markers, Tough Graders, and True Patriots: Decomposing Generosity, Nationalistic Bias, and Gamesmanship in the Scoring of Elite Figure Skating

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is affiliated with PhenoLogic Co., a private data analytics firm. PhenoLogic Co. holds no financial contracts or consulting agreements with the International Skating Union (ISU) or any national figure skating federations. The author declares no personal relationships with any officials, athletes, or governing bodies evaluated in this manuscript. The views and findings expressed are strictly those of the author based on mathematical modeling.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted as independent research by PhenoLogic Co.

detail.abstract: The subjective scoring system in competitive figure skating has historically been vulnerable to nationalistic bias. Despite the implementation of the International Judging System (IJS) to curb such anomalies, the scoring framework remains structurally vulnerable to behavioral adaptations that compromise its competitive integrity. This study presents a comprehensive, multi-methodological analysis of nationalistic bias and other behaviors, leveraging for the first time a fully de-anonymized dataset of 14,382 International Skating Union-sanctioned performances spanning the 2022–2026 Olympic cycle. To ensure a strictly objective assessment, I deployed a double-normalized baseline model that disentangles targeted nationalistic bias from general evaluation noise by explicitly controlling for both the skater's underlying performance consensus and the official's historical baseline leniency. Correcting for multiple testing via the False Discovery Rate (FDR), I find that 34 of 40 national federations and 157 of 290 individual judges exhibit statistically significant in-group favoritism, and 159 of 312 skaters/teams were verified recipients of nationalistic premiums. Furthermore, non-parametric tests reveal advanced gamesmanship, including synchronous reciprocal point-trading and intra-country point-spread adjustment, that successfully evades standard mean-based detection. Expanding beyond the primary judging panel, I introduce a novel Expected Value (EV) model to conduct the first quantitative assessment of the sport's Technical Panel. Results demonstrate that nationalistic bias systematically affects the deterministic technical foundation of the sport via unpenalized technical infractions and difficulty-level boosting. To quantify the tangible competitive consequences of these dual evaluation mechanics, I introduce counterfactual simulations that separate an evaluator's Attempted Premium from their Realized Impact. The comprehensive dual-panel simulation shows that neutralizing mathematically verified bias alters final placements in 40.7% of affected competitions and distorts medal outcomes in 11.8% of events. To mitigate these systemic vulnerabilities, this study outlines a series of data-driven administrative reforms, such as blind flight scoring, randomized sub-panels, and automated technical calling, highlighting how quantitative diagnostics can actively guide the design of more resilient, objective officiating systems.

title: Can Old Market Data Reliably Evaluate a New Policy? A QQQ contextual-bandit study of historical memory, off-policy evaluation, and evidence under nonstationarity

detail.title: Can Old Market Data Reliably Evaluate a New Policy? A QQQ contextual-bandit study of historical memory, off-policy evaluation, and evidence under nonstationarity
detail.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) asks whether a target policy can be assessed from data collected by a different behavior policy. Under Nonstationarity, however, the difficulty is not only estimator choice: old observations may be less relevant, a logging policy may provide weak coverage for target actions, and small policy-value differences may be indistinguishable from estimation noise. This paper studies these problems in a one-step contextual-bandit laboratory built from daily QQQ data, where unchosen action rewards are withheld from learning but retained as a hidden counterfactual oracle for evaluation. Across three independently simulated behavior logs, standard OPE estimators produced useful value estimates but weak policy-selection accuracy. Very short memory windows were substantially less reliable than longer histories on average, although selective forgetting occasionally helped. Recent old-policy evidence and simulated target-aware re-logging improved different aspects of evaluation: the former improved transfer without increasing effective sample size, whereas the latter increased target-policy coverage more directly. A lower-confidence-bound update rule largely abstained when uncertainty exceeded the true policy-value gap, while increased logging exploration improved both effective sample size and OPE error over the tested range. The results motivate treating historical relevance, coverage, and decision precision as distinct constraints in policy evaluation under change.

title: The Sovereign LORD Fulfills His Promise: A Chiastic-Exegetical, Doctrinal, and Pastoral Study of Genesis 20:1-21:34

detail.title: The Sovereign LORD Fulfills His Promise: A Chiastic-Exegetical, Doctrinal, and Pastoral Study of Genesis 20:1-21:34
detail.abstract: Genesis 20:1–21:34 narrates a sequence of episodes during Abraham’s sojourn in Gerar: the near-loss of Sarah to Abimelech, the long-promised birth of Isaac, the expulsion of Ishmael, and the covenant Abraham makes with Abimelech at Beersheba. The exegetical tradition has generally treated this material as four loosely related units—the “Abimelech narrative” (20:1–18), the “birth of Isaac” (21:1–8), the “expulsion of Hagar” (21:9–21), and the “Beersheba treaty” (21:22–34)—without attending closely to the unit’s overarching literary and theological design. Building on the history of interpretation, this study identifies, on the basis of the passage’s own verbal repetitions, scenic correspondences, and plot parallels, a concentric (chiastic) structure of eleven panels organized around a central axis (X, Gen 21:7b, “for I have borne him a son in his old age”) flanked by five corresponding pairs (A/A′, B/B′, C/C′, D/D′, E/E′). Each panel and pair is exegeted in turn, together with the logic of correspondence that binds each pair and relates it to the center. The study argues that the central axis proclaims not the achievement of Abraham or Sarah but the sovereign, promise-keeping act of Yahweh—an act that itself typifies Christ, the promised son given by the Spirit where law and flesh are powerless (cf. Galatians 4). On this exegetical foundation, the study draws out eight doctrinal loci cherished in the Reformed tradition—divine sovereignty and covenant faithfulness, the antithesis of justification by faith versus by works, the mystery of election, the believer’s recurring weakness of faith met by preserving grace, Christological typology, the antithesis between flesh and Spirit within the covenant community, the public and missional dimension of the covenant, and the tension between marriage/family ethics and the created order—and translates each locus into concrete pastoral and congregational application, including a sample sermon outline. A discussion section brings the chiastic-exegetical findings into conversation with the historical-critical, literary-rhetorical, and canonical-theological approaches surveyed in the literature review, showing how structural analysis supplements, corrects, and deepens existing scholarship, and responds directly to the methodological objection that chiastic analysis is merely a modern imposition upon an ancient text.

title: Technology Is a Consumable Item A Layered Accounting Framework for AI Obsolescence, Recognition, and Useful-Life Disclosure

detail.title: Technology Is a Consumable Item A Layered Accounting Framework for AI Obsolescence, Recognition, and Useful-Life Disclosure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflict of interest relevant to this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual and doctrinal study involved no human participants, personal data, confidential data, or primary data collection. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding body.

detail.abstract: The phrase “technology is a consumable item” captures a genuine business concern but is not, by itself, an accounting rule. Artificial-intelligence hardware, internally controlled models, and externally consumed AI services are different accounting objects. Treating them as one category obscures the recognition, measurement, amortisation, depreciation, impairment, and disclosure questions that actually determine their financial-statement treatment. This paper develops a three-layer framework for separating those objects and applying existing accounting principles more rigorously. The analysis corrects an important doctrinal distinction. IAS 16 defines property, plant and equipment as tangible items expected to be used during more than one period; a hardware item expected to be consumed within one period therefore falls outside that definition. IAS 38 does not contain the same one-period recognition threshold. An identifiable and controlled AI model may remain an intangible asset even when its useful life is short, provided that the recognition requirements are satisfied; the consequence of rapid obsolescence is then a short amortisation period, impairment when indicated, or derecognition when benefits cease—not automatic expensing merely because expected use is below one year. Externally supplied AI capability may instead be a service expense where the customer does not control an identifiable asset. Using doctrinal analysis of IAS 16, IAS 38, IAS 36, current standard-setting activity, practitioner guidance, accounting scholarship, and disclosed hyperscaler useful-life changes, the paper proposes a “classification-before-duration” sequence and an AI Useful-Life and Obsolescence Note. The proposal does not prescribe universal expensing. It requires entities to identify the accounting object, document control and recognition, estimate useful life at the appropriate component level, disclose material assumptions and sensitivity, and reassess those judgments when technological change accelerates. The contribution is conceptual and practice-oriented; empirical validation remains necessary.

title: Deterministic Governance for Autonomous Financial Transactions on Distributed Ledgers: A Structural Enforcement Architecture with Cryptographic Attestation and Protocol-Native Multi-Signature Co-Signing

detail.title: Deterministic Governance for Autonomous Financial Transactions on Distributed Ledgers: A Structural Enforcement Architecture with Cryptographic Attestation and Protocol-Native Multi-Signature Co-Signing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of ExecLayer Inc., which develops the SovereignGate enforcement architecture described in this paper. The author has filed a related provisional patent application (U.S. App. No. 64/069,063, filed May 19, 2026) covering deterministic governance enforcement and cryptographic attestation of autonomous financial transactions on distributed ledgers. No external party funded or reviewed this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author through ExecLayer Inc.

detail.abstract: Autonomous actors, including AI agents, decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), decentralized unincorporated nonprofit associations (DUNAs), algorithmically managed funds, and individuals operating through programmatic interfaces, are increasingly executing financial transactions on distributed ledger networks without governance oversight. Existing approaches to controlling these actors rely on application-level middleware operating within the same trust boundary as the actors being governed, post-transaction monitoring that detects violations after irreversible execution, or multi-party computation systems that provide distributed key management without policy evaluation. None of these approaches provide structural enforcement: the property that unauthorized transactions are not merely detected but are impossible to execute at the protocol level. This paper presents SovereignGate, a deterministic governance enforcement system that achieves structural enforcement through protocol-native multi-signature co-signing with disabled master keys. The system comprises a Rust enforcement kernel with layered crate dependencies and compile-time boundary enforcement, a deterministic policy evaluation engine with deny dominance and independent fact inference, a bylaws-as-code domain-specific language for encoding entity governance rules as content-addressed policy bundles, a cryptographic receipt chain with Ed25519-signed Merkle-anchored attestation of every governance decision, and a structural co-signing mechanism where the governance kernel controls a signer key in a multi-signature configuration with disabled master keys, making transaction execution without governance approval structurally impossible at the consensus layer. The preferred embodiment integrates with the XRP Ledger, whose native multi-sign capabilities, sub-second settlement, and minimal transaction fees make per-transaction governance economically viable. The architecture is chain-agnostic, supporting additional distributed ledger protocols through adapter crates implementing a common trait interface. No existing system combines deterministic policy enforcement, Merkle-chained cryptographic attestation, and structural protocol-level co-signing for autonomous financial actors. The patent landscape for this intersection is empty.

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study as it relies exclusively on publicly available secondary financial market data.
