detail.abstract: The objective of the paper is to create a GARCH/ARCH model to predict future volatility on a rolling basis and based on it suggest recommendations related to the use of the model for risk management. The dataset is extracted from yahoo finance. The financial instruments used for the prediction were Brent Oil Futures, WTI ETF, E-Mini Oil futures, ZKB gold ETF, Micro gold futures, E-mini gold futures for energy commodities, and gold futures. The dataset has been taken from the period of August 2014 to February 2022. The dynamic GARCH model was implemented using Python. As an outcome, the Brent Oil Prices (BZ=F) GARCH (1,2), E-mini-Crude Oil Futures (QM=F) GARCH (1,0) and Wisdom Tree WTI Crude Oil (CRUD.MI) GARCH (1,1) model was applicable and showed better results as compared to other GARCH models. In the instance of gold prices, Micro Gold Futures (MGC=F) GARCH (1,0), E-Mini Gold Futures (QO=F) GARCH (1,2), ZKB Gold ETF (ZGLD.SW) GARCH (1,1) was applicable and predicted accurate results with fewer errors.

title: Protecting Those Who Serve: Legal Protections, Liability, and Risk Management for Emergency and Disaster Volunteers

detail.title: Protecting Those Who Serve: Legal Protections, Liability, and Risk Management for Emergency and Disaster Volunteers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This publication did not involve human participants, animals, or research requiring institutional ethics review.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: Volunteers provide critical personnel, expertise, and surge capacity during emergencies and disasters, yet their participation occurs within a complex legal and organizational environment. Liability protections, credentialing requirements, scope-of-practice limitations, workers’ compensation provisions, interstate mutual-aid arrangements, and organizational riskmanagement practices can affect both the utilization of volunteers and the conditions under which they serve. This white paper examines legal protections and liability considerations affecting emergency and disaster volunteers in the United States, with particular attention to affiliated and spontaneous volunteers, volunteer health practitioners, interstate deployments, and the responsibilities of organizations that recruit, deploy, supervise, or integrate volunteer personnel. Contemporary scholarly evidence is considered alongside applicable primary legal authorities to distinguish individual volunteer protections from organizational liability and other forms of legal protection. The analysis emphasizes that volunteer protection is not a single or uniform legal concept and that protections may depend on jurisdiction, volunteer status, professional credentials, organizational affiliation, deployment mechanism, and the circumstances of an emergency. Evidence-informed recommendations are presented to support emergency-management leaders in strengthening volunteer planning, credentialing, training, supervision, documentation, risk management, and organizational preparedness. Protecting those who serve requires not only legal safeguards but also deliberate systems that enable volunteers to contribute safely, effectively, and responsibly.

title: Futures Before Fungibility: Compute Derivatives and the Financialization of an Unstandardized Market

detail.title: Futures Before Fungibility: Compute Derivatives and the Financialization of an Unstandardized Market
detail.abstract: Compute derivatives are moving from conjecture to exchange design. CME Group has announced cashsettled futures linked to Silicon Data H100 and B200 rental indices for planned listing on 5 October 2026, while Architect's AX venue and Intercontinental Exchange have announced Ornn-linked alternatives based on transaction-derived compute indices. The institutional novelty is therefore real, but the underlying economic mechanisms are not: the proposed contracts inherit familiar problems from electricity, freight, weather, telecommunications capacity, cloud contracting, and cash-settled commodity markets. This critical integrative review argues that compute derivatives are distinctive because financialization is arriving before the underlying service has become fully fungible or organized around a unified spot market. It calls this sequencing reversal the benchmark-before-market paradox. A private benchmark is being asked not merely to measure a market, but to help constitute it by deciding which hardware, service quality, location, rental term, and delivery conditions count as comparable compute. The paper develops a standardization trilemma among tradability, exposure representativeness, and technological durability. It shows why a liquid benchmark can improve price discovery while still leaving users and providers with material cross-hedging risk, and why rapid chip obsolescence makes contract relevance endogenous to innovation. The review concludes with testable propositions and a post-launch research agenda that separates market liquidity, benchmark adoption, and real hedging effectiveness.

title: The Integrated Executive Decision Framework (IEDF): Structuring Analytical Evidence for Executive Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Integrated Executive Decision Framework (IEDF): Structuring Analytical Evidence for Executive Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on forecasting, financial evaluation, risk analytics, scenario simulation, and sensitivity analysis to support managerial decisions under uncertainty. However, these analytical capabilities frequently operate as specialized and partially disconnected processes, creating what this study defines as the Analytical-to-Decision Gap: the disconnect between generating analytical evidence and systematically transforming that evidence into structured executive recommendations. This study proposes the Integrated Executive Decision Framework (IEDF), a structured decision architecture that integrates complementary analytical evidence while preserving the methodological independence of established analytical disciplines. The framework organizes five analytical dimensions-forecast quality, financial evaluation, risk analytics, scenario analysis, and sensitivity analysis-into an integrated executive decision process and introduces Decision Confidence as a construct for assessing the strength and coherence of the analytical foundation supporting a recommendation. An initial operationalization is proposed via the Decision Confidence Index (DCI). The framework was evaluated through an exploratory expert assessment using purposive sampling. Twenty experienced executives were invited to participate, of whom 16 completed the evaluation (80% response rate). Participants assessed the IEDF across four predefined dimensions using an 11-item, seven-point Likert-scale instrument complemented by five openended questions. The evaluation generated 176 quantitative ratings together with qualitative executive feedback. Across the four evaluation dimensions, median scores ranged from 6.00 to 6.50, while mean scores ranged from 6.02 to 6.38. The proportion of ratings classified as Agree or Strongly Agree ranged from 72.9% to 87.5% across dimensions. Qualitative analysis identified five recurring themes: integration of analytical evidence; transparency, traceability, and decision structure; implementation guidance and operationalization; additional components and extensions; and organizational application and future development. The findings provide initial expert-based empirical support for the perceived coherence and usefulness of the IEDF, but do not constitute evidence of improved organizational outcomes or definitive validation of the framework. The DCI remains a provisional methodological construct requiring calibration and empirical validation. The study contributes a structured architecture for connecting fragmented analytical evidence with executive judgment and establishes an empirical research agenda for evaluating its effectiveness in real organizational decision environments.

title: The Suppressed Effect: Five Systemic Profiles of Blocked Potential in Organisational Performance A Working Paper from the Pragadian Model of Human Synergy (PMHS)
affiliations: East Bridge University

detail.title: The Suppressed Effect: Five Systemic Profiles of Blocked Potential in Organisational Performance A Working Paper from the Pragadian Model of Human Synergy (PMHS)
detail.abstract: Organisational psychology has long concentrated diagnostic attention on output-level dysfunction, investigating why performance fails to reach expected levels. A structurally distinct and previously unnamed category of systemic risk operates in the opposite direction: conditions in which internal resources, namely capacity, relational safety, cognitive clarity, intrinsic drive, and feedback channel integrity, are present and reading above their functional threshold while the Behavioral State remains below its Minimum Functioning Threshold. This white paper introduces the Suppressed Effect as a novel theoretical construct within the Pragadian Model of Human Synergy (PMHS). The Suppressed Effect describes a systemic condition in which the infrastructure for performance exists but is prevented from converting into observable output by a blockage that sits between upstream state health and downstream execution. That blockage may be structural, environmental, psychological, or physiological in nature. Five discrete profiles are introduced: the Latent Effect (Minimum Functioning Threshold above threshold, Behavioral State below threshold), the Idle Effect (Humanistic State above threshold, Behavioral State below threshold), the Paralysed Effect (Cognitive State above threshold, Behavioral State below threshold), the Pressure Effect (Motivational State above threshold, Behavioral State below threshold), and the Hollow Effect (Signal Fidelity above threshold, Behavioral State below threshold). Each profile is defined, theoretically grounded, and examined against historical and contemporary organisational evidence. The Suppressed Effect constitutes a structurally distinct risk category from the Masked Effect and requires a distinct diagnostic and intervention logic.

title:
The Pragadian Model of Human Synergy 
Why Human Performance Fails and Where to Look Before It Does
An Introduction to the PMHS Framework and Its Novel Constructs
affiliations: East Bridge University

detail.title:
The Pragadian Model of Human Synergy 
Why Human Performance Fails and Where to Look Before It Does
An Introduction to the PMHS Framework and Its Novel Constructs
detail.abstract: Organisational performance fails in predictable ways. Leaders apply training when the problem is values. They redesign structures when the problem is perception. They introduce incentive programmes when the problem is that motivation has already hollowed. They do these things because they are measuring the one dimension of their system that is visible behaviour while the dimensions that drive behaviour remain unexamined and unmeasured. The Pragadian Model of Human Synergy (PMHS) was developed to close this diagnostic gap. It is an integrated theoretical framework that maps human functioning across four interdependent states: the Humanistic State, the Cognitive State, the Motivational State, and the Behavioral State. These four states do not operate in sequence. They operate as a system. What happens in one state shapes what happens in all others simultaneously and the quality of signal transmission between them determines whether synergy emerges or fails. The PMHS names this signal quality Synaptic Coherence. The PMHS introduces three principal theoretical constructs as its proposed novel contribution to the existing literature, together with a primary diagnostic phenomenon arising from their interaction. Synaptic Coherence establishes that synergy is produced not by the strength of individual states but by the fidelity of the connections between them. The Upstream Priority Principle establishes that the Humanistic State is the non-negotiable foundation of the system and that no downstream intervention produces sustainable change when that foundation is compromised. The Synergistic Amplification Effect proposes that the four states operate multiplicatively rather than additively, such that small upstream changes produce disproportionate downstream effects in both directions. The Masked Effect is the primary diagnostic phenomenon arising from this architecture: a condition in which observable performance appears healthy while upstream states are collapsing, producing false synergy that conventional monitoring cannot detect. The framework was developed through a Theoretical Integration Review synthesising foundational psychological scholarship and examined against six purposively selected historical cases spanning elite team performance, crisis management, ethical collapse, and catastrophic industrial failure. The six propositions governing state interaction identified consistent explanatory patterns across the cases. This white paper introduces the PMHS framework for professional and academic audiences. It presents the four states, the three principal theoretical constructs and the Masked Effect diagnostic framework, the six formal propositions, and the practical implications for leaders, practitioners, and researchers. White Paper No. 2 in this series elaborates the Masked Effect and its five systemic profiles in dedicated depth.

reference: Tibet, Ladakh and the Politics of Contested Sovereignty in the Himalayas
title: The Tibet Question in Global Politics: Between Realpolitik and Moral Diplomacy

detail.title: The Tibet Question in Global Politics: Between Realpolitik and Moral Diplomacy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Tibet, Ladakh and the Politics of Contested Sovereignty in the Himalayas

detail.abstract: The Tibet question is not only about a lost autonomy; it is about the world's lost moral voice. It is still one of the most difficult and longlasting problems that comes up when politics, sovereignty, and global morality meet. Tibet represents a struggle for cultural identity and sovereignty, but it also exemplifies the constraints of international moral diplomacy when faced with the strategic demands of Realpolitik. Since it became part of the People's Republic of China in 1951, Tibet has been under strict political supervision from Beijing, which claims of modernisation and unity have justified. Still, resistance in Tibet and among Tibetans living abroad across the world challenges this authority and raises worries around the world. Even while people around the world know that Tibet has its own culture, they don't say much about it because they depend on China for money and have political links to the country. This chapter looks at Tibet's political situation from two points of view: Realpolitik and moral diplomacy. It examines how state interests, strategic alignments, and normative discourses influence the international community's perception of Tibet. It also looks at how Tibet's visibility is changing, notably because of shifts in the global balance of power and the rethinking of Western liberal 2 » Tibet, Ladakh and the Politics of Contested Sovereignty in the Himalayas values. Ultimately, the paper contends that the Tibet issue exemplifies a broader challenge of moral diplomacy in an era where ethics often yield to strategic silence.

title: Representing Organizational Negotiations: Explicit Representations for Human and AI Reasoning

detail.title: Representing Organizational Negotiations: Explicit Representations for Human and AI Reasoning
detail.abstract: Organizations rely on explicit representations like financial statements, engineering models and project plans to support reasoning in complex domains. Negotiations are a conspicuous exception: preparation still relies on documents, meetings, and individual expertise rather than on any structured, persistent representation of the negotiation itself. In its absence, two practices prevail: individual judgment alone, and, increasingly, unstructured conversation with an AI system that reconstructs the situation from scratch in each session. Both leave reasoning to proceed over heterogeneous, session-bound information rather than an explicit, governable representation. This paper argues that recent advances in artificial intelligence change the economics of explicit organizational representation. AI can substantially reduce the effort required to construct, maintain, and reason over rich representations, while also providing powerful new ways to analyze negotiations directly. The paper's contribution is an approach that treats these as complementary rather than mutually exclusive, examining how organizational representations of complex negotiations can provide a foundation for Human-AI co-reasoning and analysis. Unlike financial statements, negotiation representations do not resolve to determinate conclusions; the ambiguity inherent in negotiations cannot be eliminated. The aim is accordingly not the perfection of reasoning but a sound, shared basis from which human and AI reasoning can proceed. Building on a distinction between knowledge acquisition, representation, and reasoning as separable organizational concerns, the paper develops design principles for organizational negotiation representations emphasizing explicitness, decision relevance, support for reasoning, evolvability, and practical usefulness over theoretical completeness. A companion paper derives the corresponding engineering principles.

title: The Inversion: From Petrodollar Anchor to Compute-Dollar Anchor

detail.title: The Inversion: From Petrodollar Anchor to Compute-Dollar Anchor
detail.abstract: The structural demand base of the US dollar is migrating from an anchor located outside American jurisdiction to one located inside it. For five decades, dollar demand was generated exogenously, by the world's need for oil, which was priced in dollars by arrangement and recycled into US claims by bargain. It is now increasingly generated endogenously, by the world's need for computation, an input manufactured, priced, and licensed within the American legal and technical system. An exogenous anchor is here defined as an object generating structural currency demand that the issuer cannot create, unilaterally withhold, or legally define. An endogenous anchor is one created within the issuer's jurisdiction, governed by its law, and deniable by its administrative act. The paper reconstructs the petrodollar loop as balance-sheet plumbing and documents the withdrawal of its load-bearing mechanisms, among them producer self-sufficiency, the diversion of recycling flows, and the reserve freeze of 2022. It then specifies the successor arrangement, a compute-dollar regime in which dollar demand takes the form of platform rent, meaning metered and revocable access to a compute stack whose chokepoints are legally coded as American capital. Building on Mehrling's hierarchy-of-money framework, Pozsar's cartography of the dollar system, and Pistor's account of legal coding, it maps the resulting demand sink, which comprises dollar-invoiced rents, foreign equity inflows, internal capital-expenditure circulation, and compute assets entering the collateral hierarchy. The structural implication is a dollar system more centralized and more cheaply enforced at its core and more reflexive at its edges, a closed loop whose strength and fragility derive from the same property, namely the anchor's location inside the system it anchors. The operational implication is a reserve system whose demand base no longer depends on foreign resource exporters but on access to American compute infrastructure.

title:
Office, Function and Attribution 
On the Normative Designation of the Conducting Agent in Electronic Public Asset Disposition

detail.title:
Office, Function and Attribution 
On the Normative Designation of the Conducting Agent in Electronic Public Asset Disposition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author was a named petitioner, together with the National Association of Judicial Auctioneers, in the administrative control proceeding discussed in Part V, and drafted the legal opinion that supported it. He serves as President of the National Association of Judicial Auctioneers and of the São Paulo State Auctioneers' Union, professional bodies whose members benefit from the rule under discussion. The account of the proceeding rests on published decisions rather than on the author's recollection.

detail.abstract: In 2022 the Internal Affairs Office of the São Paulo State Court of Justice issued a communication providing that technology companies would not be credentialed, since the activity belongs exclusively to auctioneers registered with the Commercial Registry, who will be the managers of the electronic judicial sale system. The sentence repays attention. A court had to declare that the auctioneer is the manager of the system. It had to do so because the word had been taken, and because, in the vocabulary that had by then consolidated, whoever operated the system was the one who managed it, and whoever managed it was the one who answered for it. This article argues that the displacement of vocabulary, from delegated agent to operator or system manager, was not a consequence of the dissolution of personal responsibility in electronic public sales. It was its condition of possibility. The argument draws on three contributions. J. L. Austin showed that certain utterances do not describe but perform, and that their success depends on who utters them: uttered by someone without the required authority, the intended performative act does not come off. Dennis Thompson described the problem of many hands, the difficulty of attributing responsibility where many contribute to an outcome. Mark Bovens defined accountability as a relationship between an actor and a forum, and cautioned that transparency, though often taken as a synonym, does not constitute it. Taken together, the three show that substituting a category of office for a category of technical function is not a terminological adjustment. It alters the structure that makes accountability possible. The article is conceptual. It does not estimate the incidence of unlawful conduct, quantify loss, or claim that any institutional arrangement produces superior outcomes.

title: Climate-health Recognition and Organisational Action Across Academic, Professional, and Industrial Organisations in the Health Sector in Japan: A National Cross-sectional Survey
affiliations: University of Tokyo, Nagasaki University, Yokohama City University - Department of Health Data Science, Gunma University, National Center for Global Health and Medicine - Institute for Global Health Policy Research, Kyoto University, Nagasaki University, University of Tokyo, National Center for Global Health and Medicine - Institute for Global Health Policy Research and University of Tokyo - Department of Global Health Policy

detail.title: Climate-health Recognition and Organisational Action Across Academic, Professional, and Industrial Organisations in the Health Sector in Japan: A National Cross-sectional Survey

declarations.declarationOfInterest: AS, HH, MK, AO, and JS are affiliated with the Health and Global Policy Institute, which funded this study; JS holds senior positions at the institute. HGPI is an independent, non-profit health policy research institute and was not among the organisations surveyed. All other authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained at the start of the survey. Institutional Review Board of the Health Outcome Research Institute approved the study (2025-02).
declarations.funderStatement: Health and Global Policy Institute.

detail.abstract:
Background: Health-sector organisations are critical to climate action, yet their responses are poorly characterised. We assessed perceptions, knowledge, actions, and policy views among health-sector organisations in Japan. 

Methods: We conducted a national cross-sectional survey of academic societies, professional associations, and industrial federations between October 3–28, 2025. We compared complete response distributions between academic societies and industrial federations using two-sided Fisher exact tests, with Holm adjustment across 15 comparisons, and estimated Cramér’s V with approximate 95% confidence intervals (CI) from noncentral χ² inversion. Professional associations were too few and excluded from inferential analyses. 

Findings: Of 408 organisations contacted, 154 (37·7%) provided valid responses: 120 academic societies, 29 industrial federations, and five professional associations. Recognition that climate change is occurring and affects health was near-universal. Holm-adjusted comparisons showed that industrial federations more frequently reported action and governance than academic societies, including environmental countermeasures (14/28 [50·0%] vs 8/120 [6·7%]; V=0·485, 95% CI 0·315–0·640), climate countermeasures (12/29 [41·4%] vs 6/120 [5·0%]; V=0·448, 95% CI 0·278–0·602), biodiversity countermeasures (8/29 [27·6%] vs 5/120 [4·2%]; V=0·339, 95% CI 0·164–0·491), and dedicated environmental committees (9/28 [32·1%] vs 6/120 [5·0%]; V=0·373, 95% CI 0·200–0·527). Majorities considered advocacy for greater climate-health investment and stronger climate policies appropriate, although 30–40% selected “don’t know”. 

Interpretation: Recognition of climate-related health threats coexisted with limited organisational actions, particularly among academic societies. The underlying barriers were not directly assessed. Future research should identify mechanisms and evaluate interventions addressing governance, incentives, and capacity.

title: Treatment With Immune Cytokine GM-CSF Reduces Pancreatic Amyloid, Islet Apoptosis, and Blood Glucose Levels in the hIAPP Type 2 Diabetes Mouse
affiliations: University of Colorado, Aurora - Anschutz Medical Campus, University of Colorado, Aurora - Anschutz Medical Campus, University of Colorado, Aurora - Anschutz Medical Campus, University of Colorado, Aurora - Department of Neurology, University of Colorado, Aurora - Anschutz Medical Campus, University of Colorado, Aurora - Anschutz Medical Campus and University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus - Department of Neurology

detail.title: Treatment With Immune Cytokine GM-CSF Reduces Pancreatic Amyloid, Islet Apoptosis, and Blood Glucose Levels in the hIAPP Type 2 Diabetes Mouse
detail.abstract: Previous studies showed that granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) treatment reduced cerebral amyloidosis, cognitive impairment, and neuronal death in animal models of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and improved MMSE scores and plasma measures of AD neuropathology and neuronal death in a Phase 2 trial. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by pancreatic amyloid deposits of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP), islet b- and a-cell apoptosis, and elevated blood glucose levels. We report that GM-CSF treatment of hIAPP transgenic male mice decreased pancreatic amyloid (P=0.0140) and decreased islet apoptosis (P=0.0057) compared to saline-treated mice. GM-CSF treatment also led to a sustained decrease in pancreatic islet amyloid at 45 days post-treatment (DPT) in homozygous hIAPP mice (P=0.045; especially in males, P=0.0214) and reduced blood glucose levels from baseline through 45 DPT (P=0.0002 compared to saline treatment). Recombinant human GM-CSF (sargramostim), long-approved for other indications, may prevent/treat T2D and potentially reduce AD associated with T2D.

title: Trading Data, Shifting Shares: The Labor Share Consequences of Data Marketization
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance, University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance and Capital University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Trading Data, Shifting Shares: The Labor Share Consequences of Data Marketization
detail.abstract: The institutionalized tradability of data is crucial for unlocking their full economic potential in digital era. Exploiting the pilot data exchange establishments in China, we show that data factor marketization significantly but passively increases corporate labor share. Driven by downward wage rigidity, this rise stems from a temporary contraction in labor efficiency. Dynamic analyses reveal a "dip-and-recovery" pattern in TFP and profit margins, exhibiting short-term frictions consistent with the "New Productivity Paradox." Data marketization augments labor in laborintensive firms but substitutes labor with capital in capital-intensive ones. The findings offer micro-level insights on the trajectory of digital transformation.

title: Strategic Cancer-System Data for Radiation Medicine: Value-Feasibility Gaps in Global Planning and Decision-Making from the SUNRISE Initiative
affiliations: International Atomic Energy Agency, , Dalhousie University, University of Leeds, Ghent University, Maastricht  University and International Atomic Energy Agency

detail.title: Strategic Cancer-System Data for Radiation Medicine: Value-Feasibility Gaps in Global Planning and Decision-Making from the SUNRISE Initiative
detail.abstract: Background: Reliable cancer-system data are needed for capacity planning, resource allocation and accountability. We assessed which patient- and department-level data elements professionals consider important for cancer-service planning and how feasible they are to collect across diverse settings.Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of cancer-system professionals and service leaders. Respondents rated the importance and local feasibility of 27 data elements linked to 14 recurring planning questions on parallel 5-point scales. Value-feasibility gaps were calculated as importance minus feasibility and summarised by domain and World Bank income group.Results: Among 82 valid respondents from 75 institutions in 48 countries, importance ratings were consistently high, while feasibility was lower and more variable. All 14 planning questions showed positive mean gaps. The largest concerned outcomes, toxicity, patient-reported outcomes, patient experience and treatment-related economic burden. In the small low-income subgroup, substantial gaps also affected baseline patient and tumour characteristics, diagnosis and treatment counts, and timelines. Equipment and workforce data were more closely aligned.Conclusions: Cancer-system data are widely valued for planning but are not consistently feasible to collect. The findings support a harmonised minimum indicator set with staged implementation adapted to local data maturity and resources.

title: From Experience to Employability: Using Gibbs' Reflective Cycle, the ERA Model, and Skills Auditing to Support Postgraduate Academic and Leadership Development
affiliations: University of Huddersfield - Business School

detail.title: From Experience to Employability: Using Gibbs' Reflective Cycle, the ERA Model, and Skills Auditing to Support Postgraduate Academic and Leadership Development
detail.abstract: Reflective practice has become an integral part of higher education, but it is still a great challenge for students to go beyond the mere telling of what happened to the point of being critical and assessable in their reflections. The current article provides an account of a scholarly reflective practice study that has resorted to autoethnography to investigate the role of structured frameworks in supporting meaningful learning. The researcher has used Gibbs' Reflective Cycle, the ERA model, a skills audit, and a five-year personal development plan to synthesize portfoliobased evidence into a coherent academic analysis. The results of the study show that structured reflective frameworks lead systematically from experience to evaluation, theory-informed analysis, and actionable development planning. The combination of skills auditing and design of SMART PDP has increased the awareness of employability, self-regulated learning, and feedback-as-feedforward practices. Comparative analysis with reflective learning literature supports the claim that structured scaffolding not only reduces descriptive writing but also increases reflective depth and transparency. The research introduces a "portfolio-to-paper" model that is replicable and demonstrates how reflective portfolios can be turned into academically rigorous written outputs. Despite its one case, self-reports nature, the method however has practical implications on both students who need reflective clarity and teachers who need to measure reflection in high-fidelity. In general, the paper is evidence reflective of maturity in reflective assessment, employment ability, and a consistent methodology in higher education.

title:
An Incident of Ownership: 
The Lessee, the Tenant at Sufferance, and the Right to Demolish and Redevelop Demised Land under Indian Law
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
An Incident of Ownership: 
The Lessee, the Tenant at Sufferance, and the Right to Demolish and Redevelop Demised Land under Indian Law

keywords: Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act
Section 499 of the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act

detail.abstract:
This article asks a question that decides the fate of thousands of old buildings in
Indian cities. When land is held on lease, who has the right to demolish the
building standing on it and to build something bigger in its place? Is it the lessee,
or the cooperative society and occupants who claim through the lessee, or is it the
owner of the land alone? The method is doctrinal. The statute is read first, and the
leading judgments of the Supreme Court and the Bombay High Court are then
examined in the courts’ own words, in language a law student can follow. The
article defends a single thesis in four connected planks. A lease transfers only a
right to enjoy, never ownership. The right to demolish, to redevelop, and to
exploit the development potential of land, meaning its Floor Space Index and
Transferable Development Rights, is an incident of ownership and stays with the
lessor unless expressly granted away. A lessee’s right, at its highest, is to
reconstruct what stood before, inch for inch and area for area. A tenant at
sufferance holds no estate at all, and so has nothing from which any right of
redevelopment can be carved. It follows that a municipal sanction obtained
without the lessor’s consent is illegal and confers no rights. The strongest
objections, drawn from the society-supremacy cases and from the statutory
redevelopment regimes, are stated fairly and answered.

title: Uncovering Niche Insights in Long-Tail Markets: A Unified LNRE Framework
affiliations: University of Kalyani

detail.title: Uncovering Niche Insights in Long-Tail Markets: A Unified LNRE Framework
detail.abstract: In long-tail markets, analysis is predominantly skewed towards the "head," while the "tail," rich with niche insights, often goes uninvestigated. The tail, however, stores valuable information that can expose emergent trends, sometimes contradictory to general findings derived from the head. This research highlights that while conventional machine learning algorithms struggle to model rare events due to token sparsity, our model successfully captures these elusive insights. By leveraging the mathematical properties of G-functions and Q-functions, this study integrates them into the traditional fabric of machine learning frameworks, thereby improving rare-event modelling. We show that uniform partitioning of data into subintervals facilitates granular analysis, enabling the detection of rare events. The findings highlight how long-tail contributions not only dominate but also grow with specific thresholds, uncovering emergent trends. Additionally, our approach analyzes temporal trends, dynamically tracking their evolution over time. This research highlights the need to integrate LNRE models with partitioning and convergence techniques, offering a robust tool for decoding the hidden value in long-tail market and empowering businesses to access previously invisible opportunities.

title: Volatility Smiles and Structural Non-Identification under Black-Scholes Inversion

detail.title: Volatility Smiles and Structural Non-Identification under Black-Scholes Inversion
detail.abstract: Implied volatility is widely used as a reduced representation of option prices, serving as a standard object for model calibration, comparison, and interpretation. In this paper, we analyze implied volatility as a transformation induced by the inversion of the Black-Scholes pricing map on the space of arbitrage-free option price functions. We show that, while this operator is injective when strikes are treated as a continuum, its restriction to any finite set of observed strikes (the setting relevant in practice) is not injective, and that the operator does not preserve structural properties of admissible price functions in either case. In particular, monotonicity and convexity constraints in price space do not imply corresponding properties of the implied volatility function, and non-monotonic implied volatility profiles arise on a non-empty open subset of the admissible domain. These results imply that, at the level of finite observation, implied volatility is a non-unique and non-structure-preserving representation of option prices. From an applied perspective, this limits its use as a basis for structural inference: similar implied volatility patterns may correspond to distinct admissible price configurations. The contribution of the paper is to identify a structural property of the implied volatility representation that is relevant for its interpretation and use in practice. The limitation arises at the level of the transformation itself and persists independently of model specification or calibration procedures.

title: When Should Marketing Managers Rely on Artificial Intelligence? A Conceptual Framework for Calibrated Reliance in Marketing Decision-Making
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Should Marketing Managers Rely on Artificial Intelligence? A Conceptual Framework for Calibrated Reliance in Marketing Decision-Making

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper and did not involve human participants, personal data, or empirical data collection
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly advises marketing managers on segmentation, targeting, pricing, forecasting, churn prediction, and campaign allocation. Yet effective AI use depends not simply on adoption or trust, but on whether managers rely on AI advice to a degree warranted by its diagnostic value in the decision at hand. This conceptual paper develops a framework of calibrated reliance in AI-assisted marketing decisionmaking. Drawing on judge-advisor system research, Weight of Advice, algorithm aversion and appreciation, trust in automation, explainable AI, and recent human-AI decision research, it distinguishes trust, behavioural reliance, calibrated reliance, and managerial decision quality. The framework proposes that actual AI advice quality and perceived advice quality should be analytically separated: perceived quality and trust shape behavioural reliance, whereas calibration concerns the alignment between observed reliance and the advice's case-specific value. Decision uncertainty, task ambiguity, transparency and explainability, confidence cues, managerial expertise, prior AI experience, accountability, and advice source are theorized as boundary conditions. The paper's contribution is a marketing-specific integration that reframes the managerial problem as quality-aligned advice taking rather than maximal AI use. It also proposes behavioural operationalisations of calibration and an experimental agenda using judge-advisor designs. The framework offers testable propositions for examining when AI advice improves, rather than merely influences, managerial judgment.

title: Payment Flexibility and Household Shopping Routines
affiliations: University of Notre Dame - Mendoza College of Business

detail.title: Payment Flexibility and Household Shopping Routines
detail.abstract: This study examines how retailers' payment menus shape household shopping behavior. We leverage credit-card acceptance events among U.S. grocery retailers, where an already-used payment instrument becomes newly usable at a retailer without changing household credit access. Using a triple-difference design, we compare retailers that begin accepting credit cards with control stores, across households with different pre-event credit use at other grocery retailers. Households that used more credit elsewhere shift both spending and trips toward newly accepting retailers. The source of that gain differs by household income. Lower-and middle-income gains draw mainly from product categories previously bought at control stores, while higherincome gains deepen categories already bought at the retailer. For lower-and higher-income households, that gain also appears within the month. Households shop at the retailer in more parts of the month, and their spending becomes less concentrated. The results point to payment flexibility, the ability to use a routine payment instrument at a retailer without immediately drawing on cash or debit balances, as a retailer-side demand margin.

title: ExploraTwin, a Non-Profit Research Platform for Digital Twin Simulations
affiliations: Columbia University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Marketing and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Marketing

detail.title: ExploraTwin, a Non-Profit Research Platform for Digital Twin Simulations
detail.abstract: Digital twin simulations show promise, but current empirical evidence suggests that the approach should be tested before being deployed in any particular context. To lower the friction for researchers and practitioners to test and deploy digital twin simulations, this brief commentary introduces \href{https://exploratwin.org}{ExploraTwin}, an open-access, non-profit research platform for digital twin survey simulations. ExploraTwin supports two modes. In survey mode, researchers can upload a Qualtrics survey file or create a survey within the platform; select an available sample of digital twins; configure and run the simulation, and export analysis-ready data. In panel mode, researchers can assemble a small group of twins for open-ended conversations, document annotation, and moderated, focus-group-style voice discussions. We also developed CroissantTwin, a standardized data format for adding samples of digital twins to the platform. We demonstrate the survey mode workflow by using the platform to replicate 19 experiments on digital twins from the Twin-2K-500 dataset. ExploraTwin's survey execution fidelity is high: 99.6\% of 197,000 answer units returned a structurally valid response on the first run.

title: The Value of an Icon: Dynamic Investment in Wildlife Identity Assets
affiliations: and University of Oxford - Department of Biology

detail.title: The Value of an Icon: Dynamic Investment in Wildlife Identity Assets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no personal or financial relationship with others that have (or perceived to have) influenced our study.,

detail.abstract: Rather than providing ecological services alone, natural capital can shape consumer value through culture and identity. However, how these cultural values of nature generate value remains poorly understood. Building on earlier work demonstrating that wildlife icons are associated with highvalue brands, we develop a dynamic game-theoretic model linking brand competition, consumer behaviour, and prospect theory to investigate the value of wildlife icons. We show that wildlife icons function as dynamic identity assets whose value depends on the competitive environment in which brands operate. Icon investment is most valuable in competitive environments where differentiation is important, while amplification is required in risky environments where costs dominate. Once established, consumers respond strongly to their loss. Overall our findings provide a theoretical explanation for why brands continue investing in wildlife icons and establish wildlife icons as dynamic identity assets capable of generating long-term value.

title: How Can Non-Fungible Tokens Bring Value to Brands
affiliations: University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS)

detail.title: How Can Non-Fungible Tokens Bring Value to Brands

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Research in Marketing, volume 40, issue 1, 2023[10.1016/j.ijresmar.2022.07.003]

detail.abstract: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) have registered tremendous growth in the past year, and their importance is expected to increase with the expected development of Web3. From a brand perspective, NFTs can be seen as representations of the brand components, such as the product, the logo, or the image. I argue that NFTs have immense potential to become standalone brand assets. I illustrate how this can be achieved by relating the brand's NFT strategies to the marketing funnel stages. Brands can turn into an NFT their physical products such as shoes, shirts, or art to attract brand awareness, generate cross-selling opportunities, and spark stronger perceived ownership of certain brand elements. Importantly, NFTs can allow brands to form a highly engaging brand community that can support the brand, blend online and offline product ownership, and potentially create a bond between the brand and consumers. These exciting possibilities generate a rich research agenda I present in this paper.

title: Artificial Intelligence as Adaptive Marketing Intelligence: A Literature Review

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as Adaptive Marketing Intelligence: A Literature Review

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in digital marketing is the process of using AI technology to help collect data, data-driven analysis, and machine learning (ML) to provide customer insights and automate crucial decisions for marketers (IBM, n.d.). Artificial intelligence (AI) has been playing a larger role in marketing in recent years. Many businesses are now experimenting with AI to help analyze consumer behavior, trends, provide effective communications, and in helping to support decision-making requirements for marketing campaigns. Although researchers and marketers have used and studied AI as a technology to help improve marketability and efficiency with tasks, some of these professionals have begun to explore how AI can learn through machine learning by continual input by the user and in helping to create more effective marketing outreaches.

title: The AI Sovereign Wealth Fund: A Legal and Economic Framework for Public Capital in an Age of Labor Displacement

detail.title: The AI Sovereign Wealth Fund: A Legal and Economic Framework for Public Capital in an Age of Labor Displacement
detail.abstract: The American redistributive state is financed by the very thing artificial intelligence threatens to erode. Income and payroll taxes, wage-linked social insurance, and the safety net's fiscal base all assume that wages are the main channel through which national income reaches households. If AI shifts income from labor to capital, that assumption fails, and it fails just when displacement makes the safety net most necessary. This paper develops a legal and economic framework for a response that matches the problem: a sovereign wealth fund holding a claim on the capital AI makes productive and paying a universal dividend. The remedy for a capital-driven shift in income is a public capital claim, not a patch on a wage-based system. The paper makes three contributions. First, a task-based overlapping-generations model shows that a safety net financed from wage taxes alone can no longer keep its current promise once AI automates roughly a quarter of task content, a threshold stable across plausible substitution elasticities and whether AI proves highly profitable or nearly competitive, even as the rents a capital claim could capture rise as wages fall. Second, it compares three ways to capitalize the fund, a mandatory equity issuance, a windfall tax paid in shares, and a compute levy, scoring each on one rubric that joins economic distortion to constitutional exposure under the Takings Clause, the direct-tax rule left open in Moore v. United States, and the law of government share-ownership; the two axes point to a staged design. Third, it turns the same structural critique on the proposal itself, confronting the conflict of a state that both regulates and owns the firms in question.

title: The Brand as a Legal Construct: A Doctrinal Inquiry into an Undefined Concept at the Crossroads of Intellectual Property Law and the Polish Doctrine of Personal Interests

detail.title: The Brand as a Legal Construct: A Doctrinal Inquiry into an Undefined Concept at the Crossroads of Intellectual Property Law and the Polish Doctrine of Personal Interests
detail.abstract: The brand is among the most ubiquitous notions of contemporary commerce and, paradoxically, it does not appear as an autonomous legal category in any of the major intellectual property regimes. Management scholarship defines it in mutually incompatible ways —as logo, as legal instrument, as identity system, as personality, as relationship, as semiotic marketing system—, while Aaker’s paradigmatic brand equity model compresses the whole edifice of intellectual property into a single residual entry called “other proprietary brand assets”. This article carries out a doctrinal inquiry into the legal place of the brand as a concept. It starts from the definitional vacuum in intellectual property law, contrasts the conceptual architecture of management with the legal categories that are actually on offer, decomposes Aaker’s fifth heading into its real normative regimes and proposes a “protection gap” matrix that exposes the systemic asymmetry between value-creation and legal protection. Finally, the paper articulates a reading of the brand as a new personal interest under Polish civil law, in the light of recent jurisprudence.

title: Predict, Observe, Retrain: Can a Language Model Learn to Pick A/B Test Winners from Its Own Feedback Loop?
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Predict, Observe, Retrain: Can a Language Model Learn to Pick A/B Test Winners from Its Own Feedback Loop?
detail.abstract: Companies spend a lot of money running A/B tests on headlines, ads, and email subject lines. A model that could predict the winner before the test runs would save much of that money. Recent work suggests large language models (LLMs) can simulate human responses, but most evaluations are one-shot: the model predicts, and that is the end of it. Real deployment would be a loop. The model predicts, the real test runs anyway, the outcome comes back, and the model retrains before predicting the next batch. This paper runs that loop on real data. We take 2,599 headline A/B tests from the Upworthy Research Archive (43 million impressions of real reader behavior), sort them into ten time-ordered rounds, and require every model to predict each round's winners using only outcomes revealed in earlier rounds. We compare a frozen zero-shot LLM, a fewshot prompted LLM, a gradient-boosted trees baseline on text features, and a small LLM (Qwen2.5-3B) that is LoRA fine-tuned from scratch each round on all outcomes revealed so far. The full loop was run twice with independent random seeds. The fine-tuning loop wins clearly. It picks the winner of decisive tests 52.8% of the time on average across the two runs (53.7% and 52.0%) against a 25.6% random baseline, beating the best non-LLM baseline by 15 points in both runs and in every round. The gain arrives almost entirely with the first round of feedback and holds steady, rather than climbing round over round. Zero-shot and few-shot prompting barely beat the trees baseline, echoing prior reports that prompting alone captures little about real preferences. Two checks back the result up. A memorization probe finds the base model cannot reproduce a single archive headline verbatim (0 of 200). And the fine-tuned model transfers: trained only on Upworthy tests, it ranks 1,803 news headlines from the Microsoft MIND dataset with Spearman correlation 0.37 against real click-through rates, where the base model manages 0.04. The loop works, the gains arrive early, and what the model learns is general clickability rather than one site's quirks. But at 53% accuracy on decisive pairs, the model prunes candidate pools; it does not replace testing.

title: Sticky Wage Norms and the Real Wage Cost of Unexpected Inflation
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, ADP Research and ADP Research

detail.title: Sticky Wage Norms and the Real Wage Cost of Unexpected Inflation
detail.abstract:
We use a sample of administrative payroll data covering a large and nationally representative share of U.S. workers to study how wages adjusted during the recent inflation period. Most firms apply a single modal annual nominal wage increase to the majority of their workers, and these firm-level norms changed little during the recent period of unexpected inflation. As a result, nominal wages did not keep pace with prices for a large share of workers who stayed at their firms. Forty-three percent of workers continuously employed at the same firm over the four years spanning 2021–2024 experienced a real wage decline, with a mean loss of roughly nine percent among those who fell behind. Workers could escape sticky wage norms by changing employers — job-changers’ wages rose nearly one-for-one with inflation — but switching was too infrequent to matter for most. Even accounting for job-changers, 37 percent of all workers saw real wages decline over the 4-year period. Indexing firms’ modal raises one-for-one to inflation would have closed roughly 40 percent of the resulting shortfall relative to prepandemic trend. Drawing on cross-country evidence from Belgium, whose wages are automatically indexed to inflation, we show that incomplete wage indexation, rather than inflation itself, helps explain the persistence of depressed consumer sentiment during the 2021–2024 period.
